item.title: Kelsey Mitchell's 2027 free agency: three teams, three paths to the Finals
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: How the Aces, Valkyries and Dream could sign Kelsey Mitchell, what each would sacrifice, and how their proposed lineups could reach the WNBA Finals.
item.content:encoded:
AnalysisFull Court Buckets

Kelsey Mitchell's 2027 free agency: three teams, three paths to the Finals

By Ryan MoalemiNovember 7, 2026Updated November 7, 2026

At an unchanged $7 million cap, Golden State could add Kelsey Mitchell and have $45,672 left above minimum roster charges. That cushion is $800,972 at the $7.91 million ceiling. Las Vegas fits her at a lower cap if Jackie Young leaves. Indiana's first-year supermax is $210,000 above an outside team's standard maximum at $7 million, and $237,300 above it at $7.91 million.

What each team could afford

Here is what signing Mitchell would leave at three caps, after minimum charges to reach 12 players:

Team and scenarioBalance at a $7.00M capBalance at a $7.50M capBalance at a $7.91M cap
Golden State signs Mitchell$45,672$460,672$800,972
Las Vegas signs Mitchell; Young leaves$100,800$415,800$674,100
Las Vegas signs Mitchell; Young returns at 20% of cap-$1,010,600-$795,600-$619,300
Atlanta signs Mitchell; keeps nine listed contracts-$948,030-$533,030-$192,730

Source: FCB calculations from Her Hoop Stats 2027 contract columns and the signed CBA. Data through November 7, 2026 (PST). Methods: Mitchell at 17 percent of the cap, Wilson at 20 percent for Las Vegas, and a $288,600 charge on each open spot through 12 players. The columns are a $7 million unchanged cap, a $7.50 million sensitivity case, and the $7.91 million ceiling. Download CSV (CC0)

A positive balance is money left for an upgrade above those minimums. A negative balance is the shortfall in this veteran-filled model. Player salary inputs and trade scenarios use the same contracts.

Where each roster first fits

A salary-clearing move can work under one cap and fail under another. These are the cap levels at which each proposed roster first fits, including minimum-cost replacements.

Proposed rosterBreak-even capInside the $6.09M to $7.91M range?
Las Vegas signs Mitchell; Young leaves$6,839,998Yes
Golden State signs Mitchell; keeps seven contracts$6,944,973Yes
Atlanta signs Mitchell; trades Jones for no salary$7,254,975Yes
Atlanta signs Mitchell; trades Hillmon for no salary$7,465,819Yes
Atlanta signs Mitchell; trades Canada for no salary$7,706,782Yes
Las Vegas keeps Young at 20%, signs Mitchell, trades Loyd and Evans for no salary$7,811,161Yes
Las Vegas keeps Young at 20%, signs Mitchell, trades only Loyd for no salary$8,067,903No
Atlanta signs Mitchell; keeps nine contracts$8,142,204No
Las Vegas keeps Young at 20% and signs Mitchell; no trade$9,350,231No

Source: FCB calculations from the same contract inputs and the signed CBA. Data through November 7, 2026 (PST). Methods: the smallest whole-dollar cap at which the scenario formula is no longer negative. Seventeen percent of the cap is cap times 17, divided by 100 in whole dollars. Twenty percent is the cap divided by 5 in whole dollars. Each open spot, including a replacement for a departed player, costs $288,600. Download CSV (CC0)

Golden State is still the preferred basketball fit, because the seven contracted players include an All-Defensive core. The budget result is separate. Las Vegas without Young first fits at $6,839,998, which is below Golden State's $6,944,973. At an unchanged $7 million cap, that Las Vegas roster also has more left over: $100,800, against Golden State's $45,672.

The signed agreement lets a team send qualifying offers from January 30 through February 3, opens negotiations on February 4, and allows new contracts to be signed starting February 16, the day after the 2026-season moratorium ends (CBA). On October 23, 2026, Pacers Sports & Entertainment announced that Kelly Krauskopf will step down as Fever president and that general manager Amber Cox is departing, effective immediately (Krauskopf; Cox).

Why Mitchell changes the conversation

Mitchell averaged 24.7 points in 2026 while shooting 50.9% from the field, 45.0% from three and 85.1% at the line. Her 1,086 regular-season points established a WNBA record (Mitchell statistics; WNBA records).

Her scoring is not confined to one area. FCB's calculation from her season totals assigns 492 points to two-point baskets, 405 to threes and 189 to free throws. Her effective field-goal percentage was 60.0%, reflecting the additional value of her made threes (Mitchell statistics).

For a contender, the practical appeal is having another player whose defender must stay engaged. Mitchell could attack space created by a teammate, occupy a defender away from the main action, or take responsibility when a possession runs short of time.

An Indiana Fever release credits Caitlin Clark with 96 assists to Mitchell out of 333 total assists, or 28.8%. That describes where Clark's assists went. It does not tell us what percentage of Mitchell's scoring depends on Clark or what would disappear if she left (Fever release).

Mitchell also shot 18-for-55 in Indiana's three-game playoff loss to Las Vegas. Three games cannot settle a player's postseason value, but they illustrate why a contender should preserve other ways to initiate offense (Mitchell statistics).

The best fit would offer more than a second famous scorer. It would offer passing, screening, spacing and a defense that can keep the team competitive when her jumper is not falling.

Golden State: give a championship defense more ways to score

Golden State won 32 games and the 2026 championship. Basketball-Reference's possession estimates ranked it first defensively and seventh offensively. Adding an elite scorer would address the less dominant side of an already successful team (team statistics; WNBA playoffs).

The contracted personnel are a major part of the appeal. Gabby Williams, Veronica Burton and Kiah Stokes earned 2026 All-Defensive honors. All three appear on Golden State's 2027 contract list, alongside Janelle Salaün, Kaila Charles, Iliana Rupert and Justė Jocytė (contract sources; All-Defensive selections).

A proposed closing lineup is Veronica Burton, Kelsey Mitchell, Gabby Williams, Janelle Salaün and Kiah Stokes.

This version gives Mitchell an organizer next to her, defenders who can take difficult initial assignments, and an interior presence behind the perimeter.

The first offensive objective would be to make the defense react before Mitchell needs to create a shot. Burton could initiate a possession that sends Mitchell around a screen. If the defense chases, Mitchell could turn toward the basket. If two defenders step toward her, the pass out should give Williams or another teammate a brief advantage against a rotating defense.

A second option would use Mitchell as a screener. If she screens for Williams and then moves back to the perimeter, defenders must decide whether to switch, stay attached, or send help. The action matters because it makes both players part of the same decision rather than asking them to take turns.

The risk is spacing around the action. If an opponent can leave another player unattended, it can crowd Mitchell without paying much of a price. Stokes's defensive value would need to be weighed against how the opponent guards the other end.

That creates a second closing possibility: Charles replaces Stokes, with Salaün handling center responsibilities.

The smaller group could provide more movement and different screening combinations. It would not automatically provide five credible shooting threats. That depends on which players the opponent is willing to leave and how effectively they punish that choice.

It would also have to rebound. A lineup that improves shot creation but surrenders repeated second chances may not improve the team.

What Golden State would sacrifice

The model keeps the seven listed contracts, not every member of the championship rotation. Tiffany Hayes and Kayla Thornton are unrestricted free agents; Cecilia Zandalasini is restricted. Their returns would need to be funded from the remaining budget (contract sources).

Four minimum positions are already in the model. The money above them is $45,672 at an unchanged $7 million cap, $460,672 at $7.50 million, and $800,972 at $7.91 million. Putting the entire surplus into one open spot, and leaving the other three at $288,600, would pay $334,272, $749,272, or $1,089,572 for that one player. At the unchanged cap, that is a modest raise over the minimum, not another star.

They could not assume that every unsigned contributor returns at a convenient price.

The roster question is therefore whether Golden State can add Mitchell while retaining enough bench passing, shooting and size to support different closing lineups.

What Game 7 showed

Golden State won the championship, 68-63, and trailed 30-24 at halftime (Game 7 recap). Gabby Williams scored 30 of those 68 points. Veronica Burton, the organizer who is under contract for 2027, was 3-for-13 from the field and 0-for-5 from three, with 10 points and 5 assists. Kiah Stokes had 13 rebounds. Tiffany Hayes scored 11 and is not one of the seven contracts in this model (Game 7 box score). The team shot 24-for-64, including 5-for-20 from three (WNBA box score).

Mitchell could be a second high-volume scorer so a closeout game does not rest on one player's second half. She would not have supplied Burton's five assists or Stokes's 13 rebounds in that game. Hayes's 11 points are also outside the contracted seven. One Game 7 does not prove the offense fails without another scorer. It shows where the points came from.

FCB assessment: Golden State offers the clearest role for Mitchell with the fewest required changes to the contracted defensive foundation.

Las Vegas: adding Mitchell is easier than keeping Young, too

Wilson and Mitchell would give Becky Hammon a compelling pairing. A defense responding aggressively to Mitchell's shooting could open space for Wilson. A defense concentrating on Wilson could give Mitchell cleaner opportunities on the perimeter.

The Aces' problem is deciding who remains around them.

Wilson's listed future salary floats at 20% of the cap. The $1.47 million displayed in the salary table is not the figure used here. She accounts for $1,400,000 at a $7 million cap, $1,500,000 at $7.50 million, and $1,582,000 at $7.91 million (contract sources). Wilson's salary is modeled at 20% of the cap, the supermax, so it scales up as the cap rises, which is why a Loyd-only trade first fits at $8,067,903, above the $7.91 million ceiling, while clearing room under that ceiling requires moving both Loyd and Evans and first fits at $7,811,161.

The other four listed commitments total $2,577,600: Chelsea Gray, Jewell Loyd, Dana Evans and Janiah Barker. Young is a free agent.

If Young leaves

Las Vegas could sign Mitchell at 17% of the cap, keep those five contracts, and budget six minimum positions. The money left above the minimums is $100,800 at an unchanged $7 million cap, $415,800 at $7.50 million, and $674,100 at $7.91 million.

Loyd and Barker are the contracted players who can fill the wing and forward minutes next to Gray, Mitchell and Wilson. Loyd is already paid $840,000. Basketball-Reference lists her as a guard who started 3 of 42 games in 2026 and averaged 8.0 points in 25.9 minutes, so the in-model answer is that she comes off the bench, as she did, or starts if the coaches change that role. She is a scorer. The contract list does not include another player hired to guard a perimeter star. (Aces 2026). Barker is the only other contracted frontcourt player besides Wilson, at the $288,600 minimum. The same page lists her as a forward, and its per-game table does not include her, so this model does not treat her as a proven rotation forward. She can take those minutes or sit if an open spot is upgraded. Evans, at $399,000, is the other contracted guard who can spell Gray. Basketball-Reference lists her in 14 games.

The surplus pays one of the six open spots above the minimum. It does not raise Barker's existing contract. Spending all of it on one open spot, and leaving the other five at $288,600, would pay $389,400 at a $7 million cap, $704,400 at $7.50 million, or $962,700 at $7.91 million. At the unchanged cap, that is not another maximum salary. This comparison does not name a free agent the Aces have not signed.

Gray could still organize the first action, Mitchell could attack off a screen, and Wilson could be the interior target. The cost is Young's departure. Her 2026 averages included 18.9 points, 6.8 assists and 4.4 rebounds. Mitchell's scoring does not replace that combination (team statistics).

If Young stays

Gray, Mitchell, Young and Wilson would be four closing pieces, with Young as another ball handler. The fifth spot is already on the sheet: Loyd on the wing, with Barker off the bench, or Barker in the forward minutes and Loyd off the bench in the role she played in 2026. There is no upgrade money in that version. The shortfall is $1,010,600 at $7 million, $795,600 at $7.50 million, and $619,300 at $7.91 million. Wilson and Young at 20% each, plus Mitchell at 17%, use 57% of the cap before the other contracts and the minimums.

Moving Loyd's $840,000 salary for no returning salary saves $551,400 after a replacement charge. The Aces would still be short by $459,200 at $7 million, $244,200 at $7.50 million, and $67,900 at $7.91 million. Also moving Evans's $399,000 salary saves another $110,400 after a second replacement. That double move leaves $42,500 only at the $7.91 million cap, with seven minimum spots. It is still short by $348,800 at $7 million and $133,800 at $7.50 million (contract sources; FCB calculations).

That is a budget construction, not a reported plan or evidence of a trade partner. Once Loyd is gone, Barker is the remaining contracted forward next to Wilson. The $42,500 at the ceiling is the only leftover in the Young-retained path, and it exists only at that ceiling.

The $67,900 gap after a Loyd-only move at $7.91 million could also be closed by an equivalent cut in the combined modeled salaries of Young and Mitchell. That does not mean either would accept it.

What the semifinal opener showed

Las Vegas scored 60 points on 33.9% shooting in Game 1 at Golden State, and Golden State won the rebounding battle 52-25. The AP recap on WNBA.com called 60 the Aces' lowest point total of the season. Becky Hammon said, "We lost the game on the boards, no question about that." The same recap says Jewell Loyd left early in the third quarter with a left leg injury (Game 1 recap). Basketball-Reference has Loyd at 0-for-2 and 0 points in 16:34, and Young at 11 points on 4-for-15 (Game 1 box score).

Mitchell could be another scorer on a night when a perimeter player is out and the shot is not falling. She does not fix a 25-52 rebounding gap. Young was on the floor for that game and still shot 4-for-15, so the cold night was not only Loyd's absence. One game does not settle the series. Golden State won the next two as well (WNBA playoffs).

FCB assessment: The star pairing is attractive in both versions. The Young-retained version has the more complete basketball case, but it does not fit at any cap tested here without moving more salary. The Young-leaves version fits even below $7 million, with Loyd and Barker as the contracted wing and forward, and a limited pile of money for one upgrade.

Atlanta: another scorer comes with a continuity decision

Atlanta reached Game 7 of the Finals with a roster that already had several ways to influence a game. Jordin Canada organized, Allisha Gray and Rhyne Howard supplied perimeter scoring, and Angel Reese contributed rebounding and interior activity (team statistics; WNBA playoffs).

Adding Mitchell would give that group another defender to occupy and another player to use when an initial action stalls.

The challenge is preserving enough of the existing structure.

Atlanta has $6,180,830 committed to nine listed players. Adding Mitchell at the standard maximum and two veteran minimums leaves a shortfall of $948,030 at $7 million, $533,030 at $7.50 million, and $192,730 at $7.91 million (contract sources).

Three possible routes produce three different teams.

Keep Canada and move frontcourt salary

A proposed closing lineup is Canada, Mitchell, Gray, Howard and Reese.

This is the clearest offensive fit. Canada would continue to organize, Mitchell would provide another scoring threat, and Gray and Howard could attack openings created by the first action.

A Mitchell-Reese screening action would ask the defense to manage the perimeter shot and the interior movement together. If two defenders follow Mitchell, Reese would need to make a prompt decision with the release pass. If the defense switches, Atlanta could choose whether to attack the new matchup or exploit a rebounding advantage.

The physical tradeoff is substantial. Howard would assume some larger forward assignments, and Reese would handle center responsibilities. That could work as a closing option against certain opponents without being the correct lineup for every series.

Moving Brionna Jones or Naz Hillmon would create different amounts of room, but either choice would require a credible plan for the lost frontcourt minutes. Madina Okot's development and the quality of an affordable replacement would matter.

Move Canada and retain more frontcourt size

A proposed group of Mitchell, Gray, Howard, Reese and Jones would preserve more conventional size.

It would also redistribute Canada's organizing responsibilities. Canada averaged 7.3 assists in 2026; Mitchell averaged 2.8. Those figures do not establish that Mitchell cannot create, but they show why adding her should not be treated as a direct replacement for Canada's role (Mitchell statistics; team statistics).

Atlanta would need a dependable answer for advancing the ball against pressure, beginning the first action and getting into a second action when the defense disrupts it.

The risk is an offense with more scoring names but less reliable organization.

Moving Canada for no incoming salary fits at $7.91 million, with $168,670 left, and misses at the two lower caps: short $586,630 at $7 million and $171,630 at $7.50 million. Trading Jones or Hillmon for no salary also misses at an unchanged $7 million cap, by $211,630 and $386,630. The break-even table puts the Jones move first among the Atlanta trades, at $7,254,975. That is still above $7 million. None of those one-player moves is a reported discussion.

Atlanta also traded its own 2027 and 2028 first-round picks to Chicago in the Reese deal. That reduces one source of near-term trade capital without preventing the Dream from making other moves (Reese trade).

Keep all nine and pay Mitchell less

Keeping the nine listed players and two veteran minimums would leave $241,970 for Mitchell at $7 million, $741,970 at $7.50 million, and $1,151,970 at $7.91 million.

At the ceiling, $1,151,970 is $192,730 below the modeled new-team maximum and $430,030 below Indiana's modeled supermax. At an unchanged $7 million cap, $241,970 is $948,030 below the $1,190,000 standard maximum and $1,158,030 below Indiana's $1,400,000 supermax. There is no verified reporting here that she would accept a discount.

Keeping the nine listed players also would not mean retaining every Finals contributor. DeWanna Bonner is among the unsigned players outside that total (contract sources).

What Game 7 showed

Rhyne Howard played 37:37 in the 63-68 loss and scored 6 points on 3-for-14 shooting, including 0-for-7 from three. She also had 3 steals. Jordin Canada scored 18 points with 5 assists, and Allisha Gray scored 16 (Game 7 box score). Atlanta shot 6-for-30 from three (WNBA box score).

Mitchell could be another perimeter scorer on a night Howard's shot is not there. She would not replace Canada's 5 assists, and Howard's 3 steals would still have to come from someone. Mitchell's own three-game series against Las Vegas was 18-for-55 (Mitchell statistics). One closeout game does not mean Howard would shoot 3-for-14 again. Paying Mitchell the standard maximum may also mean moving Canada or a frontcourt player, which is the cap problem above.

FCB assessment: Atlanta has a credible path only after a salary concession or a higher cap. The front office has to weigh Mitchell against the specific player that concession removes. At an unchanged $7 million cap, even trading Jones, Hillmon, or Canada for no salary does not clear the max.

Indiana still sets the financial benchmark

Mitchell's outside options must be compared with what she already has: an established partnership with Clark, continuity with Aliyah Boston, and the opportunity for a higher starting salary.

Beginning in 2027, the signed agreement limits new core designations to players with six or fewer years of service. Mitchell has completed nine seasons, so Indiana cannot use a new core designation to keep her off the market (CBA; Mitchell statistics).

The signed agreement allows the relevant Indiana supermax at 20% of the cap, compared with 17% for a new-team signing. The first-year difference is $210,000 at a $7 million cap, $225,000 at $7.50 million, and $237,300 at $7.91 million. An agreed sign-and-trade cannot provide a first-year salary above the standard maximum (CBA).

That advantage does not determine her decision. It does mean that a new team needs a persuasive explanation of the role, roster and competitive opportunity it is offering.

Golden State can point to a contracted defensive core and to Game 7, when Williams scored 30 of 68. Las Vegas can point to Wilson, with the Young decision deciding whether the roster fits. Atlanta can point to a team that reached Game 7, and to Howard's 3-for-14 in that game, but it has to say who leaves if Mitchell is paid the maximum.

Methodology

The comparison uses the 2027 contract columns of the Her Hoop Stats WNBA Salary Cap Database, checked November 7, 2026 (PST). Those team sheets displayed October 1 updates. The inputs are a snapshot of those public records, not league-certified future rosters and not a report of offers, negotiations, or Mitchell's preferences. The lineups are hypothetical.

The model retains every listed contract and applicable option in the relevant scenario, including unprotected contracts. Unsigned free agents and unsigned draft rights are excluded unless a scenario adds them. Developmental contracts do not fill any of the 12 regular spots. Mitchell's salary is 17 percent of the assumed cap, in whole dollars: cap times 17, divided by 100, with the remainder dropped. Young is 20 percent, cap divided by 5 in whole dollars, only in the labeled retention scenarios. Wilson uses that same 20 percent rule. Las Vegas's other four contracts total $2,577,600.

Each open regular-roster spot costs $288,600 until the roster reaches 12. That figure is the 2027 minimum cap charge for a player with one to three years of service. It is not the cash minimum for every veteran. At the three caps in the first table, 17 percent and 20 percent land on whole dollars, so this whole-dollar formula matches an exact percentage. The break-even search uses the same formula at every dollar in between. A continuous 17 percent and 20 percent, rounded up to the next dollar, is $1 to $4 higher on these nine rosters. The break-even file keeps that continuous figure in the column continuous_round_up_cap. The number in the article is the smallest whole-dollar cap at which the whole-dollar formula is no longer negative. At that cap, the modeled room is $0.

Trade examples assume the recipient takes the entire outgoing salary, nothing comes back, and each vacated spot is filled at $288,600. For Loyd, the net savings are $840,000 minus $288,600, or $551,400. For Loyd and Evans together, the outgoing salary is $1,239,000 and the replacement charge is $577,200.

The $7 million column is the 2026 cap, carried forward with no change. Article VII, Section 1(a) sets that cap at $7,000,000 and limits the 2027 move, up or down, to 13 percent. The permitted 2027 range is therefore $6,090,000 to $7,910,000. The $7.91 million column is that ceiling, not an announced cap. The $7.50 million column is an FCB sensitivity case, not a league projection and not the floor.

These are the rules this model uses, and where they are in the signed agreement:

Rule in this modelWhere it is
The standard maximum for a salary-cap year is 17 percent of that year's capArticle V, Section 8(b)
The supermax for a salary-cap year is 20 percent of that year's capArticle V, Section 8(a)
A qualifying veteran free agent with five or more years of service can sign the supermax with her prior teamArticle V, Section 8(c)
A new contract that the parties agree to trade within 48 hours cannot set a first-season base salary above the standard maximumArticle V, Section 3(f)
Beginning with the 2027 season, only a player with six or fewer years of service may receive a core designation in the designation windowArticle VI, Section 7(b)
The 2026 salary cap is $7,000,000, and the 2027 cap cannot rise or fall by more than 13 percentArticle VII, Section 1(a)
Each team must keep 12 players on its rosterArticle XXXIII, Section 4
2027 minimum base salary is $280,800 with zero years of service, $288,600 with one to three, $296,400 with four to six, $304,200 with seven to nine, and $312,000 with 10 or moreArticle V, Section 7(a)
A minimum contract for a player with four or more years of service counts against the cap at the one-to-three-year minimumArticle I, definition of Salary
Before the regular season, a team with fewer than 11 players in its team salary is charged the one-to-three-year minimum for each missing player, up to 11Article VII, Section 2(d)

Article VII, Section 2(d) stops that automatic charge at 11. This model also prices a 12th player at $288,600 because Article XXXIII, Section 4 requires 12 roster players. That 12th charge is a modeling choice about the player the team still has to sign, not a claim that Section 2(d) bills an empty 12th spot.

The model adds no new dead money, trade bonus, unannounced extension, or other transaction charge. It does not establish a willing trade partner, player consent, or a salary a player would accept. A different mix of rookies and veterans would change the budget. Team efficiency rankings use Basketball-Reference's possession estimates, which differ from the league's. No championship probabilities or 2027 win forecasts are assigned.

Data dictionary and reuse

The scenario CSV contains one row per team scenario and cap, including the $7 million cap. It reports the retained contract total, Wilson and Mitchell salaries, any added Young salary, the minimum charge, open positions, modeled payroll, and remaining balance. The salary-input file identifies each player, the source, and the cap hit at $7 million, $7.50 million, and $7.91 million. Wilson is the only player whose hit changes with the cap.

The trade file reports outgoing salary, replacement charge, net savings, and the resulting balance at each of the three caps. In the Loyd-plus-Evans rows, the replacement charge covers two positions. The break-even file reports retained fixed commitments, the cap-share percentage, minimum positions, the whole-dollar break-even, the room at that cap, the continuous round-up for comparison, and whether the break-even sits inside $6,090,000 to $7,910,000. All dollar values are nominal U.S. dollars. A positive balance is room. A negative balance is a shortfall.

FCB's original calculations are free to use and republish (CC0). Scenario CSV, player salary inputs, trade scenarios and break-even caps. Contract inputs are attributed to Her Hoop Stats; the CC0 dedication covers FCB's original calculations, not rights in third-party material.

For corrections to an input or calculation, contact Full Court Buckets.

Sources

  • Signed 2026 WNBA-WNBPA Collective Bargaining Agreement, hosted by the WNBPA. The rule-to-source table in the methodology gives the article and section for each cap rule used here.
  • Golden State's salary cap sheet, Las Vegas's salary cap sheet and Atlanta's salary cap sheet, Her Hoop Stats. The 2027 columns supply the contract inputs; Wilson's contract-cell note identifies the floating salary.
  • Mitchell's season and playoff statistics, Basketball-Reference; cross-checked against Her Hoop Stats' regular-season and playoff pages.
  • WNBA's 30th-season record release, October 14, 2026; also NBA Communications' official version. Confirms Mitchell's 1,086-point record.
  • 2026 WNBA playoff bracket and format and Finals Game 7 recap, WNBA. Series results, seeding, the 68-63 final, and the 30-24 halftime. Game 7 box score, WNBA, for team shooting. Game 7 player lines, Basketball-Reference.
  • Semifinals Game 1 recap, Aces at Valkyries, AP, published by WNBA.com. The 71-60 final, 33.9 percent shooting, the 52-25 rebounding margin, Hammon's boards quote, the season-low description, and Loyd's left leg injury. Game 1 player lines, Basketball-Reference.
  • Golden State's 2026 season, Las Vegas's 2026 season and Atlanta's 2026 season, Basketball-Reference. Records, ratings and regular-season player averages.
  • Golden State All-Defensive selections, Valkyries team release, October 15, 2026.
  • Fever backcourt season release, republished by OurSports Central, October 24, 2026. Source for 96 of Clark's 333 assists going to Mitchell. The directly linked Fever page exposed only its title in this review, so the accessible republication was checked for the full text.
  • Atlanta acquires Reese, Dream team release, April 6, 2026. Draft consideration in the Chicago trade.
  • Kelly Krauskopf to step down as Indiana Fever team president, Pacers Sports & Entertainment release, October 23, 2026.
  • Pacers Sports & Entertainment announces departure of Amber Cox, Fever team release, October 23, 2026.

Update, November 7, 2026, 10:34 p.m. PT: Added the unchanged $7 million cap, moved the break-even caps above the team sections, and replaced the open Aces lineup spots and the generic playoff paths with contracted players and sourced 2026 games. Wilson's salary is still 20 percent of the cap.

Update, November 7, 2026, 11:50 p.m. PT: Added section anchors, the 2027 free-agency calendar, the October 23 Fever front-office announcements, and the first-year supermax gap in the opening summary. The byline date is the November 7 Pacific publish time.

AI assisted research and editing. Full Court Buckets is responsible for the published analysis. Sources and calculation methods are provided above. How we make Full Court Buckets

item.title: Diana Taurasi headlines Women's Basketball Hall of Fame Class of 2027
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Diana Taurasi is the ninth UConn inductee in the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame Class of 2027. Induction is June 26, 2027, in Knoxville.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Diana Taurasi headlines Women's Basketball Hall of Fame Class of 2027

By Ryan MoalemiNovember 6, 2026

The Women's Basketball Hall of Fame named Diana Taurasi to the Class of 2027 on Thursday, Nov. 5. She is the ninth person from UConn on the school's list. Induction is Saturday, June 26, 2027, at the Tennessee Theatre in Knoxville.

The Class of 2027

The Hall page lists these six, in this order, and does not print a category word.

NameCategoryKnown forPrimary source
Diana TaurasiPlayerWNBA's all-time leading scorer, 10,646 points, Mercury 2004-2024. Three titles. 11 All-Star teams.Hall page
Sandy BrondelloCoachWNBA titles with the Mercury in 2014 and the Liberty in 2024. Coach of the Year in 2014. First Tempo head coach.Hall page
Mike ThibaultCoachSun head coach 2003-2012. Mystics head coach 2013-2022. Mystics' first title in 2019. Retired at 379-289.Hall page
Dee KantnerOfficial26 NCAA Women's Final Fours, including 16 national championship games.Hall page
Molly Bolin KazmerPlayerFirst player signed in the WBL, 1978. Scoring champion at 32.8 points per game in 1980. Single-game record of 55.Hall page
Judith HollandContributorUCLA women's athletics director, 1975-1980. First full scholarship for a woman at UCLA, to Ann Meyers.Hall page

Source: names, order and the known-for lines are the induction page, checked Nov. 6, 2026. Category is the job those bullets describe. Contributor is USA TODAY's word for Holland. The Hall page does not print it. USA TODAY's story puts Bolin Kazmer second. This table follows the Hall page. The data dictionary defines each column. Data through Nov. 6, 2026. Methods: one row per name on the Hall page, in that order. Download CSV (CC0)

UConn in the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame

Taurasi is the ninth. The Nov. 5 UConn release names these eight ahead of her.

NameYearRole
Geno Auriemma2006Head coach
Rebecca Lobo2010Player
Jennifer Rizzotti2013Player
Kara Wolters2017Player
Chris Dailey2018Associate head coach
Swin Cash2021Player
Maya Moore2024Player
Sue Bird2025Player
Diana Taurasi2027Player

Source: the nine names and the years are the Nov. 5, 2026 UConn release. Auriemma is "head coach" and Dailey is "associate head coach" on the June 11, 2018 UConn release. Lobo is "the first player from the program" on the July 25, 2009 UConn release. Bird is "a member of the UConn women's basketball team from 1998-02" on the June 15, 2025 UConn release. Rizzotti, Wolters, Cash and Moore have no role word on a release opened for this page. They are marked Player. The reason is in the data dictionary. Full Court Buckets has player pages for Cash, Moore, Bird and Taurasi. Data through Nov. 6, 2026. Methods: one row per name in the Nov. 5 sentence, then Taurasi. The count of nine is the count of that list. Download CSV (CC0)

The Nov. 5 release gives her UConn career as 2,156 points, 10th in the program, 648 assists, third, and 318 made threes, third. She played from 2000 to 2004. The NCAA titles on that release, and on the Hall page, are 2002, 2003 and 2004.

The June 15, 2025 release gives Sue Bird 1,378 points and 585 assists at UConn. The other seven rows do not have a college line in this file. A blank in the CSV is not a zero.

Class of 2027 WNBA ties

Three of the six are tied to a WNBA team on the Hall page.

NameJobTeamsWhat the pages say
Diana TaurasiPlayerPhoenix Mercury10,646 points, 2004-2024. Titles in 2007, 2009 and 2014. Finals MVP in 2009 and 2014. MVP in 2009. Rookie of the Year in 2004.
Sandy BrondelloCoachMercury, Liberty, TempoTitles in 2014 and 2024. Coach of the Year in 2014. First Tempo head coach, 2025.
Mike ThibaultCoachSun, MysticsSun 2003-2012. Mystics 2013-2022. Title in 2019. Retired at 379-289. Reeve's 380th regular-season win was July 8, 2026. She finished at 397.

Source: the team lines are the Hall page. Brondello's 2014 Coach of the Year award, Thibault's awards in 2006, 2008 and 2013, and Cheryl Reeve's 380th regular-season win on July 8, 2026, and her 397 at the end of that regular season, are the WNBA.com release of Sept. 28, 2026. The 379 and the 397 are the two pages' figures. This table does not add playoff wins to either one. Kantner was WNBA Supervisor of Officials in 1997-1998 and 2005-2016, on the Hall page, and is not a row here because that page names no team for her. The 2026 Tempo season is in the Nov. 4 coaching count. Open jobs are in the coaching tracker. Data through Nov. 6, 2026. Methods: one row per Hall-page inductee whose bullets name a WNBA team. Download CSV (CC0)

The statement, and two spellings

Michelle Marciniak, the Hall's CEO, in a statement USA TODAY published Nov. 5, 2026: "For nearly thirty years, the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame has honored the greatest of the game, and we are thrilled to welcome these six inductees into the distinguished seats of the Hall of Fame. Selection for this esteemed recognition celebrates the hard work, success, and record-breaking journeys for those to join this global class. We cannot wait to welcome the Class of 2027."

Sportsnet carried the same statement that day and spells it honoured. The induction page, checked Nov. 6, lists the six and the June 26 date. It does not include the sentence.

The Hall page spells the building Tennessee Theatre. The UConn release spells it Tennessee Theater. USA TODAY calls June 26, 2027, a Saturday. The Hall page gives the date and does not give the weekday.

Where the write-ups disagree

The UConn release says Taurasi was a 10-time All-WNBA first-team selection and a four-time second-team pick, and an 11-time All-Star. The Hall page says 11 All-Star teams and does not list All-WNBA. USA TODAY says 14 All-WNBA selections and does not split first and second team. Ten plus four is 14. This page uses the UConn split. A 2021 WNBA.com feature lists the same 10 first-team years and says the 2021 team was not out yet. It also gives her 9,174 points, so it is a 2021 snapshot.

USA TODAY says she led the league in scoring five times, and that she is the league's all-time leader in 3-pointers made and in free throws made. The Hall page and the UConn release do not say that. The 2021 feature lists five scoring titles, in 2006 and from 2008 through 2011, and lists her first in threes and free throws at that feature's totals. This page does not use five, and it does not use those leader lines.

The UConn release says she is the only player with more than 10,000 points, the only six-time Olympic gold medalist in basketball, a seven-time Russian National League champion, and a four-time USA Basketball Female Athlete of the Year. It also says she has three World Championship gold medals and one bronze. The Hall page names the gold years, 2010, 2014 and 2018, and the Olympic years, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. It does not mention a bronze or the Russian league. The EuroLeague years on the Hall page are 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2013 and 2016.

Sportsnet says Brondello's Opals won World Cup silver in 2018 and in 2022. The Hall page says silver in 2018 and bronze in 2022, plus Olympic bronze in 2024 and Asia Cup gold in 2025. Basketball Australia's Oct. 21, 2026 story also says bronze in 2022. This page uses the Hall page.

That Basketball Australia story says Brondello was named to the Sport Australia Hall of Fame Class of 2026, with the gala on Nov. 24, 2026, at Centrepiece, Melbourne Park. The Sport Australia member page says she was inducted in 2026. Sportsnet's Oct. 20 story says the Tempo announced the selection that day. This page does not pick one announcement date.

USA TODAY says Holland was UCLA's director of women's athletics from 1975 to 1981. The Hall page says first full-time director from 1975 to 1980, then senior associate athletic director from 1980 to 1996. This page uses the Hall page. USA TODAY also says Ann Meyers led UCLA to a pair of national titles. The Hall page says Holland oversaw UCLA's AIAW national title in 1978, the first won by a major university. It does not say a pair.

USA TODAY calls Bolin Kazmer "Machine Gun Molly." The Hall page uses Molly Bolin Kazmer and does not use the nickname. The same Hall page says she averaged 54.8 points a game in a season at Moravia High School in Iowa, scored 83 in a game there, and was WBL co-MVP with Ann Meyers in 1980.

The Hall page says Kantner and Violet Palmer were the first two women hired as NBA referees, for 1997-2002, and that ESPN hired Kantner as a women's college basketball rules analyst in 2025. USA TODAY adds 247 NBA games, 11 years as WNBA supervisor, and world championships in 1994 and 1998. Those three are not on the Hall page. The supervisor years on the Hall page are 1997-1998 and 2005-2016.

USA TODAY says Thibault was a U.S. women's assistant in 2008 and again in 2024, and that Belgium reached the 2026 FIBA World Cup quarterfinals. The Hall page says he was a U.S. assistant for the 2008 Olympic gold, and that he led Belgium to the 2025 EuroBasket title. It does not mention 2024 or a 2026 quarterfinal.

NBC Connecticut, Jennifer Lambert, Nov. 5, repeats the UConn figures for 2,156 points, 648 assists and 318 threes, the three NCAA titles, the three WNBA titles, the two Finals MVPs, the six Olympic golds, and the eight earlier UConn names.

How the rows were counted

One row per name on the Hall page. Nine UConn rows: the eight in the Nov. 5 sentence, then Taurasi. Three WNBA rows: the inductees whose Hall-page bullets name a team. Column definitions are in the data dictionary. The files are free to use and republish (CC0).

newsFull Court Buckets

Wings and Tempo each send 6 players to Unrivaled Season 3 rosters

By Ryan MoalemiNovember 5, 2026

The Dallas Wings and the Toronto Tempo each have 6 of the 48 players on Unrivaled's 2027 rosters. The Golden State Valkyries, the 2026 WNBA champions, have 5, and no two of them are on the same club. Unrivaled named the eight clubs on Nov. 4, 2026.

Every player on the Unrivaled Season 3 rosters

Each club has six players. The position is the one on that club's Unrivaled page. A blank 2026 club means the player is not on any of the eight 2026 stats pages.

Source: clubs and the 48 names are the Nov. 4, 2026 Unrivaled release. Position is Guard, Wing or Forward on the club roster page. The 2026 WNBA team and the college come from that team's WNBA.com roster page on Nov. 5, 2026, except Aaliyah Edwards, whose college is on the Phantom roster page because the Sun table does not list one. Champion means the player is on the Valkyries roster page and the Game 7 blog says Golden State won the title. The 2026 Unrivaled club is the stats page with the most games. Courtney Williams also has 4 games on Breeze. Aziaha James also has 1 game on Lunar Owls. Data through Nov. 5, 2026. Methods: one row per name in the release. The team counts and the data dictionary use the same rows. Download CSV (CC0)

Which WNBA team sent the most

Source: team counts are the player file above. A number in parentheses is how many players from that WNBA team are on that club. Data through Nov. 5, 2026. Download CSV (CC0)

Jessica Shepard and Maddy Siegrist are the only Wings teammates on the same club, both on Laces. Paige Bueckers is on Breeze, Arike Ogunbowale on Mist, Li Yueru on Phantom and Aziaha James on Rose.

Tempo has two pairs. Marina Mabrey and Temi Fágbénlé are on Lunar Owls. Kiki Rice and Isabelle Harrison are on Mist. Brittney Sykes is on Rose. Aneesah Morrow is on Vinyl.

Three Atlanta Dream players are on Vinyl: Allisha Gray, Rhyne Howard and Jordin Canada. Naz Hillmon is the Dream player on Hive. Hive also has Cameron Brink and Rae Burrell, the two Sparks players on Hive. Dearica Hamby is the Sparks player on Vinyl.

Sporting News wrote that the 48 players were assigned to six teams. The Nov. 4 release lists eight clubs, six players each. The same Sporting News headline is right about the Valkyries: Gabby Williams and four teammates.

Kelsey Plum was a Los Angeles All-Star in the July 7 release. The WNBA.com trade-deadline story says the Sparks traded her to Phoenix on Aug. 2. The Mercury roster on Nov. 5 lists her, which is why the table says Mercury. She and Kahleah Copper are Mercury teammates on Phantom and Breeze.

Who is back on the same club

20 of the 48 are on the club where they played the most games in 2026. Lunar Owls, Mist, Phantom and Rose each have 3. Breeze, Hive, Laces and Vinyl each have 2. Twelve played for a different club. Sixteen are on none of the 2026 stats pages.

The Nov. 4 release says half the league is returning to a club from season one or season two, and that more than 75 percent are on multiyear deals. The 20 above are the players whose 2026 stats page matches the club they are on now.

The Oct. 28 roster update says the league signed Kaitlyn Chen and Isabelle Harrison to one-year deals. Neither has a 2026 stats line.

Mist beat Phantom 80-74 on March 4, 2026, for its first title, in the league recap. Breanna Stewart scored 32 and was the Championship MVP. She is back, with Arike Ogunbowale and Veronica Burton. Allisha Gray scored 12 in that game and is on Vinyl. Alanna Smith played 14 games for Mist in 2026 and is not one of the 48. Plum scored 40 in that game and is back with Phantom.

Breeze coach Jarell Christian, in the Nov. 4 release: "I'm excited to welcome Paige and Dom back for their second season with the Breeze."

Phantom coach Roneeka Hodges, in the same release: "I welcome the professionalism, skill and energy KMac, Li and Aaliyah will add to the Ghost Gang!" Kayla McBride, Li Yueru and Aaliyah Edwards are the players she welcomes. Plum, Natasha Cloud and Tiffany Hayes played for Phantom in 2026.

All-Stars, the rookie, and who is not here

14 of the 48 were 2026 All-Stars. Copper is in that 14 because the commissioner named her on July 22 to replace the injured Plum. Plum had already been selected, so she stays in the 14 too. Rose is the only club with no 2026 All-Star. Chelsea Gray is on Rose. The Oct. 28 reveal announcement calls her the 2026 Unrivaled MVP and an inaugural champion.

Olivia Miles received all 74 Rookie of the Year votes. She is on Hive with Sonia Citron. Gabby Williams is the Finals MVP, on Laces with Jackie Young. The roster release calls Williams an Unrivaled newcomer, and she has no 2026 club stats line. The WNBA.com Game 7 blog says she scored 30 points in Game 7 and averaged 19.6 points and 2.6 steals in the series. Our recap is Game 7.

Six of the 10 All-WNBA players are on a roster. Miles and Stewart are first team. Shakira Austin, Bueckers, Rhyne Howard and Young are second team. The other four are Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell, A'ja Wilson and Angel Reese. Wilson won the 2026 MVP. She is not on a club.

Also selected as All-Stars and not on a club: Natasha Howard, Kiki Iriafen, Jonquel Jones and Nneka Ogwumike. Iriafen played 14 games for Phantom in 2026. Sabrina Ionescu is on the Liberty roster page and is not one of the 48. Brittney Griner played 13 games for Vinyl in 2026 and is not one of the 48. The Sun roster page lists her.

Aliyah Boston was an All-Star starter and is out for 2027. The Oct. 28 update says she is recovering from a procedure the Fever had already announced, and that she is expected back in 2028. The reveal announcement that day says Rickea Jackson and Ezi Magbegor are out for 2027 with injuries. The same update says Unrivaled and Kate Martin ended her contract.

The Nov. 4 release says the rosters include four 2026 WNBA champions. The Valkyries roster page lists five of the 48: Burton, Chen, Hayes, Thornton and Williams.

Four players are marked rookies on a WNBA roster page: Miles, Rice, Flau'jae Johnson and Sydney Taylor.

Who might be a free agent after 2026 is in 2027 free agents.

Arenas on the schedule

The schedule page on Nov. 5 listed dates and buildings. The club names were blank. The Nov. 4 release says the matchups come out Nov. 6.

item.title: Liberty fire Chris DeMarco: only 3 WNBA coaches have lasted more than two seasons
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Only 3 of 15 WNBA head coaches have lasted more than two seasons. Reeve has 17 with the Lynx. Six coaches at two seasons and four at one have 16 combined.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Liberty fire Chris DeMarco: only 3 WNBA coaches have lasted more than two seasons

By Ryan MoalemiUpdated November 4, 2026

The New York Liberty will not keep Chris DeMarco. Only 3 of 15 WNBA head coaches have lasted more than two seasons with their current team. Cheryl Reeve has 17 with the Lynx. The six coaches with two seasons and the four with one have 16 seasons combined. Open-job day counts are in the 2027 WNBA coaching tracker.

Every WNBA head coach, Nov. 4, 2026

Cheryl Reeve, Becky Hammon and Nate Tibbetts are the three. New York and Los Angeles have no head coach on their WNBA.com team pages.

TeamHead coachHire dateSeasonsRegular seasonWin %2026 playoffs
Minnesota LynxCheryl ReeveDec. 8, 200917397-201.6640-2
Las Vegas AcesBecky HammonDec. 31, 20215148-56.7252-4
Phoenix MercuryNate TibbettsOct. 18, 2023362-66.484Missed
Atlanta DreamKarl SmeskoNov. 13, 2024260-28.6828-4
Golden State ValkyriesNatalie NakaseOct. 10, 2024255-33.6259-4
Indiana FeverStephanie WhiteNov. 1, 2024252-36.5911-2
Washington MysticsSydney JohnsonDec. 23, 2024244-44.5000-2
Chicago SkyTyler MarshNov. 3, 2024226-62.295Missed
Connecticut SunRachid MezianeDec. 4, 2024222-66.250Missed
Dallas WingsJose FernandezOct. 27, 2025127-17.6141-2
Toronto TempoSandy BrondelloNov. 4, 2025111-33.250Missed
Portland FireAlex SaramaOct. 17, 2025117-27.386Missed
Seattle StormSonia RamanOct. 28, 202518-36.182Missed
New York LibertyVacantNov. 3, 20260
Los Angeles SparksVacantSept. 25, 20260

Source: hire dates are the dateline or publish date on the linked team or WNBA.com release. For New York and Los Angeles, the date is the day the job opened. Regular-season wins and losses are that team's line on the WNBA.com standings for each season in the stint. The 2026 playoffs column is that postseason only. White's row is her current stint. The Fever hiring release says she also coached Indiana in 2015 and 2016, a 37-31 overall record and a 6-6 playoff record. Data through Nov. 4, 2026. Methods: one season is one WNBA regular season the coach was that team's head coach, in the current uninterrupted stint. The coach is the name on the WNBA.com team page on Nov. 4, 2026. Missed means no 2026 playoff game. No current row is an interim. Download CSV (CC0)

The median stint among the 13 coaches still in a job is 2 seasons.

Liberty head coaches, 2022 through 2026

Sandy Brondello coached 2025 and Chris DeMarco coached 2026, so the next hire is the third Liberty coach in three seasons. Brondello coached the team from 2022 through 2025, the Toronto Tempo release says, and that release calls her a 2024 WNBA champion.

SeasonCoachRegular seasonSeedPlayoff result
2026Chris DeMarco26-18 (.591)No. 8Beat Minnesota 2-0, then lost to Atlanta 0-3
2025Sandy Brondello27-17 (.614)No. 5Lost to Phoenix 1-2
2024Sandy Brondello32-8 (.800)No. 1Won the title, beat Minnesota 3-2
2023Sandy Brondello32-8 (.800)No. 2Lost the Finals to Las Vegas 1-3
2022Sandy Brondello16-20 (.444)No. 7Lost to Chicago 1-2

Source: regular-season lines are the WNBA.com standings. Seeds are the league playoff seeds. The coach for 2022 through 2025 is the Tempo release. DeMarco's season is the Liberty hiring release of Dec. 3, 2025. The 2024, 2023 and 2022 results are the Liberty team history page. The 2025 series is the WNBA.com bracket, Phoenix wins 2-1. The 2026 series is the 2026 bracket. Data through Nov. 4, 2026. Download CSV (CC0)

Why New York moved on

On Nov. 3, 2026, the Liberty account posted "Thank you, Coach DeMarco." The graphic reads "THANK YOU" and "CHRIS DEMARCO." The same morning, Alexa Philippou of ESPN reported that sources said the team will not retain him. That story's publish time is 1:03 p.m. UTC, which is 5:03 a.m. Pacific. Philippou also reported that after the semifinal sweep, DeMarco said he expected to return in 2027. The WNBA.com team page lists no Liberty head coach.

The hiring release, published Dec. 3, 2025, says the Liberty hired DeMarco, a Golden State Warriors assistant, that day. General manager Jonathan Kolb is the person quoted.

In 2026 the Liberty went 26-18 and were the No. 8 seed. On June 30 they beat Las Vegas 93-85 in the Commissioner's Cup final at Barclays Center, on the WNBA.com game page. They then beat the No. 1 Lynx 2-0, in our recaps of Game 1 and Game 2. Atlanta, the No. 4 seed, swept the semifinals, 92-82, 101-98 in overtime and 85-83, in our recaps of Game 1, Game 2 and Game 3.

The WNBA named Cheryl Reeve Coach of the Year on Sept. 28, her fifth time, with 40 of 74 votes, after a 33-11 season. The release puts her career regular-season wins at 397, the win total in the Lynx row above, and says the Lynx trailed New York 1-0 in that first-round series. New York finished the sweep in Game 2. What the roster does next, including Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu and Jonquel Jones, is in five moves after the sweep. Service time is in the 2027 free-agent file.

Both Finals coaches were in their second season

Natalie Nakase and Karl Smesko were hired 34 days apart, on Oct. 10 and Nov. 13, 2024. Both coached in the 2026 Finals in their second season. Nakase's Valkyries won the series. The WNBA.com recap of Game 7 says Golden State beat Atlanta 68-63. Our recap is Game 7.

Smesko's two seasons sum to 60-28. Atlanta's 2026 line on the standings is 30-14, so 2025 was 30-14 too. Nakase's two seasons sum to 55-33. Golden State was 32-12 in 2026, so 2025 was 23-21. Down 2-1 in the Finals, Nakase started Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles in Game 4, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Hayes scored 11 points in Game 7 on the WNBA.com box score.

Eight hires had a first season in 2025: Nakase (Oct. 10, 2024), White (Nov. 1), Marsh (Nov. 3), Smesko (Nov. 13), Roberts (Nov. 19), Meziane (Dec. 4), Johnson (Dec. 23) and Chris Koclanes in Dallas (Dec. 23, 2024). Koclanes was not the 2026 coach. Fernandez's Oct. 27, 2025 release names him as the next Wings coach.

Leave out Golden State, Portland and Toronto, the expansion teams whose current coach is the first, and leave out the two vacancies. Seven of those 10 jobs are in a first or second season.

Connecticut's row is 22-66. The Sun were 11-33 in 2026, so 2025 was 11-33 too. Morgan Tuck told USA TODAY Sports on Oct. 30 that the plan is to keep Meziane when the franchise plays in Houston in 2027. "Our plan is to keep Rachid and that he'll be with us next year," she said. The table still lists the Connecticut Sun, the name on the WNBA.com team page on Nov. 4.

Hires whose first season was 2026

Five of those hires have a date on a release: Alex Sarama (Oct. 17, 2025), Fernandez (Oct. 27, 2025), Sonia Raman (Oct. 28, 2025), Sandy Brondello (Nov. 4, 2025) and DeMarco (Dec. 3, 2025). The Fire release is dated Oct. 17, 2025 on the team's news list. DeMarco's job is the one that opened on Nov. 3.

Los Angeles

The Sparks parted ways with Lynne Roberts on Sept. 25, 2026, effective that day. Special advisor Farhan Zaidi's quote on the release thanks her through "our last game last night." The hiring story, dated Nov. 20, 2024, says the team announced it Tuesday, which was Nov. 19. Her two seasons were 21-23 in 2025 and 16-28 in 2026, 37-51 (.420). Both seasons were outside the eight-team playoff field. The 2026 Sparks were 16-28, 11th on the standings.

How to read the count

Tenure is the number of WNBA regular seasons in the current uninterrupted stint, through Nov. 4, 2026. Vacancies are rows, and they are left out of the median. Stephanie White is counted from 2025. The files are free to use and republish (CC0). Column definitions are in the data dictionary.

Correction, Nov. 4, 2026: Liberty seeds are the league playoff seeds. An earlier version of this page added an East tag. In 2023 the Liberty were first in the East and the No. 2 seed, per the team history page.

item.description: Las Vegas got 96.3% of its 2026 points from players with five or more seasons, the unrestricted group if the deal ends. That group scored 56.0% of WNBA points.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Las Vegas got 96.3% of its 2026 points from players with five or more seasons

By Ryan MoalemiNovember 3, 2026

The Las Vegas Aces got 96.3% of their 2026 regular-season points from players with five or more seasons in Full Court Buckets' file, and that group scored 56.0% of all WNBA points. Five seasons is the CBA line for unrestricted free agency once a contract ends.

Share of 2026 points scored by players with 5+ seasons

Las Vegas also got 96.0% of its minutes from that five-season group. League-wide, the four-season group scored 6.9% of the points and the three-or-fewer group scored 37.1%.

Source: Full Court Buckets regular-season file for 2026 (ppg and mpg multiplied by games). Data through the end of the 2026 regular season. The Finals ended Oct. 31, 2026, and these rows leave out the playoffs. Methods: a player is in the 5+ group when the 2008-2026 season files show at least five regular seasons with a game. Four seasons is the restricted group. Three or fewer is the reserved group. The WNBA row includes every player. Team rows leave out Lexi Held (Toronto and Phoenix on one row, 225.1 points) and Aneesah Morrow (Connecticut and Toronto, 295.9 points) because the file does not split their games. Shares can move by a fraction of a point because averages are stored to one or two decimals. Rounded shares can miss 100 by a tenth. Kelsey Mitchell's row is 24.68 points times 44 games, or 1,085.9, against 1,086 points on the WNBA.com season awards story. Class if contract ends is the CBA result if the contract ends after 2026. It is not the league's February list. The data is free to use and republish (CC0). Download CSV (CC0)

Every 2026 player, by the CBA test

Class if contract ends is what Article VI assigns if the contract has ended. Restricted and reserved players get that status only if the old team sends a qualifying offer from Jan. 30 through Feb. 3, 2027. If it does not, they are unrestricted. The league has not published the 2027 list. Click a column heading to sort.

Source: the same 2026 regular-season file, plus season files back to 2008 for the season count. Data through the end of the 2026 regular season. Methods: Class if contract ends is UFA at five or more seasons (CBA Article VI, Section 9), RFA at four (Section 5(b), only if the team sends a qualifying offer), and Reserved at three or fewer (Section 8, only if the team sends a qualifying offer). An asterisk means one of those seasons had fewer than seven games. Article I does not credit a year for a 7-day contract, a developmental contract, or replacement contracts covering fewer than seven games. A standard contract that reaches the active list does count. The file does not record contract type, so those seasons are counted and marked. The data is free to use and republish (CC0). Download CSV (CC0)

Key dates

The dates below are the ones in the CBA text. The lottery date is from the league's Oct. 28 release.

WhenWhat the document saysWhere
Nov. 15, 2026Draft lottery, 7:30 to 8:00 p.m. ETWNBA release: ESPN in the U.S., TSN in Canada. The release does not name a separate streaming service.
Jan. 30 to Feb. 3, 2027Qualifying offers, and core designationsCBA Article VI, Sections 5, 7(c) and 8
Feb. 4, 2027Negotiations may startArticle V, Section 17, and Article VI, Section 1(a)
Feb. 15, 2027The moratorium endsArticle V, Section 17, for the offseason after the 2026 season
Feb. 16, 2027Contracts may be signedArticle VI, Section 1(a): the day after the moratorium

The 2026 salary cap is $7 million, Article VII, Section 1(a) of the same CBA. What clubs take in at the gate and on sponsorships is a different ledger, on FCB's team revenue page. The 2026 season ended Oct. 31, when the Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7. The game recap has the series.

Houston, Los Angeles, Portland, Seattle, Toronto and Washington are in the Nov. 15 drawing. The release says Phoenix had traded its first-round pick to Los Angeles, and Chicago had traded its first-round pick to Washington.

Where the public lists disagree

Statuses are official when the league publishes its list in February. Until then, a season count can show which label the CBA rule supports, and where it cannot.

Awak Kuier played 41 games at 6.3 points, 3.9 rebounds and 1.1 assists per game (18.6 minutes, 50.8% from the field, 39.0% from three). The file has 4 regular seasons with at least one game (2021, 2022, 2023, 2026). She did not appear in 2024 or 2025. Article VI, Section 5(b) makes four years of service restricted if Dallas sends a qualifying offer. Section 9's unrestricted status needs five. Her Hoop Stats and the CBS Sports ranking of Nov. 2 both list her as restricted. A four-season count agrees with that label and does not support an unrestricted label. The league's own service ledger is the piece this file does not have.

Emily Engstler played 44 games at 10.1 points, 5.7 rebounds and 2.1 assists per game (24.7 minutes, 46.5% from the field, 37.1% from three). The file has 5 regular seasons with at least one game (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). Five seasons, none shorter than 12 games, is unrestricted under Section 9 if the contract has ended. CBS and Her Hoop Stats list her as restricted, which is the four-year status in Section 5(b). This file does not show a four-season count.

Rae Burrell played 43 games at 14.6 points, 2.4 rebounds and 2.5 assists per game (28.8 minutes, 45.5% from the field, 38.3% from three). The file has 5 regular seasons with at least one game (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). The short season is 2022 (3 games). If 2022 counts, Section 9 makes her unrestricted. If that season was only a 7-day contract, a developmental contract, or replacement contracts covering fewer than seven games, Article I drops the year and she has four, which is restricted if the Sparks send a qualifying offer. CBS and Her Hoop Stats list her as restricted. The 2022 contract type is not in this file, so both readings stay open.

Zaay Green played 7 games at 2.1 points, 1.0 rebounds and 0.1 assists per game (9.6 minutes, 30.0% from the field, 21.4% from three). The file has one regular season with a game (2026). Section 8 makes three or fewer years reserved if Toronto sends a qualifying offer, and unrestricted if it does not. Her Hoop Stats lists her as unrestricted. A one-season count does not require that label. It also does not rule it out, because skipping the qualifying offer produces an unrestricted free agent. No waiver wire release in this reporting shows that she already cleared.

Rebecca Allen played 29 games at 5.8 points, 2.6 rebounds and 0.6 assists per game (18.1 minutes, 42.0% from the field, 40.6% from three). The file has 11 regular seasons with at least one game (2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026). The short season is 2015 (2 games). Her Hoop Stats still lists her as an unrestricted free agent. This reporting did not find a league or team release that announces a retirement, so she stays on the table. A podcast comment is not that release.

The names on the November rankings

CBS Sports ranked ten players on Nov. 2. The lines below use the season file and the CBA. Contract length is included only where a team document states it.

Napheesa Collier played 16 games at 16.8 points, 6.9 rebounds and 2.6 assists (29.3 minutes, 50.0% from the field, 44.4% from three). Seasons in the file: 2019 through 2026, eight in all, with 2022 limited to 4 games. The Lynx game notes of June 19, 2026 say the team re-signed her to a one-year contract on April 16, and the bio line calls 2026 her 8th year. The roster table in those same notes lists her experience as 7, matching the seven seasons before 2026. The notes also say she had surgery on her left ankle on March 24 and, as of June 19, had missed the first 15 games. Article VI, Section 7(b) allows a 2027 core designation only for a player with six or fewer years of service. Eight seasons is past that line, and so is seven if the four-game 2022 season is set aside.

Jackie Young played all but one game: 43, at 18.9 points, 4.4 rebounds and 6.8 assists (32.3 minutes, 48.8% from the field, 38.3% from three). Her eight seasons run 2019 through 2026, with none under seven games. The Aces' April 11 release announces the re-signing and does not state the length. Eight seasons is past the six-year core line in Section 7(b).

Kelsey Mitchell played 44 games at 24.7 points, 1.7 rebounds and 2.8 assists (32.5 minutes, 50.9% from the field, 45.0% from three). That is nine seasons, 2018 through 2026. The Fever's April 11 release says she returns for a ninth season and does not state the length. WNBA.com's awards story says she scored 1,086 points, which the story calls the record for most points in a season, at 24.7 per game in 44 games. Nine seasons is past the core line in Section 7(b).

Kelsey Plum is split across two rows: 12 games with the Los Angeles Sparks at 23.9 points per game, and 5 games with the Phoenix Mercury at 15.8. Seasons in the file: 2017, 2018, 2019, then 2021 through 2026. No 2020. WNBA.com's trade-deadline story says the Sparks sent her to the Mercury for Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick, and says she had signed a one-year deal with the Sparks. That length is in the deadline story, not in a signing release read for this page. Nine seasons is past the core line.

Natasha Cloud played 40 games at 11.1 points, 3.4 rebounds and 4.8 assists (28.2 minutes, 49.0% from the field, 35.7% from three). Eleven seasons in the file, 2015 through 2019 and 2021 through 2026, is unrestricted under Section 9 if the Chicago contract has ended. No release read for this page states the 2026 term.

Nyara Sabally played 24 games at 12.3 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists (23.9 minutes, 52.7% from the field, 39.2% from three). Four seasons, 2023 through 2026, is restricted if Toronto sends the qualifying offer, and unrestricted if it does not.

Sophie Cunningham played 43 games at 7.9 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.2 assists (22.2 minutes, 46.0% from the field, 41.9% from three). Eight seasons, 2019 through 2026, is unrestricted under Section 9 if the Indiana contract has ended, and it is past the core line. No release read for this page states the 2026 term.

Pauline Astier played all 44 games at 9.3 points, 2.7 rebounds and 3.3 assists (23.3 minutes, 54.6% from the field, 33.3% from three). The file has one season, 2026. That is reserved under Section 8 if New York sends a reserved qualifying offer, and unrestricted if it does not. Her Hoop Stats lists her as reserved. She is not in the CBS top ten.

A'ja Wilson led that five-season group with 26.2 points per game in 41 games, 1,073.0 points in this file, with 9.4 rebounds and 3.2 assists. Those points sit inside the Las Vegas share. Her 2026 contract length is not in a release read for this page, so 96.3% is a service-class share. It is not a count of points already headed to free agency.

Who can be cored, and who cannot

Article VI, Section 7(a) lets each team designate one veteran free agent as a core player. A player who is still under a contract she signed while designated counts against that one spot. Section 7(d) says the designation ends when the original term ends, or when she is traded, the contract ends, or she retires.

Section 7(b) limits designations made before the 2026 season: a player who had already played two seasons on a core contract could not be designated again. For 2027, the same section says only a player with six or fewer years of service may be designated. The example in the text is that a player may not be designated after the season in which she accrues a seventh year.

On that 2027 test, Collier, Young, Mitchell and Plum cannot be cored. The same is true of anyone else with seven or more seasons in the player file. Four seasons or fewer is not a core candidate in the ordinary case, because Section 7(a) applies the designation to a player who would otherwise be unrestricted or restricted. Reserved players are not in that sentence.

Exhibit 4 lists core service after the 2025 season, including Kelsey Mitchell in 2025, Kelsey Plum in 2025, and Breanna Stewart in 2024 and 2025. It does not say which of those contracts, if any, still run in 2027. This page does not mark any team's 2027 core spot as already used.

What this file does not say

It does not say the contract is over. A player with eight seasons can be unrestricted and still be signed. The only 2026 term confirmed here from a team document is Collier's one-year deal in the Lynx notes. The February list is the one that will match names to statuses after the qualifying offers go out.

Salaries are not in the file. Developmental contracts are not marked, and Section 8 also reserves a player who finished the season on one of those if the team sends the offer. Players who did not appear in the 2026 regular-season file, including anyone whose contract expired while suspended, are not in the table. Article VI, Section 3 keeps a player who withheld services off the free-agent list unless the old team agrees.

item.title: Williams scores 30 and the Valkyries beat the Dream 68-63 for the title
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Valkyries beat the Dream 68-63 in Game 7 and won the 2026 WNBA Finals 4-3. They were outscored 500-472 in the series and won the only game they trailed at halftime.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Williams scores 30 and the Valkyries beat the Dream 68-63 for the title

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 31, 2026

Every play: Dream at Valkyries, Game 7 →

The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 on Saturday at Chase Center and won the 2026 WNBA Finals, 4-3. Gabby Williams scored 30 points, 15 of them in the third quarter.

2026 Finals series trend: score, pace and the halftime lead

The Valkyries won the series 4-3 while being outscored by 28 points, and Game 7 was the only game the team that trailed at halftime won.

GameFinalMarginHalftime (Dream-Valkyries)PaceDream FGDream threesValkyries FGValkyries threesScoring leader
1Valkyries 68, Dream 64439-4279.621-644-2525-787-33Gabby Williams, 26
2Dream 79, Valkyries 651439-3782.421-627-2521-617-24Angel Reese, 30
3Dream 97, Valkyries 712646-4083.134-699-2224-6912-30Angel Reese, 21
4Valkyries 67, Dream 62526-4273.218-544-2326-724-25Rhyne Howard, 19
5Valkyries 64, Dream 55922-2571.419-656-2624-616-24Rhyne Howard, 20
6Dream 80, Valkyries 691146-2679.627-6213-3022-707-27Gabby Williams, 26
7Valkyries 68, Dream 63530-2472.823-696-3024-645-20Gabby Williams, 30
1-7Dream 500, Valkyries 472Dream by 28Leader won 6 of 777.5163-44549-181166-47548-183Williams 137, Reese 90 reb

Source: official WNBA.com box scores (Game 1, Game 2, Game 3, Game 4, Game 5, Game 6, Game 7). Data through Game 7, Oct. 31, 2026. Methods: pace is the average of the two teams' estimated possessions. Possessions = field-goal attempts + 0.44 x free-throw attempts - offensive rebounds + turnovers, using player rebounds and player turnovers, not team rebounds or team turnovers. Each game was 40 minutes, so pace is possessions per 40 minutes. The 1-7 pace uses the series possession totals, not a simple average of the rounded game paces. Halftime is the sum of the first two quarters. The scoring leader is the game's high point total. The 1-7 leader cell is Williams' series points and Reese's series rebounds. Games 1-6 come from Full Court Buckets game files checked against those box scores. Game 7 comes from the official box score. The data is free to use and republish (CC0). Download CSV (CC0)

Atlanta shot 163 of 445 (36.6%) in the series and Golden State 166 of 475 (34.9%). From three, Atlanta was 49 of 181 (27.1%) and Golden State 48 of 183 (26.2%). Game 7's pace, 72.8, was the second-lowest of the series. Game 5 was 71.4.

A 9-point hole, then 15 points from Williams

The Dream led 30-24 at halftime and 37-28 with 5:59 left in the third, after DeWanna Bonner's layup. That was Atlanta's largest lead. Golden State then scored 17 points to Atlanta's 7 and led 45-44 at 1:05 of the third. Williams scored 15 of Golden State's 21 third-quarter points. After the score reached 37-34, the Valkyries' last 11 points of the quarter were hers: threes at 2:58, 2:22 and 2:00, then a turnaround jumper at 1:05. Those three threes came 58 seconds apart, from the first to the third.

Williams finished with 30 points on 10 of 23 shooting, 4 of 8 from three and 6 of 6 at the line, with 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals, 4 blocks and a plus-7. She had 2 points at halftime. Watch the sequence on the Game 7 play-by-play.

The fourth quarter was tied at 57 with 2:41 left, after Rhyne Howard's layup. Williams' 31-foot three at 2:18, assisted by Veronica Burton, made it 57-60. Golden State led the rest of the way. Williams made two free throws at 1:40 for her 30th point and a 62-57 lead. Kiah Stokes tipped in a miss with 53.8 seconds left to make it 64-57. Allisha Gray answered with a three at 34.2 seconds, assisted by Howard, to make it 64-60. Burton made two free throws with 5.1 seconds left for the final margin, 68-63.

What the box score adds

  • Shooting. Atlanta shot 23 of 69 (33.3%) and 6 of 30 from three (20.0%). Golden State shot 24 of 64 (37.5%) and 5 of 20 from three (25.0%). Golden State made 15 of 16 free throws. Atlanta made 11 of 15.
  • The glass and the extra points. Player rebounds were 37-35, Golden State. Atlanta had 18 second-chance points to Golden State's 9, and 12 points off turnovers to Golden State's 7. Points in the paint were 30-28, Golden State. Fast-break points were 2-2. Turnovers were 10 for Atlanta and 9 for Golden State, plus 2 team turnovers each. The official box score lists those team turnovers on top of the player totals.
  • Blocks and the lead. Golden State blocked 8 shots to Atlanta's 2. Williams had 4 of the 8. The box lists 4 lead changes and 4 ties. Atlanta's biggest lead was 9. Golden State's was 8, at 8-0. Atlanta led for 19:25 and Golden State for 17:14.
  • Who scored. Jordin Canada led Atlanta with 18 points on 6 of 15 shooting, with 5 assists. Gray had 16 on 5 of 16, including 4 of 4 at the line. Howard had 6 points on 3 of 14 shooting and 0 of 7 from three, with 3 steals. Angel Reese had 8 points, 12 rebounds and 4 turnovers. Her seven-game rebound totals are 12, 16, 12, 9, 15, 14 and 12, which is 90. Burton had 10 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists on 3 of 13 shooting, and she made 4 of 4 free throws. Stokes had 8 points, 13 rebounds and 2 blocks. Tiffany Hayes had 11 points and fouled out. Atlanta's bench scored 12, Golden State's 5.

The crowd, the series and where it was shown

Game 7 drew 18,064, a sellout, at Chase Center (WNBA.com game page). That is the same attendance figure on the official pages for Games 1, 2 and 5 at Chase Center. The FCB Finals attendance file now has 123,553 fans through seven games.

Saturday was the first seventh game since the WNBA made the Finals a best-of-seven in 2025 (WNBA announcement). The Las Vegas Aces swept Phoenix in four games in that first series (WNBA). The FCB Finals file from 2002 through 2025 includes no seventh game.

The series result, the schedule and the links are on the 2026 Finals schedule. This game's preview was published before tip.

TV: USA Network and CNBC. Stream: Peacock.
