item.title: WNBA Finals Game 7: Atlanta's shooting vs. Golden State's defense
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Dream outscored the Valkyries by 33 points, but the series is tied. Gray's shooting, Reese's playmaking and Golden State's center rotation could decide it.
item.content:encoded:
Halloween Finals 2026

newsFull Court Buckets

WNBA Finals Game 7: Atlanta's shooting vs. Golden State's defense

By Ryan MoalemiUpdated October 31, 2026

This preview was published before the game. For the result, read our game recap. 2026 WNBA Finals ratings tracker.

Follow the play-by-play: Dream at Valkyries, Game 7 →

The Dream have outscored the Valkyries by 33 points, but the series is tied. Gray's shooting, Reese's playmaking and Golden State's center rotation could decide the championship.

Atlanta has outscored Golden State 437-404 through six games. The series is still tied.

On Saturday at Chase Center, the WNBA's first Game 7 will decide which franchise wins its first championship. The Dream have produced the bigger offensive performances. The Valkyries have won the tighter, lower-scoring games. Each has already won on the other's floor.

Atlanta forced the deciding game with an 80-69 victory Thursday, making six threes in the opening quarter. That matched its total from all of Game 5.

The question now is whether the Dream can create those opportunities again before Golden State's defense takes control.

Where to watch

  • When: Saturday, October 31, at 5 p.m. PT / 8 p.m. ET.
  • Where: Chase Center, San Francisco.
  • TV: USA Network and CNBC.
  • Streaming: Peacock.
  • Series: Tied 3-3. The winner earns its first WNBA championship.

Odds snapshot: Covers' October 30 preview listed Golden State as a 1.5-point favorite, a total of 142.5 and win probabilities of 51% for Golden State and 49% for Atlanta. Those figures describe that published market snapshot, not an FCB forecast, and can change before tipoff.

Why Atlanta is plus-33 in a tied series

Golden State's wins have come by 4, 5 and 9 points. Atlanta's have come by 14, 26 and 11.

GameWinnerScoreAtlanta's cumulative scoring margin
1Golden State68-64-4
2Atlanta79-65+10
3Atlanta97-71+36
4Golden State67-62+31
5Golden State64-55+22
6Atlanta80-69+33

Source: FCB series data through Game 6. Download the series scoring CSV: series-margin-games-1-6.csv

Golden State has won the three lowest-scoring games and lost the three highest. Atlanta has scored at least 79 points in every win and no more than 64 in any loss.

That makes Atlanta's offense the clearest dividing line in this series. Golden State has not scored more than 71 in any game. Its path has depended on keeping the Dream within reach.

The plus-33 margin shows how convincing Atlanta's wins have been. It does not give the Dream a head start Saturday.

Gray's hand and Atlanta's biggest offensive question

Allisha Gray has been playing through dislocated pinky and ring fingers on her shooting hand, an injury suffered in the semifinals.

In Game 6, she scored 23 points and made five of seven threes. Angel Reese described the encouragement she had given her teammate: "You're a superstar. Act like a superstar and we'll follow behind you."

Gray and Rhyne Howard combined for 44 points and nine of Atlanta's 13 threes Thursday. Gray's final three, with 56 seconds remaining, pushed the lead to 80-69 and stopped Golden State's comeback.

Across the series, Atlanta has shot 37.7% from three in its wins and 18.9% in its losses. Gray is 8-for-17 from deep in the wins and 2-for-16 in the losses.

The task is to keep creating clean looks for Gray and Howard. Atlanta cannot assume Thursday's shooting will repeat, but it can repeat the movement and passing that produced those opportunities.

For current participation designations, consult the WNBA injury report.

Reese can influence the game before she shoots

Reese enters Game 7 with 78 rebounds, a WNBA Finals series record. That total has come over six games, an important distinction when comparing it with records from the previous, shorter Finals formats.

Her rebounding has remained productive in both wins and losses. The bigger difference has been her scoring: 66 points on 22-for-46 shooting in Atlanta's three wins, compared with 29 points on 9-for-31 shooting in its losses.

She has also made at least one three in every Atlanta victory in this series and none in its defeats. That is an interesting pattern, but the stronger Game 7 lesson is how she helped create shots for others.

Reese finished Game 6 with six assists. As The Athletic's Sabrina Merchant detailed, Atlanta used her in the middle of the floor as a passing option and let her advance the ball after defensive rebounds. Those possessions helped the Dream play earlier in the shot clock and work around Golden State's pressure on their guards.

Atlanta needs that version of Reese: active on the glass, decisive with the ball and involved in getting its shooters open.

Golden State's biggest adjustment may be at center

Kiah Stokes has been central to Golden State's best performances. Game 6 gave Natalie Nakase a reason to consider a different closing lineup.

Stokes finished scoreless with seven rebounds and a minus-25 in 20 minutes. Laeticia Amihere contributed five points and 10 rebounds in 20 minutes and finished plus-14. Nakase said Stokes' legs were not moving as well as Amihere's.

Those numbers do not isolate either player's individual impact. They do make the rotation worth watching. If Amihere is moving better and helping Golden State sustain its pressure, Nakase has already shown she will give her important minutes.

The bench presents another question. Golden State's reserves scored a playoff-low 14 points Thursday, all from Cecilia Zandalasini and Amihere. Janelle Salaün, the 2026 Sixth Player of the Year, did not play and has exceeded five minutes only once in the series, according to the Valkyries' official preview.

Will Nakase keep the rotation tight, or look for another source of offense if the starters struggle?

The player splits behind the series

PlayerIn her team's winsIn her team's lossesSeries plus-minus
Angel Reese66 points, 42 rebounds, 22-for-46 FG29 points, 36 rebounds, 9-for-31 FG+32
Allisha Gray49 points, 8-for-17 from three34 points, 2-for-16 from three+35
Kiah Stokes26 points, 31 rebounds, +52 points, 29 rebounds, -46-41
Tiffany Hayes28 points43 points-56
Naz Hillmon24 points13 points+40

Source: FCB player data through Game 6. Win and loss splits refer to each player's own team. Download the player splits CSV: series-player-splits-games-1-6.csv

Hillmon has the best cumulative plus-minus in the series. Hayes has the lowest, despite scoring more points in Golden State's losses than its wins.

Plus-minus measures the team's scoring margin while a player is on the floor. It is affected by teammates, opponents and game situations. Hayes was minus-17 in Golden State's Game 4 victory, so it would be inaccurate to say her individual plus-minus consistently tracks the result.

Turning mistakes into points has mattered most

The team with more points off turnovers has won all six games. Across those games, the winners have outscored the losers 118-54 in that category.

GameWinnerAtlanta points off turnoversGolden State points off turnovers
1Golden State817
2Atlanta2413
3Atlanta227
4Golden State816
5Golden State621
6Atlanta1812

Game 6 showed why the distinction matters. Atlanta committed 15 turnovers to Golden State's 11, yet won the points-off-turnovers comparison 18-12.

Forcing a mistake is only the first step. Converting the resulting possession has been more closely associated with winning than the raw turnover count.

The halftime leader has also won every game, although three of those leads were three points or fewer. These are patterns from six games, not guarantees about the seventh.

History gives Golden State another reason to value home court

Golden State earned home-court advantage with a 32-12 regular-season record, two wins better than Atlanta's 30-14. No tiebreaker was needed.

According to the Valkyries, home teams have won 11 of the previous 13 winner-take-all WNBA Finals games.

The recent deciding games also offer context for Golden State's preferred style. In the last five, only the 2019 Washington Mystics reached 80 points. The other winning scores were 67, 70, 77 and 69. That history suggests a low-scoring finish would be unsurprising, although it does not determine how these teams will play.

The atmosphere should be familiar even if the stakes are not. All six games in this series have sold out, drawing a combined 105,489 fans. Atlanta has already won once at Chase Center in these Finals.

What each team needs to do

Atlanta: create space before the defense gets set

Push after defensive rebounds, use Reese as a passing option and move the ball quickly enough to make Golden State defend the whole floor. Gray and Howard need opportunities to catch and shoot rather than repeatedly create against a set defense.

The Dream also need cleaner possessions after halftime. Their 20-point Game 6 halftime lead provided room for mistakes. A close Game 7 may offer much less.

Golden State: disrupt Atlanta's start and stay flexible

The Valkyries cannot give Atlanta another opening quarter of comfortable perimeter looks. They need to pressure the ball, contest without losing rebounding position and make the Dream work deeper into possessions.

Nakase's center choice could be crucial. Stokes has helped Golden State win this matchup, while Amihere supplied its most productive reserve minutes Thursday. The decision should follow how they are playing Saturday.

Golden State also needs more from Veronica Burton offensively after her 2-for-13 shooting performance in Game 6. Gabby Williams' 26 points kept the Valkyries competitive, but relying on another comeback would leave little margin for error.

The pick: Atlanta 76, Golden State 72

Golden State has home court and a defense capable of holding Atlanta in the 60s. The Dream have shown the greater offensive upside, and Game 6 offered a workable approach: Reese initiating possessions, Gray and Howard benefiting from the spacing, and mistakes becoming points at the other end.

The pick is Atlanta in a close game. Getting into the mid-70s would mean the Dream had avoided the offensive struggles that defined their three losses. It would not guarantee a championship, but it would put the game closer to the conditions in which they have played their best.

Prediction: Dream 76, Valkyries 72. This is an editorial pick, not a statistical model projection.

item.title: Dream hit 13 threes, beat Valkyries 80-69 to tie Finals 3-3
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Dream beat the Valkyries 80-69 in Game 6 and tied the WNBA Finals 3-3. Atlanta's 13 threes were the most by either team in a game this series.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Dream hit 13 threes, beat Valkyries 80-69 to tie Finals 3-3

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 29, 2026

The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 80-69 in Game 6 of the WNBA Finals on Thursday at State Farm Arena to tie the series 3-3. Atlanta scored 32 first-quarter points and led 46-26 at halftime.

Finals data: threes, turnovers and the halftime lead

Atlanta and Golden State have each made 43 threes in this series, and the team that led at halftime has won every game. Game 6 is the first the team with more turnovers won. Here is every game:

GameFinalHalftimeDream threesValkyries threesDream TOValkyries TOFewer turnovers won?
1Valkyries 68, Dream 64Valkyries 42-394-257-33128Yes
2Dream 79, Valkyries 65Dream 39-377-257-241418Yes
3Dream 97, Valkyries 71Dream 46-409-2212-30815Yes
4Valkyries 67, Dream 62Valkyries 42-264-234-25179Yes
5Valkyries 64, Dream 55Valkyries 25-226-266-24157Yes
6Dream 80, Valkyries 69Dream 46-2613-307-271510No
1-6Dream 437, Valkyries 404Leader 6-043-15143-16381675 of 6

Source: official WNBA.com box scores (Game 1, Game 2, Game 3, Game 4, Game 5, Game 6). Data through Game 6, Oct. 29, 2026. Methods and sources: finals, halftime scores, three-point makes and attempts, and turnovers from Full Court Buckets game files, checked against those box scores. Turnovers are the box-score turnover total and do not add separate team turnovers. Golden State had 1 team turnover in Game 6 on top of its 10. The data is free to use and republish (CC0). Download CSV (CC0)

Atlanta has shot 43 of 151 threes (28.5%) and Golden State 43 of 163 (26.4%). Atlanta has also outscored Golden State 437-404, a 33-point edge, with the series tied.

A 2-0 lead, then a 13-0 run

The WNBA moved the Game 6 tip from 8 p.m. ET to 12:30 p.m. ET so it could be played at State Farm Arena. The Hawks moved their game that night to 8 p.m. ET to make room (WNBA announcement, Oct. 26).

Veronica Burton made a step-back with 9:19 left in the first quarter to give Golden State a 2-0 lead, the only lead the Valkyries held. Allisha Gray answered with a three at 9:04, and the official WNBA.com box score has Golden State leading for 15 seconds. The game was never tied.

Naz Hillmon was called for a defensive three-second technical, and Gabby Williams made the free throw to make it 6-5. Atlanta then scored 13 straight points to go up 19-5 before Williams hit a three at 3:49. The Dream led 32-15 after the quarter. Those 32 points are the most by either team in any quarter of this series, and the 17-point margin is the largest end-of-quarter lead. Atlanta led 46-26 at halftime. Golden State made 9 of 34 shots in that half, with three blocked shots counted as attempts on the Game 6 play-by-play.

Gray, Howard and a flagrant call

Atlanta shot 13 of 30 from three (43.3%) and 27 of 62 overall (43.5%). Golden State shot 7 of 27 from three (25.9%) and 22 of 70 overall (31.4%). Gray made 8 of 12 shots and 5 of 7 threes for 23 points, with 6 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 steals and 3 blocks. On Friday, Oct. 23, with Atlanta up 2-1, she told the AP, "I am literally playing with eight fingers" (AP). Rhyne Howard scored 21 on 6 of 11 shooting, 4 of 6 from three and 5 of 5 at the line, with 4 assists. She picked up her sixth foul, a shooting foul, with 1:15 left.

With 7:23 left in the third, Gray stole a Tiffany Hayes pass. Burton was called for a flagrant-1 on the possession after officials reviewed the play and ruled she made an unnecessary windup and contact with Howard's face as Howard drove to the basket (ESPN). The play log marks that review as a call overturned, and Howard made both free throws. Atlanta led 53-28. Golden State won the third quarter 21-17 but still trailed 63-47 entering the fourth. Kaila Charles made threes at 1:06 and with 1.2 seconds left in the quarter, her only 6 points of the game.

Angel Reese finished with 15 points, 14 rebounds and 6 assists, and 6 turnovers, on 5 of 18 shooting and 2 of 8 from three. This was her fourth points-and-rebounds double-double of the series, following Games 1, 2 and 3. She has 78 rebounds in the six games: 12, 16, 12, 9, 15 and 14, the most by any player in a single WNBA Finals (Sporting News). The previous mark was Sylvia Fowles' 75 rebounds (15.0 per game) in the five-game 2017 Finals (WNBA). "The job is not done, and I'm looking forward to it. One more. Job's not done," Reese said after the game (The Guardian). Atlanta's bench scored 4 points, all from Isobel Borlase. DeWanna Bonner was 0 of 2.

Williams scored 26 but finished minus-15

Williams scored 26 points on 8 of 22 shooting and 7 of 8 free throws, added 3 steals and finished minus-15. Twenty-two of her 26 points came after halftime (Game 6 play-by-play). She matched her Game 1 performance of 26 points on 8-of-22 shooting and 7-of-8 free throws, though she was plus-16 in that 68-64 Valkyries win. Her three at 4:06 of the fourth, then a running layup and free throw at 1:15, got Golden State to 77-69. Laeticia Amihere had 10 rebounds and was plus-14 in 20 minutes.

Gray answered both of Golden State's early fourth-quarter pushes. Her three at 9:03, assisted by Howard, made it 66-47, and after the Valkyries cut the lead to 68-55, her three at 6:33, again from Howard, made it 71-55.

Atlanta led 74-55 with 5:43 left after Reese's second three. Golden State scored 9 of the next 10 points, and the lead was 75-64 with 2:36 left. Gray's fifth three, assisted by Reese with 56 seconds left, made it 80-69.

Kiah Stokes scored 0 points on 0 of 2 shooting, with 7 rebounds, 0 blocks and a minus-25. She had at least 3 blocks in each of the first five games and 17 blocks through Game 5. Burton scored 8 points on 2 of 13 shooting and 0 of 6 from three, made all 4 free throws, and had 0 turnovers and 3 steals. Hayes, who played her first 10 WNBA seasons with the Dream (Valkyries), scored 15 on 6 of 10 shooting. Cecilia Zandalasini scored 9 off the bench on 3 of 12. Jordin Canada scored 10, and Hillmon had 7 points and was plus-15.

What the box score adds

  • Turnovers and the glass. Atlanta committed 15 turnovers to Golden State's 10, plus 1 Golden State team turnover (official box score). Atlanta scored 18 points off turnovers to Golden State's 12. Golden State edged Atlanta in player rebounds 36-35, and each team had 9 team rebounds.
  • Paint, second chance, bench. Points in the paint were 26-26. Atlanta had 11 second-chance points to Golden State's 4. Golden State had 10 fast-break points to Atlanta's 4, and 14 bench points to Atlanta's 4.
  • Blocks. Atlanta blocked 8 shots to Golden State's 2, Golden State's fewest blocks of the series.
  • The lead. One lead change. Atlanta's biggest lead was 25, at 44-19. Golden State's was 2, at 2-0. Atlanta led for 39:04.

Watch every possession on the Game 6 play-by-play page.

The crowd and Game 7

Game 6 drew 17,099, a sellout, matching Games 3 and 4 at State Farm Arena. The FCB Finals attendance file now has 105,489 fans through six games. That is more than the prior record of 92,599 at the 2024 Finals, the highest series total in that file from 2002 through 2025. Game 7 has not been played, so the series total is not finished.

Game 7 is Saturday, Oct. 31, at 5 p.m. PT (8 p.m. ET) at Chase Center in San Francisco, Dream at Valkyries (WNBA.com game page). Oct. 31 is Halloween. TV: USA Network and CNBC. Streaming: Peacock.

Saturday will mark the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history. In 2025 the league replaced the best-of-five Finals with a best-of-seven (WNBA announcement). The Las Vegas Aces swept Phoenix in four games in that first series (WNBA). The FCB Finals file from 2002 through 2025 includes no seventh game, as the 2025 series ended in four.

TV: USA Network and CNBC. Stream: Peacock.

item.title: WNBA 2026 Finals: Valkyries can clinch in Game 6, but road teams in this spot are 2-4
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Valkyries vs. Dream Game 6 preview: road teams are 2-4 in Finals closeout games when the home team had already won one, since 2002. Tip time, TV, odds, and original data with CSVs.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

WNBA 2026 Finals: Valkyries can clinch in Game 6, but road teams in this spot are 2-4

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 27, 2026

Follow the play-by-play: Valkyries at Dream, Game 6 →

The Golden State Valkyries lead the Atlanta Dream 3-2 and can win the title in Game 6. Since 2002, road teams in their spot are 2-4.

Road teams closing out a Finals, since 2002

Since 2002, six road teams have led the Finals with a chance to clinch on the road after the home team had already won a game in the series. That is Golden State's spot on Thursday, and only two of those road teams won. Here are those six games:

SeasonGameRoad teamAtSeries beforeFinalRoad team won?
20074DetroitPhoenix2-176-77No
20154MinnesotaIndiana2-169-75No
20194WashingtonConnecticut2-186-90No
20224Las VegasConnecticut2-178-71Yes
20234Las VegasNew York2-170-69Yes
20244New YorkMinnesota2-180-82No

Source: WNBA.com box scores, compiled in the FCB Finals database. Data through Finals Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. Methods: every Finals game since 2002 in which the road team led the series and could clinch with a win (winner-take-all deciders excluded). "Opponent had a win" means the home team had won at least one game in the series. 2020 was played at a neutral site and is excluded. Download CSV (CC0)

Since 2002, road teams leading the series with a chance to clinch are 8-8, not counting winner-take-all deciders. They are 2-4 when the home team had already won a game in the series, which is Golden State's spot Thursday. Golden State can win the title in Game 6 on Thursday at 9:30 a.m. PT (12:30 p.m. ET) at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, even though Atlanta has outscored it 357-335.

All six games were decided by 7 points or fewer, and three by 2 or fewer. Three of the four road teams that lost the closeout won the title at home in the next game: Minnesota in 2015, Washington in 2019 and New York in 2024. The 2007 Detroit Shock lost Game 5 at home to Phoenix. Road teams whose opponent had not yet won a game went 6-4 in their closeout games; the CSV has all 16 games.

Golden State's points per game would be the lowest for a champion since 2002

Golden State is averaging 67.0 points per game in the Finals. If it wins Game 6 while scoring 65 or fewer, its 66.7 average would be the lowest for a champion since 2002, just under the 2005 Sacramento Monarchs' 66.75. The table shows the lowest-scoring champions since 2002, plus Golden State's pace so far:

SeasonChampionFinals gamesPointsPer game
2005Sacramento426766.75
2004Seattle320568.33
2003Detroit320869.33
2002Los Angeles214070.00
2015Minnesota536472.80
2026 so farGolden State533567.00

Source: WNBA.com box scores. Data through Finals Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. Methods: total Finals points divided by Finals games for each champion. Download CSV (CC0)

If the series goes seven, Golden State would need 132 or fewer combined points in Games 6 and 7 to finish under 66.75. Since 2002, only the 2006 Detroit Shock (outscored by 9) and the 2016 Los Angeles Sparks (by 5) have won three of the first five Finals games while being outscored; both won the title. Golden State is at minus-22.

Series leaders through five games

Gabby Williams leads the series with 81 points, but she has made 26 of 90 shots (28.9 percent). Angel Reese is one point behind on 59 shots and has 64 rebounds. Kiah Stokes has 17 blocks and 53 rebounds while scoring 28 points. The full leaders table through five games is below:

PlayerTeamPTSREBASTBLKSTLFG3PFT
Gabby WilliamsGS81191601326-907-3522-25
Angel ReeseATL8064146726-593-525-33
Rhyne HowardATL72261361322-619-3219-25
Allisha GrayATL601993216-575-2623-27
Tiffany HayesGS5619101421-552-1712-15
Jordin CanadaATL5325342618-574-2013-18
Cecilia ZandalasiniGS48463617-448-226-10
Veronica BurtonGS45241710816-556-237-9
Kiah StokesGS2853317112-213-81-2

Source: Full Court Buckets game files built from WNBA.com box scores. Data through Finals Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. Download CSV (CC0)

The free-throw gap

Atlanta has attempted 52 more free throws than Golden State in this series, 130 to 78, or 10.4 more per game. The Dream attempted more free throws in all five games, with the widest gap in Game 4 (31 to 13), which Atlanta still lost. The table below shows the game-by-game count:

GameDream FTAValkyries FTADifferenceRunning total
12116ATL +5ATL +5
23519ATL +16ATL +21
32917ATL +12ATL +33
43113ATL +18ATL +51
51413ATL +1ATL +52
Total13078ATL +52

Source: WNBA.com box scores. Data: CC0. Data through Finals Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. Methods: team free-throw attempts (FTA) per game; the difference is Dream minus Valkyries.

Keys to victory for Game 6

Atlanta Dream

Push the pace

Atlanta's two wins were the two fastest games of the series, at about 82 and 83 possessions, and it scored 79 and 97. Its three losses ran about 80, 73 and 72 possessions, and it scored 64, 62 and 55. Speed has not tired out Stokes's shot blocking, though: she had 4 blocks in each of Games 1 and 2 and 3 in each of Games 3-5.

Get Reese going

Angel Reese scored 30 and 21 on 17 of 28 shooting in Atlanta's wins and 14, 8 and 7 on 9 of 31 in its losses.

Score at the rim

Atlanta scored 24 and 40 points on paint finishes in its wins and 22, 18 and 14 in its losses. Free throws have not decided games: Atlanta took 31 free throws to Golden State's 13 in Game 4 and still lost 67-62.

Don't leave Stokes open

Kiah Stokes missed all four of her 3-point tries in Games 1-4, then made 3 of 4 in Game 5 and scored 13, her high for the series, in a 9-point Atlanta loss.

Win the turnover battle

The team with fewer turnovers has won all five games. Atlanta had 14 and 8 in its wins, against Golden State's 18 and 15, and 12, 17 and 15 in its losses. The team with more points off turnovers has also won every game: Atlanta outscored Golden State 46-20 off turnovers in its two wins, and Golden State won that count 54-22 in its three.

Try Reese at the 4

Reese shot 22 of 39 (56 percent) for 65 points in Games 1-3 and 4 of 20 (20 percent) for 15 in Games 4-5. Court Queens LA (@courtqueens101) suggested on X that Smesko play Madina Okot at the 5 and Reese at the 4, so Stokes has to guard Okot. Okot has played 3:56 in the series, and the pair have shared the floor for under two minutes.

Golden State Valkyries

Hold Atlanta to 64 or fewer

Golden State has won every game in which Atlanta scored 64 or fewer (64, 62 and 55) and lost both games in which Atlanta scored 79 or more.

Take care of the ball

Golden State turned it over 8, 9 and 7 times in its wins and 18 and 15 times in its losses.

Win the first half

The halftime leader has won all five games. Golden State led at the half by 3, 16 and 3 in its wins and trailed by 2 and 6 in its losses.

Make it a half-court game

Golden State's last two wins were the two slowest games of the series, about 73 and 72 possessions in Games 4 and 5, and Atlanta's paint scoring fell from 40 in Game 3 to 18 and 14. Its fast-break points fell from 19 and 13 in Games 2 and 3 to 2 in each of Games 4 and 5.

Keep the Game 4 starting five

Golden State started Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini with Stokes, Gabby Williams and Burton in Games 1-3 and went 1-2. Natalie Nakase started Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes in their place in Games 4 and 5, and Golden State won both. The rotation got shorter too: seven Valkyries played at least five minutes in each of those games, down from nine, nine and 10 in Games 1-3, and Burton played about 38 and 37 minutes.

Data through Finals Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. Methods: counts from FCB's play-by-play and box-score files for Games 1-5, built from WNBA.com box scores. Possessions are estimated as field-goal attempts minus offensive rebounds plus turnovers plus 0.44 times free-throw attempts, averaged for both teams. Fast-break points, points off turnovers, starters and minutes are from the WNBA.com box scores. Paint finishes are points on layups, putbacks, hooks and tip-ins in the play-by-play. Some ideas came from fan discussion this week; we kept only the ones the numbers back up.

Attendance record watch

The 2026 Finals have drawn 88,390 fans through five games. A crowd of 4,210 on Thursday would pass the prior record of 92,599, set by the 2024 Finals, the most since 2002 before this series, and State Farm Arena seats more than 17,000. Our Finals attendance tracker has every game, and the data is free to reuse under CC0.

Where the trophy would be raised

If Golden State wins Thursday, it would celebrate on a court that has to be ready for an NBA game a few hours later. The Hawks host the Cleveland Cavaliers at State Farm Arena at 8 p.m. ET that night (NBA.com), with doors at 7 p.m. (State Farm Arena). That leaves seven and a half hours from Game 6 tip-off to the Hawks' tip, and six and a half hours to the Hawks' doors, before accounting for overtime or a trophy ceremony.

ESPN's Ramona Shelburne reported on NBA Today on Oct. 26 that the celebration "may not actually be on that court." She said, "I've heard there are discussions about whether there's enough time to turn the arena over in time for the fans to celebrate on the court. It could be moved to like a practice court" (Yahoo Sports). She later posted on X: "To clarify: There is a resolve to make sure any potential championship that is won Thursday afternoon is celebrated on the court" (The Big Lead). The WNBA's Game 6 announcement does not mention a trophy plan (WNBA), and we found no Dream or arena statement on it as of Tuesday.

Only Golden State can clinch Thursday. If Atlanta wins, Game 7 is Saturday, Oct. 31, at 5 p.m. PT (8 p.m. ET) at Chase Center in San Francisco (WNBA), and the trophy would be presented there.

A second-year champion

Golden State played its first season in 2025, when it became the first expansion team to make the playoffs in its first year (Valkyries). A title Thursday would come in its second season. The fastest expansion champion so far is the Seattle Storm, which joined in 2000 and won in 2004, its fifth season (WNBA). Neither finalist has won a WNBA title, so 2026 will crown a first-time champion (WNBA).

Follow Game 6 live

Our Game 6 play-by-play page goes live at tip-off and updates every 30 seconds. It includes every play, the running score and a downloadable CSV.

Game 1: Valkyries 68, Dream 64 (Oct. 17); Game 2: Dream 79, Valkyries 65 (Oct. 19); Game 3: Dream 97, Valkyries 71 (Oct. 21); Game 4: Valkyries 67, Dream 62 (Oct. 24); Game 5: Valkyries 64, Dream 55 (Oct. 26); Game 6: Dream 80, Valkyries 69 (Oct. 29); Game 7: Valkyries 68, Dream 63 (Oct. 31). The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.

Game 6 at a glance

  • When: Thursday, Oct. 29, at 9:30 a.m. PT (12:30 p.m. ET)
  • Where: State Farm Arena, Atlanta
  • TV and streaming: USA Network, with Peacock streaming (WNBA). E! and Syfy are also listed to carry the game.
  • Doors: 10:30 a.m. ET. The arena is cashless (State Farm Arena).
  • Series: Golden State leads 3-2. A Golden State win ends the series; an Atlanta win forces Game 7.
The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.

Injuries: the latest official WNBA injury report, for Game 5 (Oct. 26, 11 p.m. ET), listed only Atlanta's Brionna Jones as out (left leg). The Game 6 report is due by 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (WNBA injury report). Checked Tuesday, 12:40 p.m. PT.

Why it's at 9:30 a.m. PT

Game 6 was originally set for 8 p.m. ET. The WNBA moved it to 12:30 p.m. ET at State Farm Arena, which seats more than 17,000, instead of the Dream's usual home, Gateway Center Arena (about 3,500). The Hawks agreed to move their game against Cleveland that night to 8 p.m. ET (WNBA). "The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere at State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success, and we're excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line," Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said in the announcement.

Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said he was excited Atlanta could pack a big arena and joked, "I'd like to see it be a national holiday for all WNBA championship games" (Yahoo Sports). He also said there would be no pregame shootaround for either team (Yahoo Sports). The weekday midday tip drew the loudest reaction on X and r/wnba this week (Deadline).

Dream ownership answered in an open letter to fans on Tuesday. "Two months ago, when the WNBA finalized playoff dates and times, we raised concerns that the W Finals schedule conflicted with NBA games at State Farm Arena," it said, adding, "Playing a midday game on a Thursday is not what we would have chosen and not what we fought for" (CBS Sports). The Dream announced on Oct. 6 that it will play all of its home games at State Farm Arena starting in 2027 (Atlanta Dream).

Four things to watch

The third quarter. Atlanta has won the third quarter 100-68 across five games. Golden State has won the other three quarters 267-257. The team that led at halftime has won all five games, and so has the team with fewer turnovers (Game 5 recap).

Reese against Stokes. Reese averaged 21.7 points in Games 1-3 and 7.5 in Games 4-5. Stokes called Reese "the head of the snake" after holding her to 2 of 10 shooting in Game 4 (USA Today). Stokes has at least 3 blocks in every game of the series, and her 17 blocks are a Finals series record, passing Sylvia Fowles and Brittney Griner (WNBA on X).

Atlanta's Game 5 hole. The Dream shot 19 of 65 (29.2 percent), turned it over 15 times and got 4 points from the bench (WNBA.com box score). "That's going to be a very ruthless Atlanta team that really wants it just as much. You can never count them out," Golden State coach Natalie Nakase said after Game 5 (SI).

Free throws. Atlanta averaged 29.0 free-throw attempts in Games 1-4 and took 14 in Game 5. "The contact they allow on Angel compared to everybody else is just ridiculous," Smesko said after Game 5 (SI). Reese said, "It definitely shifted when we went up 2-1" (same source).

Finals MVP race

If Golden State wins, the Finals MVP debate is between Williams, its leading scorer, and Stokes, whose case rests on defense. Kalshi's Finals MVP market had Williams at 57 percent, Reese 27 and Stokes 18 on Tuesday (Kalshi). CBS Sports ranks the field after Game 5 (CBS Sports).

The odds

DraftKings opened Atlanta -3.5, with the Dream -166 and the Valkyries +140 on the moneyline, on Oct. 26 (DraftKings Network). The Dunkel Index lists a total of 147.5 (Dunkel Index). Kalshi gave Atlanta a 56 percent chance to win Game 6 on Tuesday. Prices may change before tip-off. Lines checked Tuesday.

Four of five games in this series finished under 147.5 combined points, and Game 5 finished with 119.

21+. Gamble responsibly. 1-800-GAMBLER.

Other Game 6 previews we read

RealGM, NBC Sports, San Francisco Chronicle and Valkyrie Nation.

This preview was published before the game. For the result, read our game recap.

item.title: Valkyries beat Dream 64-55 in the lowest-scoring WNBA Finals game since 2002
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Valkyries beat the Dream 64-55, the lowest-scoring Finals game since at least 2002, for a 3-2 lead despite being outscored by 22 in the series.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Valkyries beat Dream 64-55 in the lowest-scoring WNBA Finals game since 2002

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 26, 2026

The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 64-55 in Game 5 of the WNBA Finals on Monday at Chase Center, taking a 3-2 series lead. Golden State is one win from the title.

Finals data: lowest-scoring games since 2002

Game 5 broke a three-way tie at 121 points for the lowest-scoring WNBA Finals game since at least 2002. Here are the lowest-scoring Finals games in that span:

RankFinals gameFinal scoreCombined points
12026 Game 5Golden State 64, Atlanta 55119
2 (tie)2015 Game 5Minnesota 69, Indiana 52121
2 (tie)2005 Game 4Sacramento 62, Connecticut 59121
2 (tie)2005 Game 3Sacramento 66, Connecticut 55121
52003 Game 2Detroit 62, Los Angeles 61123
62006 Game 4Detroit 72, Sacramento 52124
7 (tie)2026 Game 4Golden State 67, Atlanta 62129
7 (tie)2024 Game 5New York 67, Minnesota 62 (OT)129

Atlanta made 19 of 65 shots, 29.2%, and 6 of 26 threes. Its 55 points are the fewest by either team in the series. Golden State shot 39.3% and blocked 9 shots.

The 119 combined points are the fewest in any of the 98 WNBA Finals games played from 2002 through Monday. Golden State's 64 points are the fewest by a Finals winner since Sacramento beat Connecticut 62-59 in Game 4 of the 2005 Finals.

Atlanta's 55 points tie Connecticut in 2005 Game 3 for the fourth-lowest team score in that span, behind Phoenix's 50 in 2021 Game 3 and 52-point games by Sacramento (2006 Game 4) and Indiana (2015 Game 5).

Series data: the third quarter and the point differential

Golden State leads 3-2 even though Atlanta has outscored it 357-335, and the third quarter explains most of that gap: Atlanta has won it by 32 points, while Golden State has won the other three quarters by 10. Here's how each game split:

GameFinal3rd quarterOther 3 quartersHalftime
1Valkyries 68, Dream 64Dream 17-9Valkyries 59-47Valkyries 42-39
2Dream 79, Valkyries 65Dream 21-9Dream 58-56Dream 39-37
3Dream 97, Valkyries 71Dream 25-17Dream 72-54Dream 46-40
4Valkyries 67, Dream 62Dream 19-12Valkyries 55-43Valkyries 42-26
5Valkyries 64, Dream 55Valkyries 21-18Valkyries 43-37Valkyries 25-22
TotalDream 357, Valkyries 335Dream 100-68Valkyries 267-257Halftime leader 5-0

Data through Game 5, Oct. 26, 2026. The data is free to use: all 98 Finals scores (CSV) and 2026 Finals quarter scores (CSV). Methods and sources: final and quarter scores from official WNBA.com box scores (Game 1, Game 2, Game 3, Game 4, Game 5) and WNBA.com game records for every Finals game from 2002 to 2025, the same records behind the FCB Finals database. Overtime games count full final scores. Finals before 2002 are not yet in the database.

Only two teams in the 2002-2026 database won three of a Finals' first five games while being outscored over those games, and both won the title: the 2006 Detroit Shock (365-374, -9) and the 2016 Los Angeles Sparks (386-391, -5). Golden State is at -22.

Atlanta's 8-point quarter

Golden State started Kaila Charles, Gabby Williams, Kiah Stokes, Tiffany Hayes and Veronica Burton, the same five as Game 4. Angel Reese picked up two fouls in the first quarter, an offensive foul at 2:08 and a personal foul with 58.9 seconds left, and sat until 8:28 of the second.

The Dream led 14-13 after one quarter on a Rhyne Howard three with 21.5 seconds left. That one-point edge was Atlanta's biggest lead of the night. The Dream scored 8 points in the second quarter and trailed 25-22 at halftime. Their 22 first-half points are the fewest by either team in a half this series.

Atlanta had won the third quarter in each of the first four games, 82-47 combined. This time Kiah Stokes made two threes in the period, and Golden State won it 21-18 to lead 46-40.

At 6:37 of the third, Allisha Gray was called for an offensive foul on an inbounds play with Golden State up 34-26. The Dream challenged, and replay upheld the call.

How Golden State pulled away

A Jordin Canada layup cut the lead to 46-42 with 9:53 left. Golden State then scored 10 of the next 12 points: a Gabby Williams and-one, a Stokes three at 7:21 assisted by Cecilia Zandalasini, a Veronica Burton basket and a Zandalasini basket at 4:58 for 56-44.

After two Isobel Borlase free throws, Tiffany Hayes scored Golden State's next 6 points, a basket at 3:50 assisted by Zandalasini and four free throws. Her last two, at 1:46, made it 62-46, the Valkyries' biggest lead. Atlanta did not score from 4:07 to 1:30, then hit three late threes, two by Canada and one by Howard, to close the gap.

The numbers that decided it

  • Turnovers. Atlanta 17, Golden State 9, including 2 team turnovers each, per the official WNBA.com box score. Golden State had 9 steals and scored 21 points off turnovers to Atlanta's 6.
  • Shooting. Golden State made 24 of 61 shots and Atlanta 19 of 65. Both teams made 6 threes.
  • Rim protection. Golden State blocked 9 shots to Atlanta's 3. Burton had 4, Stokes 3, and Kaila Charles and Zandalasini 1 each.
  • The glass. Atlanta won the rebounding battle 44-33, with 12 offensive rebounds to Golden State's 5, and outscored Golden State 19-6 on second-chance points. Atlanta took 65 shots to Golden State's 61 but made 13 of 39 inside the arc.
  • Paint and bench. Golden State won points in the paint 26-18 and bench points 15-4.

Free throws dried up. Atlanta averaged 29.0 free-throw attempts in Games 1-4, then went 11 of 14, its fewest attempts of the Finals by 7.

GameDream FT-FTAValkyries FT-FTAResult
118-2111-16Loss, 68-64
230-3516-19Win, 79-65
320-2911-17Win, 97-71
422-3111-13Loss, 67-62
511-1410-13Loss, 64-55

Reese's scoring. Reese's last field goal came with 1:39 left in the first quarter. Her 7 points and 4 free-throw attempts are her lows of the 2026 playoffs, and she had 3 turnovers to 2 made shots. Atlanta is 2-0 this series when she scores 20 or more and 0-3 when she scores under 15.

GameReese FGM-FGAFTM-FTAReboundsTurnoversPointsResult
15-114-712414Loss
210-169-1116230Win
37-125-512221Win
42-124-6968Loss
52-83-41537Loss
Games 1-322-39 (56.4%)18-2313.3 per game821.7 per game2-1
Games 4-54-20 (20.0%)7-1012.0 per game97.5 per game0-2

Stokes had 13 points on 5 of 6 shooting, 3 of 4 from three, with 8 rebounds and 3 blocks. She has 17 blocks in the series and at least 3 in every game. The WNBA said before Game 5 that her 14 blocks through Game 4 had already passed Sylvia Fowles and Brittney Griner for the most in a Finals series, and the league noted her sixth straight playoff game with 3 or more blocks ties Lisa Leslie for the longest such streak. After the game she told the home fans, "All we need is two hoops, 94 feet and each other," in an on-court interview the WNBA posted. Burton added 13 points, 8 rebounds, 3 assists and 4 blocks. Hayes scored 12 on 4 of 9 shooting and 4 of 4 free throws. It is her fourth straight game in double figures. Zandalasini had 12 points off the bench on 5 of 10 shooting and was +9, the best mark of the game, after a game-high +20 in Game 4. Williams scored 9 with 3 steals.

Howard led Atlanta with 20 points on 7 of 15 shooting, including 3 of 8 threes. Angel Reese had 15 rebounds, 5 of them offensive, and 5 assists, but scored 7 points on 2 of 8 shooting. Canada scored 12 on 5 of 16, Allisha Gray had 10 on 4 of 12, and Naz Hillmon grabbed 11 rebounds. Atlanta's bench went 0 of 9 from the field. DeWanna Bonner and Borlase combined for 4 points on 0 of 8.

Watch every possession on the Game 5 play-by-play page, or check the official WNBA.com box score.

Before the game, Reese arrived at Chase Center in a black "Protect Black Women" T-shirt, in a video the WNBA posted.

The series so far

The team with fewer turnovers has won all five games, and so has the team leading at halftime. Atlanta has won its two games by a combined 40 points. Golden State has won its three by a combined 18. The Valkyries, in their second season, went 32-12 as the No. 2 seed.

Game 5 drew 18,064 at Chase Center, a sellout. That brings the 2026 Finals to 88,390 fans through five games, according to the FCB Finals attendance tracker. The prior record is 92,599, set in 2024. A Game 6 crowd of 4,209 would tie it and 4,210 would break it. State Farm Arena drew sellouts of 17,099 for Games 3 and 4.

What's next

Game 6 is Thursday, Oct. 29, at 9:30 a.m. PT (12:30 p.m. ET) at State Farm Arena in Atlanta (WNBA.com game page), on USA Network, E! and Syfy and streaming on Peacock. Golden State can clinch the title with a win.

item.title: Valkyries beat Dream 67-62 to tie the WNBA Finals 2-2 as Atlanta turns it over 18 times
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Golden State beat Atlanta 67-62 in Game 4 at State Farm Arena to tie the WNBA Finals 2-2. The Dream had 18 turnovers, 14 before halftime.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Valkyries beat Dream 67-62 to tie the WNBA Finals 2-2 as Atlanta turns it over 18 times

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 24, 2026

The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 67-62 in Game 4 of the WNBA Finals on Saturday at State Farm Arena, tying the series 2-2. Golden State led by 16 late in the first half, and Atlanta got no closer than four.

The Dream had 18 turnovers, 14 of them before halftime. Golden State scored 16 points off those turnovers and Atlanta scored 8 off the Valkyries' 9. That 8-point gap was bigger than the final margin.

Built in the first half

Golden State led 16-11 after one quarter and 42-26 at the half. It made 17 of 40 shots before the break. Atlanta shot almost the same percentage, 8 of 19, but got 21 fewer shots up because of the turnovers and Golden State's 8 first-half offensive rebounds. Our first-half breakdown has the full numbers.

The lead hit 16 at 42-26 on a 24-foot three by Kayla Thornton, assisted by Cecilia Zandalasini, with 1:38 left in the second quarter.

Atlanta's comeback falls short

The Dream cut their turnovers to four after halftime and outscored Golden State 36-25, but Atlanta made just 10 of 35 shots in the second half. It won the third quarter 19-12 to trail 54-45 and the fourth 17-13.

Tiffany Hayes scored three straight Golden State baskets early in the fourth, and Veronica Burton answered an Isobel Borlase layup with a 24-foot step-back three at 4:23 for a 64-55 lead. Rhyne Howard made two free throws and Angel Reese scored on a driving layup at 1:36 to make it 64-59.

Burton's turnaround jumper with 34.6 seconds left made it 66-59. Howard answered with a layup and a free throw at 0:28.7 to make it 66-62, the closest Atlanta got in the second half. Burton made 1 of 2 free throws a second later, and the Dream did not score again.

The numbers that decided it

  • Turnovers. Atlanta 18, Golden State 9 (team totals, including team turnovers).
  • Shots. Golden State took 72 field goals to Atlanta's 54. Both teams made 4 threes.
  • Free throws. Atlanta went 22 of 31 and Golden State 11 of 13, which kept the Dream in it.
  • The glass. Kiah Stokes had 16 rebounds, 8 of them offensive, and 3 blocks. Golden State had 13 offensive rebounds to Atlanta's 12.

Gabby Williams led Golden State with 17 points on 7 of 21 shooting. Hayes and Burton scored 13 each, and Burton added 5 assists and 3 steals without a turnover. Zandalasini had 10 points off the bench and was +20, the best mark of the game.

Howard led Atlanta with 19 points and 8 rebounds. Reese had 8 points on 2 of 12 shooting, 9 rebounds and 6 turnovers. Borlase and Jordin Canada scored 10 each, and Naz Hillmon had 9 rebounds.

Watch every possession on the Game 4 play-by-play page, or check the official WNBA.com box score.

The series so far

The team with fewer turnovers has won all four games, and so has the team leading at halftime. Atlanta has won its two games by a combined 40 points. Golden State has won its two by a combined 9.

Game 4 drew 17,099 at State Farm Arena, a sellout. That brings the 2026 Finals to 70,326 fans through four games, according to the FCB Finals attendance tracker. The prior record is 92,599, set in 2024, so this series needs 22,273 more to tie it. Chase Center drew 18,064 for Game 1.

What's next

Game 5 is Monday, Oct. 26, at 5 p.m. PT at Chase Center in San Francisco (WNBA.com game page), on USA Network (simulcast on CNBC) and streaming on Peacock. The Finals are best of seven, so the winner will be one game from the title.

item.title: 40 Shots to 19 Before Halftime: How Golden State Won WNBA Finals Game 4
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Official Game 4 data show Golden State took 40 first-half shots to Atlanta’s 19 despite nearly identical shooting percentages. Download the data and charts.
item.content:encoded:
WNBA FinalsFull Court Buckets

40 Shots to 19 Before Halftime: How Golden State Won WNBA Finals Game 4

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 24, 2026

Atlanta shot almost as well as Golden State before halftime. It had 14 turnovers and just eight made field goals.

Game 4, first halfGolden StateAtlanta
Field goals made / attempted17 / 408 / 19
Field-goal percentage42.5%42.1%
Turnovers, including team turnovers414
Offensive rebounds83
Points4226

Source: FCB’s half-by-half data, calculated from the official Game 4 play-by-play. Data through Game 4, Oct. 24, 2026.

Golden State made 42.5% of its field-goal attempts in the first half of Game 4. Atlanta made 42.1%. The Valkyries still reached halftime with a 42–26 lead after attempting 40 field goals to the Dream’s 19.

Atlanta committed 14 turnovers before the break, then cut that number to four in the second half. Its comeback fell short, 67–62, leaving the WNBA Finals tied 2–2.

Full Court Buckets’ analysis of the official box scores and play-by-play found a pattern across all four games: the team with fewer turnovers has won every time. In both Golden State victories, its advantage in points off turnovers exceeded its final winning margin.

Data for reporters: Game 4 by half · All four games by half · All four games · Downloadable chart

The first-half gap: 14 turnovers, eight made baskets

Atlanta attempted more free throws, 14 to six, which accounts for part of the field-goal-attempt gap. But it also committed 10 more turnovers and collected five fewer offensive rebounds.

After halftime, Atlanta won the field-goal-attempt count 35–32 and outscored Golden State 36–25. Its shooting percentage actually fell to 28.6%. The Dream generated more attempts and more free-throw points while sharply reducing their giveaways.

Every halftime leader has won, and Atlanta owns the second halves

That first-half edge has decided the series so far, while Atlanta keeps winning after the break. Here's every game, half by half:

GameHalftime score1st-half FGA, ATL–GSV1st-half turnovers, ATL–GSV2nd-half scoreFinal
1Golden State 42–3933–375–6Golden State 26–25Golden State 68–64
2Atlanta 39–3734–318–8Atlanta 40–28Atlanta 79–65
3Atlanta 46–4038–326–10Atlanta 51–31Atlanta 97–71
4Golden State 42–2619–4014–4Atlanta 36–25Golden State 67–62

The team leading at halftime has won all four games. Golden State has built both of its wins before the break, leading by a combined 19 points at halftime in Games 1 and 4, then being outscored by 10 after it.

After halftime, the series has belonged to Atlanta. The Dream have won three of four second halves and outscored Golden State 152–110 after the break, while trailing 161–150 in first halves. Golden State has taken exactly 140 field-goal attempts in each half of the series, but made 58 before halftime (41.4%) and 38 after it (27.1%). Atlanta has attempted 67 second-half free throws to Golden State’s 31.

Game 4’s 14 first-half turnovers were not part of a series-long pattern. Atlanta had fewer first-half turnovers than Golden State in Games 1 and 3 and the same number in Game 2.

Source: FCB’s half-by-half data for all four games, calculated from official play-by-play and reconciled to full-game totals.

After halftime, Golden State stops finishing inside

Shots inside 15 feetFirst halves, Games 1–4Second halves, Games 1–4
Golden State38 / 73 (52.1%)23 / 79 (29.1%)
Atlanta33 / 69 (47.8%)34 / 77 (44.2%)
Golden State threes19 / 61 (31.1%)11 / 51 (21.6%)

Golden State’s second-half slump is mostly a two-point problem. It has taken more shots inside 15 feet after halftime than before, but has made 15 fewer. Atlanta’s inside shooting has barely changed between halves.

Source: FCB shot-zone data and every shot, Games 1–4, classified from play-by-play shot descriptions.

Steals have cost far more than dead-ball turnovers

Turnover type, Games 1–4TurnoversOpponent points within 24 secondsPoints per turnover
Live-ball (credited steal)61781.28
Dead-ball (no steal)48360.75
Atlanta live-ball29351.21
Golden State live-ball32431.34

A steal has been worth about 1.7 times as many points to the opponent as a dead-ball turnover. Golden State’s 14 live-ball turnovers in Game 2 produced 20 Atlanta points. Rhyne Howard leads the series with 12 steals, none in Game 4.

Game 4 broke that pattern for Atlanta. Ten of its 18 turnovers were dead-ball. Angel Reese’s six were three bad passes, two offensive fouls and a travel; only two were steals, and Golden State scored three points within 24 seconds of them.

Game 1’s last five minutes: Atlanta made 1 of 10 shots

Game 1, final 5:00Golden StateAtlanta
Points114
Field goals2 / 71 / 10
Three-pointers attempted25
Free throws7 / 82 / 2
Turnovers31

Atlanta led 60–57 with five minutes left in Game 1. It missed its last nine field-goal attempts, three of them blocked, and did not score after Howard’s free throws with 3:12 left. Gabby Williams scored eight of Golden State’s 11 points in that stretch, six on free throws. Her free throws with 1:18 left gave the Valkyries a 65–64 lead.

Source: Game 1 closing-stretch data, calculated from the official Game 1 play-by-play.

Golden State led the final 35:49 of Game 4

GameLead changesTiesLargest lead, ATLLargest lead, GSVBiggest run
17695Atlanta 11–0
21413216Atlanta 11–0
302260Atlanta 8–0 (twice); Golden State 8–0
412516Golden State 12–0

Game 4 had one lead change. Atlanta led 7–2 before Golden State’s 12–0 run in the first quarter. Kiah Stokes’ layup with 4:11 left in the quarter put the Valkyries ahead 9–7, and they never trailed or were tied again. Golden State never led in Game 3.

Source: scoring runs and lead tracker, from play-by-play scoring.

An eight-point edge off turnovers in a five-point win

Golden State scored 16 points off turnovers in Game 4; Atlanta scored eight. On all other scoring, Atlanta led 54–51.

The same split appeared in Game 1. Golden State won the points-off-turnovers category 17–8, while Atlanta led 56–51 on all other points.

Golden State victoryGSV margin in points off turnoversGSV margin in all other scoringFinal winning margin
Game 1, 68–64+9−5+4
Game 4, 67–62+8−3+5
Combined+17−8+9

Across its two wins, Golden State has outscored Atlanta 33–16 off turnovers while being outscored 110–102 on all other points. That is how the recorded scoring divides up; it does not tell us what would have happened if the turnovers had never occurred.

Eight more two-point baskets outweighed Atlanta’s free throws

Golden State finished Game 4 with 72 field-goal attempts to Atlanta’s 54. Those 18 additional attempts were not 18 additional possessions: Atlanta attempted 31 free throws to Golden State’s 13, and offensive rebounds also affected the shot count.

Golden State won despite shooting 4-for-25 from three. Both teams made four threes, but the Valkyries made 22 two-point baskets to Atlanta’s 14, a 16-point advantage. Atlanta made 22 free throws to Golden State’s 11, recovering 11 of those points. The remaining five were the final margin.

Four games, four wins for the team with fewer turnovers

GameResultTurnovers, ATL–GSVPoints off turnovers, ATL–GSV
1Golden State 68–6412–108–17
2Atlanta 79–6514–1924–13
3Atlanta 97–7110–1722–7
4Golden State 67–6218–98–16

Across the four games, winners have committed 43 turnovers to the losers’ 66 and scored 79 points off turnovers to the losers’ 36.

The series totals hide those swings. Atlanta has 54 turnovers and Golden State 55, almost a tie. The difference has been their distribution from game to game.

The sharpest reversal came between Games 3 and 4. Atlanta went from a 22–7 advantage in points off turnovers to an 8–16 deficit, a 23-point swing toward Golden State. The Valkyries scored four fewer points than in their Game 3 loss and still won Game 4.

Four games establish a pattern in this series, not a guarantee for Game 5.

Reese’s split shows how much Atlanta’s offense has changed

Angel Reese finished Game 4 with eight points on 2-for-12 shooting and six turnovers, one-third of Atlanta’s team total. Her production has differed sharply between the Dream’s two wins and two losses.

Reese through Game 4Atlanta wins, Games 2–3Atlanta losses, Games 1 and 4
Points per game25.511.0
Field goals17 / 287 / 23
Field-goal percentage60.7%30.4%
Rebounds per game14.010.5
Turnovers per game2.05.0

Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19 points in Game 4. Her defensive contribution also changed: she recorded 11 steals across Atlanta’s two wins and none in Game 4.

Golden State’s own scoring has barely moved: 67.5 points per game in wins, 68 in losses. Atlanta has averaged 88 in wins and 63 in losses. The Valkyries have won twice without a scoring surge. Atlanta’s offense has been the much larger variable.

Download and reuse the data

FCB’s original charts, calculations and compiled data tables are free to use and republish.

  • Team statistics, Games 1–4 (CSV)
  • Game 4, first and second halves (CSV)
  • All four games, first and second halves (CSV)
  • Reese and Howard, Games 1–4 (CSV)
  • Every turnover, with type, steal and opponent points within 24 seconds (CSV)
  • Turnovers by type, team and player (CSV)
  • Every field-goal attempt with shot zone (CSV)
  • Shot zones by team, game and half (CSV)
  • Scoring runs of 8+ points (CSV)
  • Lead changes, ties and largest leads (CSV)
  • Game 1 final five minutes (CSV)
  • Combined data and methods (JSON)
  • First-half chart (PNG)
  • Golden State’s winning margins chart (PNG)
  • Data definitions and calculation notes

Methods and sources

This analysis covers the four completed games of the 2026 WNBA Finals through Oct. 24. Full-game figures were checked against the official WNBA box scores linked above. Half-by-half counts for all four games were calculated from Full Court Buckets game data, checked against official WNBA play-by-play, and reconciled to full-game totals.

Turnovers include both player turnovers and team turnovers. Golden State’s Game 1 total is eight player turnovers plus two team turnovers; Atlanta’s Game 4 total is 17 plus one.

Shot zones use the distance or shot type in each play description: rim (0–4 feet, layups, dunks, tips), short (5–14 feet, floaters, hooks), midrange (15+ feet, two-pointers) and threes. Thirty attempts without a distance or type took their distance from the official play-by-play. “Opponent points within 24 seconds” counts the other team’s points in the 24 game-clock seconds after a turnover, in the same quarter. It is FCB’s per-turnover measure. It matches the official points-off-turnovers total exactly in six of eight team-games and totals 114 against the official 115. A live-ball turnover is one with a credited steal.

“All other scoring” means final points minus the official points-off-turnovers total. These are mutually exclusive scoring categories, not an estimate of the causal cost of turnovers. Field-goal attempts, free-throw attempts and possessions are different measures. Player shooting percentages use combined makes divided by combined attempts, not an average of individual game percentages.

Source credit: Full Court Buckets game data, verified against official WNBA box scores and play-by-play.

item.title: Angel Reese didn't get good overnight: double-digit rebounds in every full season since high school
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Angel Reese has averaged 10+ rebounds in every full college and WNBA season. Our 124-game box score ledger shows the rebounding was always there; the 2026 playoff change is her shooting.
item.content:encoded:
WNBA FinalsFull Court Buckets

Angel Reese didn't get good overnight: double-digit rebounds in every full season since high school

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 21, 2026

Angel Reese, every level, per game

In 2026 Reese set WNBA single-season records with 521 rebounds, 206 offensive rebounds and 32 double-doubles (WNBA). Her rebounding was there at every level before that. Here's her career, level by level, per game:

LevelSeasonTeamGPTSREBOff. reb shareFG%TS%Double-doublesSource
High school2016-20 careerSaint Frances Academyn/a1820n/an/an/an/aLSU bio
High school2019-20Saint Frances Academy2118.610.2n/an/an/an/aMaxPreps
College2020-21Maryland1510.06.044.4%46.753.91 (6.7%)Maryland stats, box scores in ledger
College2021-22Maryland3217.810.649.7%50.055.517 (53.1%)Maryland stats, box scores in ledger
College2022-23LSU3623.015.441.8%52.558.434 (94.4%)LSU stats PDF
College2023-24LSU3318.613.441.5%47.154.527 (81.8%)LSU stats PDF, box scores
WNBA2024Chicago Sky3413.613.138.6%39.146.426 (76.5%)WNBA stats, Sky
WNBA2025Chicago Sky3014.712.6n/a45.853.723 (76.7%)WNBA stats, WNBA
WNBA2026Atlanta Dream4316.412.139.5%45.152.432 (74.4%)WNBA stats, WNBA
WNBA playoffs2026Atlanta Dream819.410.335.4%48.159.74 (50.0%)WNBA box scores: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8

Sources: Maryland and LSU box scores for college rows; WNBA.com for WNBA rows. Data through Finals Game 3, Oct. 21, 2026. "Full season" means every season after high school except her injury-shortened 15-game Maryland freshman year. College rows include postseason games; WNBA season rows are regular season only, and the 2026 playoffs are a separate row.

TS% (true shooting) = points ÷ (2 × (FGA + 0.44 × FTA)), computed by FCB. Off. reb share = offensive rebounds ÷ total rebounds. Double-double rate = double-doubles ÷ games. College double-doubles are counted from every box score; WNBA counts are the league's published counts (26 in 2024 and 23 in 2025 on her WNBA bio, 32 in 2026). College seasons include conference and NCAA tournament games; WNBA seasons are regular season only. LSU's 2022-23 stat sheet lists 829 points while her LSU bio says 830; we use the stat sheet's 829. LSU's 2023-24 season sheet lists 441 rebounds and 183 offensive; the 33 box scores add to 442 and 184, so the table uses the season sheet. Download the season CSV or the game-by-game ledger.

Angel Reese had 21 points, 12 rebounds and 3 steals on 7-of-12 shooting as the Dream beat the Valkyries 97-71 in Game 3 on Wednesday for a 2-1 Finals lead (WNBA box score, FCB play-by-play). During the game, at 5:44 PM PT, Colin Salao posted the line the replies ran with:

“It’s actually insane how quickly Angel Reese got this good”

Colin Salao (@colincsalao on X), Oct. 21, 2026, 5:44 PM PT

By 9:41 PM PT that night the post had 22,505 views, 212 likes, 84 replies and 29 quote posts. So we went back and logged all 116 of her college games from the Maryland and LSU box scores, plus her eight 2026 playoff games. She had 10 or more rebounds in 80 of the 116 college games. The rebounding was never the thing that changed. Her shooting was.

The Angel Reese rebounding ledger

This is the dataset behind the story, one row per game. It covers every game she played at Maryland and LSU and all eight of her 2026 playoff games, with minutes, points, rebounds split into offensive and defensive, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers, shooting, true shooting, a double-double flag and a link to the official box score for each row. We have not found game-by-game WNBA regular-season box scores we can source to the league, so those seasons appear as official season totals.

SeasonTeamGTotal REB10+ REB gamesDouble-doublesLongest 10+ REB streak20+ REB gamesBest game
2020-21Maryland1590111011 vs Northwestern, Mar. 12, 2021
2021-22Maryland3234018177016 vs Nebraska and Indiana, Feb. 2022
2022-23LSU36555343423628 vs Texas A&M, Jan. 5, 2023
2023-24LSU33441272716320 three times
2024Chicago Sky34446 (Sky)n/a26n/an/an/a
2025Chicago Sky30377n/a23n/an/an/a
2026Atlanta Dream43521n/a32n/an/a26 at Los Angeles, Aug. 24, WNBA record (WNBA)
2026 playoffsAtlanta Dream882443016 at Golden State, Finals Game 2

Game counts, streaks and best games for college and the 2026 playoffs are counted from the box scores in the ledger. WNBA regular-season totals are per-game averages times games (2025) or the league's and team's published totals (2024, 2026). n/a means we could not source the game-level figure.

Download: Ledger CSV (124 games) · Season CSV

Methods: Maryland rows come from the box scores linked on umterps.com, LSU 2022-23 from LSU's individual game-by-game sheet in its season stats PDF, LSU 2023-24 from the 33 official box score PDFs on LSU's schedule page, and the 2026 playoffs from FCB game data checked against official box scores. FCB computed true shooting, double-double flags and streaks.

Cite this: Full Court Buckets, "Angel Reese rebounding ledger," Oct. 21, 2026, https://fullcourtbuckets.com/news/angel-reese-always-this-good-data/#rebounding-ledger

Embed the chart:

<a href="https://fullcourtbuckets.com/news/angel-reese-always-this-good-data/#rebounding-ledger"><img src="https://fullcourtbuckets.com/images/articles/angel-reese-always-this-good-data/chart-rebounding-ledger.png" width="800" height="450" alt="Angel Reese rebounding ledger chart"></a><br>Chart: <a href="https://fullcourtbuckets.com/news/angel-reese-always-this-good-data/">Full Court Buckets</a>

What the ledger shows

  1. The 2022-23 run is the outlier, and it was in college. Reese had a double-double in 34 of 36 LSU games that season, 23 of them in a row from the opener, and six games with 20 or more rebounds, topped by 26 points and 28 rebounds against Texas A&M on Jan. 5, 2023 (LSU stats PDF). LSU lists the 34 double-doubles as an NCAA single-season record (LSU bio). Across four college seasons she had seven 20-point, 20-rebound games.
  2. Maryland already had the rebounder. As a sophomore she had 17 double-doubles in 32 games and a seven-game run of 10-plus rebounds. Half of her rebounds that season (169 of 340) were offensive, the highest share of any season in the table (Maryland stats). Her freshman year was 15 games after a fractured right foot (Maryland notes).
  3. No WNBA player who debuted since 2009 has rebounded like this over a first three seasons. In FCB's season data, Reese has 1,344 rebounds in 107 games, 12.6 a game. Next is Tina Charles at 11.1 (2010-12), then Teaira McCowan and Breanna Stewart at 8.8 and Aliyah Boston at 8.5 (minimum 60 games over the first three seasons, 215 players). Reese also had the top rebounding average among players with 20 or more games in each of 2024, 2025 and 2026.
  4. 2026 was the record year. She set WNBA season records with 521 rebounds, 206 offensive rebounds and 32 double-doubles, became the first player to 500 rebounds in a season, and grabbed a league-record 26 against the Sparks on Aug. 24 (WNBA, AP). She was named Defensive Player of the Year with 46 of 74 votes (WNBA).
  5. The jump is shooting. Her true shooting fell to 46.4% as a rookie, then went to 53.7% and 52.4%, and is 59.7% in eight 2026 playoff games (155 points on 106 shots and 54 free throws), the highest of the periods in the table. Eight games is a small sample, and the three Finals games are part of it. In the Finals she is 22 of 39 (56.4%) with 65 points and 40 rebounds (WNBA box scores: Game 1, Game 2, Game 3).
RankPlayerFirst three seasonsGREBREB per game
1Angel Reese2024-261071,34412.6
2Tina Charles2010-121011,11711.1
3Teaira McCowan2019-21887748.8
4Breanna Stewart2016-181018888.8
5Aliyah Boston2023-251241,0518.5

Regular season only. Players whose first season in FCB's data (which starts in 2008) is 2009 or later, with at least 60 games across their first three seasons. Source: FCB season data.

Does she finish seasons stronger?

One reply said her finishing took a leap later in the season. We can't split the 2026 WNBA regular season by month yet, but the college box scores let us check whether she usually gets better late. She didn't.

SeasonFirst half FG%Second half FG%First half TS%Second half TS%
2021-22 Maryland52.447.556.254.8
2022-23 LSU57.747.662.454.7
2023-24 LSU50.544.359.150.3

Each season is split into its first and second half of games by date (16/16, 18/18 and 16/17). Second halves include conference and NCAA tournament play, so the opponents were tougher. Source: the ledger.

In all three full college seasons her shooting fell in the second half. In 2026 it went the other way: 45.1% in the regular season, 48.1% in the playoffs and 56.4% in the Finals. That is a change from her own pattern. It is still field-goal percentage, which mixes every shot type, so it can't prove her finishing improved. Showing that needs shot-location data and film.

What the replies got right and wrong

We read the replies and quote posts in the thread. Each post below was checked on X on Oct. 21 at 9:41 PM PT, and each claim is tested against the data.

“Overnight”

“😂 it’s like she came out of no where.”

@tisagraves on X

“Been doing this since high school yall just love to sound stupid”

@sdpmook on X

The data backs @sdpmook. A No. 2 national recruit with 79 college double-doubles and three seasons atop the WNBA rebounding table did not come out of nowhere. We found no primary source for her junior high stats, so that era is left out.

“Only rebounds and defense”

“The defense and rebounding were always there. Coming into her own as a scorer and the go-to for her team.”

@scism_cameron on X

Mostly right, with one fix: she was a scorer before. She averaged 23.0 points at LSU in 2022-23 and led the SEC (LSU stats, LSU bio). What dipped was her rookie WNBA scoring, 13.6 points on 39.1% shooting. It has gone up every season since: 14.7, 16.4, then 19.4 in the playoffs.

“She isn't a shooter”

“She is surrounded by a good team. She isn't a shooter. Just had some good looks tonight.”

@zechariah1680 on X

Half right. She hit 2 of 2 threes in Game 3, but shot 19.3% on 1.3 threes a game in the 2026 regular season (WNBA). She is 8 of 17 from three in the playoffs, too few to call. In 116 college games she took 32 threes. Her points come at the rim and the line, and she has made 45 of 54 free throws (83.3%) in the playoffs after 72.1% in the regular season.

“It's foul calls”

“Yeah? It’s called foul calls”

@justtradebaby on X

Box scores can't settle this. Free-throw counts show how often she got to the line, not whether any call was right. Here is what they do show. She is taking 6.8 free throws a game in the playoffs and took 6.3 in the regular season. At LSU she took 9.4 a game in 2022-23 and 8.1 in 2023-24 (2023, 2024). Per shot, her free-throw rate has dropped too: 0.61 and 0.60 free throws per field-goal try at LSU, 0.49 in the 2026 regular season, 0.51 in the playoffs. She is getting to the line less often per shot than at LSU and making more of the free throws she takes.

“She went to a loaded team”

“She went to an already loaded team cut it out 😂😂 check her record with the team that drafted her 😂😂”

@r8der_g on X

She did change teams in a trade from the Sky to the Dream (Chicago Sky), and Atlanta was already a 30-win team in 2025 (WNBA). Her own numbers went up in Atlanta: 12.9 shots a game vs. 11.1 in 2025, 16.4 points vs. 14.7, and 3.1 turnovers vs. 3.9. A better roster and her own growth can both be true, and these numbers can't separate the two. We did not verify the Sky's team records for this piece, so we don't compare them.

“3x All-Star”

“She’s a 3x All-Star, she’s been good stupid”

@wnbawanksta on X

Correct. The WNBA calls 2026 her third straight All-Star selection (WNBA), and LSU lists 2024, 2025 and 2026 (LSU).

“Her finishing took a leap”

“Angel Reese has always been an impact player. But her finishing took a leap later in the season and that’s been the difference.”

@robinlundberg on X

The data fits this, but can't prove it. See the split above: her shooting usually faded late in college seasons, and in 2026 it rose from 45.1% to 48.1% in the playoffs and 56.4% in the Finals. A month-by-month 2026 regular-season split is still missing, so we can't say which month it started, and FG% alone doesn't isolate finishing.

Why it looks overnight

  • Injuries cut her samples short. A fractured right foot limited her to 15 games as a Maryland freshman (Maryland). A wrist fracture that needed surgery ended her rookie WNBA season after 34 games (AP). She played 30 games in 2025 (WNBA).
  • Her weak stretch was her rookie shooting. The 39.1% rookie season is the low point in the table, and it came in her first WNBA year. Her rebounding that year set a league record.
  • The spotlight was on more than basketball. LSU says her Instagram grew from about 70,000 followers when she arrived to nearly 500,000 entering the 2023 NCAA tournament and more than 1 million after it (LSU), and Reebok announced a signature shoe for her (Authentic Brands). We did not measure how much coverage was about off-court topics, so this is context, not proof.
  • The big audience isn't new. Her 2023 title game drew 9.9 million viewers on ABC (ESPN press release). Finals Game 1 this year drew 2.1 million (NBC Sports) and Game 2 drew 1.33 million (USA Sports). We had not found a Game 3 audience figure as of Oct. 21.

Methods and data dictionary

Ledger columns: game_no, level, season, team, date, opponent, min, pts, reb, oreb, dreb, ast, stl, blk, tov, fgm, fga, fg3m, fg3a, ftm, fta, ts_pct, double_double, reb_10_plus, source. Each 2026 playoff row links its official WNBA.com box score, and all eight match FCB's game files. Maryland's box score totals match its season pages, and LSU's 2022-23 totals match its season sheet. LSU 2023-24 matches on points, shooting, assists, steals and blocks and is off by one rebound, as noted above. The first-three-seasons table uses FCB season data from 2008 on, so players who debuted before 2009 are left out. Left out because we could not source them: junior high stats, her first three high school seasons, 2024-26 WNBA game-by-game rows, 2025 offensive rebounds, college rebounding ranks, and Chicago Sky team records. Ledger CSV · Season CSV. Corrections: contact us.

item.title: Dream beat Valkyries 97-71 for their first home Finals win and a 2-1 series lead
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 in Game 3 of the WNBA Finals on Wednesday at State Farm Arena to lead the series 2-1. Golden State never led.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Dream beat Valkyries 97-71 for their first home Finals win and a 2-1 series lead

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 21, 2026

The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 in Game 3 of the WNBA Finals on Wednesday at State Farm Arena and lead the series 2-1. The game was tied 49-49 with 7:45 left in the third quarter, and Atlanta outscored Golden State 22-8 the rest of the quarter.

Golden State never led. It was the Dream's first home win in a WNBA Finals game, after losing all three of their earlier home Finals games, and the third quarter once again decided the game.

The third quarter, a third time

Our Game 3 preview pointed out that Golden State had scored 9 points and taken no free throws in the third quarter of Games 1 and 2. On Wednesday the Valkyries scored 17 in the third and went 3 of 4 at the line, their first third-quarter free throws of the series. They still lost the quarter 25-17, because Atlanta made 10 of its 14 shots in it.

Cecilia Zandalasini made four threes in 2:51 of game time across halftime, the last a 24-foot step-back that tied it 48-48 at 8:52 of the third. Zandalasini's free throw made it 49-49 at 7:45.

Rhyne Howard answered with a reverse layup. Angel Reese made two free throws, Isobel Borlase scored on a driving layup off a Reese pass, and Reese's running layup at 5:25 made it 57-49 and forced a Golden State timeout.

A Tiffany Hayes driving layup cut it to 59-55 at 3:41. Atlanta then scored 12 of the last 14 points of the quarter. DeWanna Bonner hit a 24-foot three off a Howard pass at 3:03 and an 11-footer at 2:07, Borlase added a running layup, and Jordin Canada and Naz Hillmon scored inside in the final minute for a 71-57 lead after three.

GameResult3rd quarterOther three quarters
Game 1Valkyries 68-64Dream 17-9Valkyries 59-47
Game 2Dream 79-65Dream 21-9Dream 58-56
Game 3Dream 97-71Dream 25-17Dream 72-54
SeriesDream 240-204Dream 63-35Dream 177-169

Atlanta has outscored Golden State by 36 points in the series, and 28 of them came in third quarters. Before Wednesday the Valkyries led the other three quarters combined, 115-105. Game 3 flipped that too.

How the first half went

Atlanta scored the first 6 points, and Golden State's first field goal, an Aminata Gueye basket, came at 4:38 of the first quarter. Golden State scored 7 straight points, 5 of them by Hayes, to make it 9-8, but Hillmon hit threes at 2:18 and 1:42, and Atlanta led 23-15 after one.

Reese and Howard hit back-to-back threes at 6:32 and 6:12 of the second quarter, and Canada's layup at 5:35 made it 35-23. Janelle Salaun kept Golden State close with three threes in the quarter. She finished with 13 points in 12 minutes. Zandalasini's three with 16.8 seconds left made it 46-40 at halftime.

The fourth quarter

Hillmon's layup off a Reese pass opened the fourth, and Howard's two free throws at 6:47 made it 80-60, Atlanta's first 20-point lead. Gabby Williams set up a Kiah Stokes layup and hit a 24-footer to make it 80-65.

After an Atlanta timeout, Borlase's floater, a Canada layup and a Bonner layup off a Borlase pass made it 86-65 at 4:33. The bench finished it: Sika Kone hit a three, Madina Okot converted a three-point play, and Kone's floater with 2.3 seconds left set the final margin at 26.

The numbers that decided it

  • Two-point shots. Golden State made 12 of 30 threes but only 12 of 39 twos. Atlanta made 25 of 47 twos.
  • Shooting. Atlanta shot 34 of 69 (49.3%). Neither team had shot better than 34.4% in the first two games.
  • Turnovers. Golden State turned it over 17 times and Atlanta 10. Atlanta had 9 steals, 5 of them by Howard.
  • Ball movement. Atlanta had 26 assists on 34 baskets. Canada had 8 and Allisha Gray 6.

Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds on 7-of-12 shooting, including 2 of 2 from three, with 3 steals. Howard scored 16 with 5 steals, 4 assists and no turnovers. Hillmon scored 15 on 3-of-5 three-point shooting, and Borlase had 12 points and was +21, the best mark on either team.

Williams led Golden State with 15 points and 8 assists but shot 5 of 18. Hayes scored 14, and Stokes had 11 rebounds and 3 blocks.

Where it ranks

From the Full Court Buckets Finals database, which lists every WNBA Finals game since 2002 with a link to its official game record:

  • Atlanta's first home Finals win. The Dream had lost Game 3 at home in 2010, 2011 and 2013, each time trailing the series 0-2.
  • The Dream's biggest Finals win and highest Finals score. Their only other Finals win was Monday's 14-point Game 2. Their previous Finals high was 95 points, in a 2011 loss at Minnesota. Their two worst Finals losses were by 25, in Games 1 and 2 in 2013.
  • A rare Finals margin. A 26-point margin is the seventh largest in a Finals game since 2002, and the largest since the Las Vegas Aces beat the New York Liberty 104-76 in Game 2 in 2023.
  • No lead changes. Game 3 had none and was tied twice. Game 1 had 7 lead changes and Game 2 had 14.

Reese has 65 points and 40 rebounds through three Finals games. Howard has 12 steals, and Hillmon is +38, the best mark in the series.

What's next

My preview pick, Atlanta to win Game 3, was right. The lean, the under 153.5, missed: the teams combined for 168 points.

Game 4 is Saturday, Oct. 24, at 10 a.m. PT at State Farm Arena (WNBA release), on NBC and Peacock. The Finals are best of seven, so Atlanta is two wins from the first championship in franchise history. One lopsided game is a small sample, and Golden State won Game 1 by doing what it did not do Wednesday: winning the quarters outside the third.

Watch every possession on the Game 3 play-by-play page.

Full Court Buckets gathers and verifies its own game data. Turnover totals include team turnovers.

TV: NBC · Stream: Peacock
