item.title: WNBA Finals Game 3 preview: Golden State hasn't taken a third-quarter free throw this series
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Golden State has scored 9 points and taken no free throws in the third quarter of both Finals games. Written before Game 3 with the series tied 1-1; Atlanta won Game 3 97-71.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

WNBA Finals Game 3 preview: Golden State hasn't taken a third-quarter free throw this series

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 21, 2026

This preview was published before the game. For the result, read our game recap. 2026 WNBA Finals ratings tracker.

Follow the play-by-play: Valkyries vs. Dream, Game 3 →

The Golden State Valkyries have scored 9 points in the third quarter of both WNBA Finals games, and they haven't attempted a single free throw in either one. The Atlanta Dream have outscored them 38-18 in third quarters, and that 20-point gap is the whole series so far.

Game 3 is tonight at State Farm Arena with the series tied 1-1, and the third quarter is where the Valkyries have to find points.

Finals Game 3 at a glance

  • When: Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 5 p.m. PT
  • Where: State Farm Arena, Atlanta
  • TV and streaming: USA Network (simulcast on CNBC) and Peacock (USA Sports release, Oct. 21, 2026)
  • Series: Tied 1-1. Golden State won Game 1 68-64, and Atlanta won Game 2 79-65.
  • Game line: Dream -3.5, total 153.5 (DraftKings, as of Oct. 21 at 11:00 a.m. PT)
  • Next: Game 4 is Saturday, Oct. 24, at 10 a.m. PT in Atlanta

Game 3 was moved up from Thursday, Oct. 22, and out of the Dream's usual home arena to State Farm Arena. It is the first WNBA Finals game in the Atlanta market since 2013, the league said when it announced the move.

Injury report

As of the league's official injury report from Oct. 21 at 3:00 p.m. ET (12:00 p.m. PT) (WNBA injury report).

Atlanta: Brionna Jones (left leg) is out. She is the only player listed for either team.

Golden State: No players are listed. Iliana Rupert has not played this season for a non-injury reason.

What happened in Game 2

Atlanta won 79-65 at Chase Center on Monday. Angel Reese had 30 points and 16 rebounds, and a 19-2 run that started at 3:52 of the third quarter turned a 45-44 game into a 64-46 lead by 9:00 of the fourth. Rhyne Howard had 6 steals, a Finals record (AP). Both teams made 21 field goals and 7 threes. Atlanta made 30 of 35 free throws and Golden State 16 of 19. Our Game 2 recap has the full sequence.

Golden State turned it over 19 times (every turnover count in this preview includes team turnovers), and Atlanta scored 24 points off those turnovers. "We have to play harder, number one, but we've got to play smarter as well," Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase said after the game (NBC Bay Area).

The third quarter is the series

Across the two third quarters, Golden State has made 8 of 40 shots: 4 of 25 in Game 1 and 4 of 15 in Game 2. It has gone to the free-throw line zero times. Atlanta has made all 16 of its third-quarter free throws, 4 in Game 1 and 12 in Game 2.

The Dream were called for 5 fouls in those two quarters, 3 in Game 1 and 2 in Game 2, and none of them was a shooting foul. Golden State was called for 9, including 5 shooting fouls.

The two quarters didn't go the same way. In Game 1, the Valkyries kept the ball (1 turnover) but missed 21 of 25 shots. In Game 2 they turned it over 8 times in the quarter. The result was 9 points both times.

Outside the third quarter, Golden State won the other three quarters of Game 1 by 12, 59-47, and Atlanta won them by 2 in Game 2, 58-56. In the other three quarters combined, Golden State leads 115-105. Two quarters is a very small sample, so this shows where the series has been decided, not what will happen tonight.

The Dream lost all three home Finals games in 2010, 2011 and 2013, each one with Atlanta down 0-2. Tonight is the first time they have played a home Finals game with the series tied.

The odds and my pick

DraftKings has Atlanta -3.5 and a total of 153.5, as of 11:00 a.m. PT Oct. 21 (The Odds API snapshot via AgentBets). The series price is Dream -135, Valkyries +115 (ESPN betting report, Oct. 20, 10:41 a.m. PT). Prices may change before tip-off.

My lean is the under 153.5: Games 1 and 2 finished with 132 and 144 points, and neither team has shot better than 34.4 percent in a Finals game. My pick is Atlanta to win Game 3.

21+. Gamble responsibly. 1-800-GAMBLER.

Frequently asked questions

How many WNBA players have famous relatives?

Full Court Buckets has verified 74 famous relatives of 58 current and former WNBA players as of November 3, 2026. Siblings are the most common tie (29), and the NBA is the most common sport (27). The list grows as new family ties are confirmed.

Who is Angel Reese's brother?

Julian Reese, her younger brother. NBA forward. Signed a two-way contract with the New Orleans Pelicans on Sept. 24, 2026, after starting 2026 with the Washington Wizards.

Is Cameron Brink related to Steph Curry?

Not a blood relative. Curry's parents, Dell and Sonya Curry, are Brink's godparents, and Brink's parents are Stephen's godparents. Brink's mother, Michelle Bain-Brink, was Sonya Curry's college roommate at Virginia Tech, and her father, Greg Brink, was Dell Curry's teammate there.

Who is Gabriela Jaquez's brother?

Jaime Jaquez Jr., her older brother. NBA forward and former UCLA All-American. The Miami Heat traded him to the Milwaukee Bucks on July 6, 2026, in the Giannis Antetokounmpo deal.

Who is Flau'jae Johnson's dad?

Jason Johnson, the rapper known as Camoflauge. Savannah, Georgia rapper who was shot and killed in May 2003, about six months before she was born.

Who are the Sabally sisters?

Satou Sabally and her younger sister, Nyara Sabally. WNBA forward. The Toronto Tempo took her in the 2026 expansion draft. Both played at Oregon and both played for Germany at the 2024 Olympics. They first faced each other in the WNBA on June 11, 2023.

Who is Candace Parker's brother?

Anthony Parker, her older brother. Former NBA guard who played for the Toronto Raptors. Orlando Magic general manager since July 2023.

Is Jordan Hawkins related to Angel Reese?

Yes. They are cousins. Won the 2023 NCAA title at UConn, the same year Reese was Most Outstanding Player of the women's Final Four with LSU. Signed a two-way deal with the Chicago Bulls on Oct. 6, 2026.

Who is Veronica Burton's grandfather?

Ron Burton. The Boston Patriots' first-ever AFL draft choice (1960) and a College Football Hall of Famer from Northwestern.

Who is Lexie Brown's dad?

Dee Brown. Won the 1991 NBA Slam Dunk Contest. Played for the Celtics (1990-98), Raptors (1998-2000) and Magic (2000-02).

Who is Breanna Stewart's wife?

Marta Xargay. Spanish guard who won a 2016 Olympic silver medal with Spain and played three WNBA seasons with the Phoenix Mercury. They married in 2021 after meeting as teammates at Dynamo Kursk in Russia.

Who is Diana Taurasi's wife?

Penny Taylor. Three-time WNBA champion with the Phoenix Mercury (2007, 2009, 2014), three-time Olympian for Australia and 2006 World Championship MVP. Later a Mercury assistant coach. They married in 2017. Taurasi and Taylor are the only players who were part of all three Mercury championship teams.

item.title: Angel Reese scores 30 as Dream beat Valkyries 79-65 to even the WNBA Finals
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 79-65 in Game 2 of the WNBA Finals on Monday at Chase Center, tying the series 1-1.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Angel Reese scores 30 as Dream beat Valkyries 79-65 to even the WNBA Finals

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 19, 2026

The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 79-65 in Game 2 of the WNBA Finals on Monday at Chase Center, tying the series 1-1. Angel Reese had 30 points and 16 rebounds, and a 19-2 Atlanta run that started late in the third quarter turned a one-point game into a 64-46 lead.

Both teams made exactly 21 field goals and exactly 7 threes. The whole 14-point margin came at the free-throw line, where Atlanta went 30 of 35 and Golden State went 16 of 19.

The third quarter, again

Golden State scored 9 points in the third quarter of Game 1. It scored 9 again on Monday.

Veronica Burton hit a 26-foot three at 9:31 of the third for a 40-39 lead, Golden State's last lead of the night. Kaitlyn Chen still had the Valkyries within 45-44 at 3:52.

From there it was all Atlanta. DeWanna Bonner scored on a running layup off a Reese assist at 3:06. Allisha Gray, Reese and Naz Hillmon all scored at the line, Reese added a layup and two more free throws, and Jordin Canada hit a 32-foot three with 0.8 seconds left for a 60-46 lead after three.

Canada and Bonner each made two free throws in the first minute of the fourth, and by 9:00 it was 64-46. Atlanta outscored Golden State 19-2 over that 6:52 stretch.

How the first half went

Chen's 5-footer with 2.0 seconds left gave Golden State a 21-18 lead after one, helped by two threes from Kaila Charles.

In the second quarter, the Valkyries scored 7 straight points at the line between 7:04 and 4:14, 5 of them from Gabby Williams, to lead 33-27. Atlanta answered with a 10-0 run, capped by Gray's 25-foot running jumper at 1:31. Tiffany Hayes tied it with two driving layups, and Bonner's 18-foot pull-up with 2.5 seconds left made it 39-37 Atlanta at the half.

The fourth quarter

Atlanta's lead hit 21 at 69-48 on two Canada free throws at 6:06. Williams hit a 26-foot three and Charles a 23-footer at 4:32 to make it 71-55. On the next trip, Reese made a 24-foot three off a Canada pass at 4:15, her only three-point try of the night. Burton's 24-foot three at 1:30 made it 78-63, and the Valkyries never got closer than the final 14.

The numbers that decided it

Our Game 2 preview focused on the turnover battle. Atlanta had won it in all five of its earlier playoff games, then lost it 12-8 in Game 1. On Monday it flipped back.

  • Turnovers. Golden State turned it over 19 times and Atlanta 14. The Dream scored 24 points off those turnovers, the Valkyries 13.
  • Steals. Atlanta had 14 steals, up from 5 in Game 1. Rhyne Howard had 6 and Bonner 4.
  • Fast breaks. Atlanta outscored Golden State 19-0 in fast-break points.
  • Free throws. Atlanta took 35 free throws after taking 21 in Game 1.

The preview also added the turnover margin and the offensive-rebound margin together. Golden State had won that combined count in all seven of its playoff games. Atlanta won it by 7 on Monday: by 5 on turnovers and 8-6 on the offensive glass. It's one game, but it's the first time this postseason the Valkyries lost that count.

Reese made 10 of 16 shots and 9 of 11 free throws and was +13. Canada had 13 points, 10 assists and 7 rebounds. Gray scored 18 and was +20, the best mark on either team.

Williams and Hayes scored 14 each for Golden State, but Williams went 3 of 15. Kiah Stokes had 11 rebounds and 4 blocks without attempting a shot, and the Valkyries had 10 assists on 21 baskets.

What's next

My preview picked Golden State to win Game 2, and that missed. The betting lean, the under 152.5, hit with 144 total points.

Game 3 is Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 5 p.m. PT at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, on USA Network (simulcast on CNBC) and Peacock.

My pick is Atlanta in Game 3. Through two games, the Dream have outscored Golden State 38-18 in third quarters.

Watch every possession on the Game 2 play-by-play page.

item.title: WNBA Finals Game 2 preview: Atlanta lost the turnover battle for the first time this postseason
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Atlanta won the turnover count in all five of its first playoff games, then lost it 12-8 in Finals Game 1. Written before Game 2 with Golden State up 1-0; Atlanta won Game 2 79-65.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

WNBA Finals Game 2 preview: Atlanta lost the turnover battle for the first time this postseason

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 19, 2026

This preview was published before the game. For the result, read our game recap. 2026 WNBA Finals ratings tracker.

Follow the play-by-play: Dream vs. Valkyries, Game 2 →

The Atlanta Dream forced 44 more turnovers than they committed across their first five playoff games, and they won the turnover count in all five. In Game 1 of the WNBA Finals, the Golden State Valkyries flipped it: Atlanta turned it over 12 times to Golden State's 8 and lost 68-64.

Game 2 is Monday at Chase Center, with Golden State up 1-0. The question for Atlanta is whether it can get its best weapon back, because the Dream also went 2 of 19 from the field in the fourth quarter of Game 1, and Golden State's late blocks came from four players other than Kiah Stokes.

Finals Game 2 at a glance

  • When: Monday, Oct. 19, at 5 p.m. PT
  • Where: Chase Center, San Francisco
  • TV and streaming: USA Network, CNBC and Peacock
  • Series: Golden State leads 1-0
  • Series odds: Valkyries -190, Dream +155 (DraftKings, checked Oct. 19 at 12:13 p.m. PT)
  • Game line: Valkyries -2.5, total 152.5 (DraftKings, checked Oct. 19 at 12:13 p.m. PT)
  • Next: Game 3 is Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 5 p.m. PT at State Farm Arena in Atlanta (Valkyries schedule update, WNBA release on Games 3 and 4)

Injury report

As of the league's official injury report from Oct. 19 at 12:00 p.m. ET (9:00 a.m. PT) (WNBA injury report).

Atlanta: Brionna Jones (left leg) is out. She is the only player on either team's list.

Allisha Gray is not listed. She was listed available for Game 1 with a left-hand injury and played 33 minutes in her return. "I felt good playing out there. My finger felt good, was able to get through the physicality," Gray said after Game 1 (AP).

Golden State: No players are listed for Game 2. Iliana Rupert has been away from the team all season for a non-injury reason.

What happened in Game 1

Golden State won 68-64 by holding Atlanta scoreless over the final 3:12. Gabby Williams scored 8 of the Valkyries' last 9 points and finished with 26. Atlanta led 64-61 after Rhyne Howard's free throws at 3:12 and missed all seven of its field-goal attempts after that. Our Game 1 recap has the full sequence.

"Unfortunately, we had kind of one bad defensive quarter where we had a few breakdowns and then one bad offensive quarter in the fourth," Dream coach Karl Smesko said (USA Today).

The turnover battle flipped

Atlanta's playoff run was built on extra possessions. The Dream won the turnover count by 15 and 11 against Washington, then by 6, 9 and 3 against New York. In Game 1 they lost it by 4, and Golden State scored 17 points off Atlanta's 12 turnovers. Atlanta scored 8 off Golden State's 8 (WNBA box score).

Golden State also won the offensive glass 12-7. Add the turnover margin and the offensive-rebound margin together, and the Valkyries have come out ahead in all seven of their playoff games, including their one loss, to Dallas. Atlanta had been ahead in all five of its games before Saturday, and finished minus-9 in Game 1.

The turnover counts here are player turnovers from FCB's game files, which leave out team turnovers. Counting team turnovers, Golden State had 10, so the official count was 12-10, not 12-8. That's also why Atlanta's semifinal margin is plus-18 here and plus-19 in our Game 1 preview. One Finals game is a small sample, so this shows what changed on Saturday, not what will happen Monday.

That's the kind of series this was expected to be. In his Finals preview, Chris Gunther of Charting Hoops pointed out that both finalists are defense-first teams in a league where offenses usually win titles, and that both went exactly 18-5 after the Fourth of July. Extra possessions are how a defense-first team wins, which is why Atlanta losing that count in Game 1 matters.

The fourth quarter, and who protected the rim

Atlanta made 2 of 19 shots in the fourth quarter, missed all 7 of its threes and scored 8 points. Five of those 19 shots were blocked.

Stokes finished with 4 blocks, but all four came in the first half. The five fourth-quarter blocks came from four different players: Veronica Burton had two, and Cecilia Zandalasini, Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes had one each. Every one of them came close to the rim, including Zandalasini's block of a 5-foot pullup and Burton's second, on Gray's floater. Burton blocked Jordin Canada at 3:33 and Gray at 2:40, with Atlanta trying to protect a one-possession lead.

Gray went 0 for 7 in the fourth. Atlanta's starting guards, Gray, Howard and Canada, shot 11 of 42 for the game. If the Dream keep driving into the same help, they need to finish those plays or turn them into kickouts before the second defender arrives.

The odds and my pick

DraftKings has Golden State favored by 2.5 points in Game 2, with the Valkyries at -105 and the Dream +2.5 at -115. The moneyline is Golden State -135 and Atlanta +114. The total is 152.5, with the over at -108 and the under at -112. DraftKings opened Game 2 at Golden State -1.5 with a 151.5 total (DraftKings Network), so both numbers have gone up a point.

The series price is Valkyries -190 and Dream +155, per DraftKings. Prices were checked Oct. 19 at 12:13 p.m. PT and may change before tip-off.

My betting lean is the under 152.5. Game 1 finished with 132 points, 20.5 under this total, and neither team made more than a third of its shots. One game is a small sample, and Atlanta scored at least 85 in every playoff game before Saturday, so this is a lean, not a lock.

My pick is Golden State to win Game 2. The Valkyries have won the combined turnover and offensive-rebound count in all seven playoff games, and that edge doesn't depend on their shots falling.

21+. Gamble responsibly. 1-800-GAMBLER.

item.title: Eligible Valkyries players are in line for $60,000 each after the 2026 title
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Eligible Valkyries players are in line for $60,000 each after the 2026 title, up from $22,908. Finals MVP Gabby Williams is in line for $30,000 more.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Eligible Valkyries players are in line for $60,000 each after the 2026 title

By Ryan MoalemiUpdated November 4, 2026

Each eligible player on the Golden State Valkyries, who won the 2026 WNBA Finals 4-3, is in line for a $60,000 bonus, up from $22,908 per player in 2025. Eligible players on the runner-up Atlanta Dream are in line for $20,000 each. Gabby Williams, named Finals MVP after 30 points in the 68-63 Game 7, is in line for a separate $30,000 award, six times the $5,000 paid in 2025. The dollar figures are the bonus schedule in the agreement the league and the players' union signed in March. The team site is the source for the series result and the MVP. The agreement does not say the awards have been paid.

A year ago, winning the midseason Commissioner's Cup paid more than winning the title. Players on the 2025 Cup champion Indiana Fever could earn up to $30,000 each, according to Sportico. The new deal keeps the Cup at $30,000 per player and pays twice that for the championship.

2025 vs. 2026 playoff bonuses

Every playoff bonus at least doubled under the new deal, and the Finals MVP award grew sixfold. Here's each one, 2025 vs. 2026:

Bonus20252026Change
WNBA champion, per player$22,908$60,0002.6x
Finals runner-up, per player$8,521$20,0002.3x
Lost in semifinals, per player$3,435$10,0002.9x
Lost in first round, per player$1,778$5,0002.8x
Finals MVP$5,000$30,0006x

Sources: 2025 figures from the league's March 2026 summary of the deal; 2026 figures from the bonus table in the signed agreement. Methods: Change is the 2026 figure divided by the 2025 figure, rounded to one decimal.

What each Finals roster stands to earn

The agreement's bonus table counts 12 players per team. On that basis:

  • The champion's roster: $720,000 in title bonuses (12 x $60,000).
  • The runner-up's roster: $240,000 (12 x $20,000).
  • The gap between winning and losing: $40,000 per player, or $480,000 across a 12-player roster.

The Finals MVP award is listed as its own line in the agreement, separate from the team bonuses, and the table does not say one replaces the other. Under that reading, Finals MVP Gabby Williams would collect $90,000 in bonuses ($60,000 plus $30,000) if she also meets the team-bonus roster test. The table does not say how the award is handled if the MVP comes from the losing team, so that case is left out here. Nothing on the team site or in the agreement says either award has been paid.

Not every player who wore the jersey this season is automatically in line for a share. To earn a team bonus, a player must be on the team's regular-season roster on the last day of the regular season. If a player was on a playoff team's roster for two-thirds of its regular-season games but not on any roster on the final day, she gets $5,000 instead, as long as she did not earn a playoff team bonus with another team. The exact headcount on each Finals roster that qualifies has not been published.

Why neither Finals team gets Cup money

The 2026 Commissioner's Cup went to the New York Liberty, who beat the Las Vegas Aces 93-85 in the Cup final on June 30 at Barclays Center. Breanna Stewart was named the game's MVP. Under the agreement, that win was worth $30,000 per player for 12 Liberty players. The Aces got $10,000 each as the Cup runner-up, and Stewart also earned the separate $10,000 Cup MVP award.

Neither the Valkyries nor the Dream reached the Cup final, so neither team adds Cup team money to its playoff bonus this season. Using the agreement's 12-player basis, the Liberty's Cup pool was $360,000, half of the $720,000 the champion's roster is in line for.

Is "nearly tripled" right?

Close, but it rounds up. The AP described the $60,000 title bonus as "nearly triple" last year's amount. The actual ratio is 2.6 times. The larger multipliers are lower in the table: semifinal bonuses are up 2.9 times, first-round bonuses 2.8 times, and the Finals MVP award is up six times.

Last year's numbers were already a raise. The 2024 champion New York Liberty got $20,825 per player. When the Finals moved from best-of-five to best-of-seven in 2025, the league raised the pool, and each Las Vegas Aces player got $22,908, Sportico reported. Some outlets still list $20,825 as the 2025 figure. That is the 2024 amount.

How the bonus compares to salaries

The agreement sets the 2026 minimum salary at $270,000 to $300,000, depending on years of service, and the league projects an average salary of $583,000. A $60,000 title bonus is 20% to 22% of a minimum contract and about 10% of the average.

Playoff bonuses are paid in addition to salary. Starting in 2027, every amount in the bonus table rises or falls at the same rate as the salary cap. The full 2026 schedule, including the Commissioner's Cup and individual awards like MVP and All-WNBA, totals $3 million.

What's next

Game 1: Valkyries 68, Dream 64 (Oct. 17); Game 2: Dream 79, Valkyries 65 (Oct. 19); Game 3: Dream 97, Valkyries 71 (Oct. 21); Game 4: Valkyries 67, Dream 62 (Oct. 24); Game 5: Valkyries 64, Dream 55 (Oct. 26); Game 6: Dream 80, Valkyries 69 (Oct. 29); Game 7: Valkyries 68, Dream 63 (Oct. 31). The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.
The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.

The Valkyries and the City of San Francisco set the championship parade for Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, from noon to 2 p.m. along the Embarcadero, starting at the Ferry Building and ending at King and 2nd Street.

Attendance for every Finals game since 2002 is in our WNBA Finals tracker and database.

Sources

  • Aces vs. Liberty, Commissioner's Cup final, June 30, 2026: game summary (WNBA.com)
  • 2026 WNBA champions, Finals results and parade (Golden State Valkyries, checked Nov. 4, 2026)
  • Key elements of the tentative collective bargaining agreement (WNBA, March 2026)
  • A landmark 7-year WNBA labor deal moves forward with a signed term sheet (AP, March 2026)
  • WNBA Finals bonus pay: champions see raise for best-of-7 victory (Sportico, 2025)
  • Caitlin Clark questions Commissioner's Cup, playoff payout disparity (Sportico, July 2025)

item.title: Goapele, Rita Moreno and Larry June set for Valkyries' Finals Game 1; Alanis Morissette sings before Game 2
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Who performs at Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals Games 1 and 2 at Chase Center: Goapele, Rita Moreno, Larry June, Alanis Morissette, Too $hort and LaRussell.
item.content:encoded:
WNBAFull Court Buckets

Goapele, Rita Moreno and Larry June set for Valkyries' Finals Game 1; Alanis Morissette sings before Game 2

By Ryan MoalemiUpdated November 4, 2026

Alanis Morissette sang the national anthem before WNBA Finals Game 2 at Chase Center on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, and Too $hort hit the pregame drum, E! News reported. Vallejo rapper LaRussell was announced for halftime, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

  • Game 2: anthem and drum per E! News (anthem also reported by SFGate). Halftime: LaRussell was announced in the San Francisco Chronicle report of Oct. 16, 2026; Full Court Buckets has not located an occurrence record for that set as of Oct. 19, 2026, 8:45 p.m. PT. The Dream won 79-65 to tie the series 1-1 (WNBA.com game record).
  • Game 1 (Oct. 17): Goapele sang the anthem, Rita Moreno hit the drum and Larry June performed at halftime, NBC Bay Area reported. The Valkyries won 68-64 (WNBA.com game record).
  • Series result, checked Nov. 4, 2026: the Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA Finals, 4-3. The team site lists Game 7 as Valkyries 68, Dream 63, and names Gabby Williams Finals MVP after 30 points in that game (Valkyries playoffs page).
  • That page set the championship parade for Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, noon to 2 p.m., along the Embarcadero from the Ferry Building to King and 2nd Street.

Oakland singer Goapele was announced to sing the national anthem before Game 1 of the WNBA Finals on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, at Chase Center, with Rita Moreno on the pregame drum and San Francisco rapper Larry June at halftime. For Game 2 on Monday, Oct. 19, Alanis Morissette sang the anthem and Too $hort took the drum, E! News reported. Vallejo rapper LaRussell was announced for halftime by the San Francisco Chronicle and the Mercury News on the night of Oct. 16. This page still has no separate occurrence record for that set.

All six have Bay Area ties, and the drum job comes with history: the Valkyries have handed the mallet to selected guests such as Angela Davis, Megan Rapinoe and Eileen Gu to start the "G! S! V!" chant before home games.

The lineup

Announced pregame and halftime lineup for Games 1 and 2 at Chase Center, per the San Francisco Chronicle (Oct. 16, 2026). Status as of Oct. 19, 2026, 8:45 p.m. PT.
Game 1: Sat. Oct. 17Game 2: Mon. Oct. 19
Tipoff12:30 p.m. PT5 p.m. PT
TVNBC, PeacockUSA Network, CNBC, Peacock
National anthemGoapeleAlanis Morissette
Pregame GSV DrumRita MorenoToo $hort
HalftimeLarry JuneLaRussell
StatusAll three appearances happened, per NBC Bay AreaAnthem and drum happened, per E! News; halftime announced (Chronicle), not independently confirmed

Both games are at Chase Center in San Francisco against the No. 4 Atlanta Dream. The WNBA's Finals preview lists CNBC for Game 2 alongside USA Network and Peacock; the Valkyries' schedule lists USA and Peacock.

Who's performing

Goapele is a Grammy-nominated R&B singer from Oakland. She already has a role with the team: the Valkyries named her to the Valkyries Collective, the group of Bay Area ambassadors the franchise announced before its first season.

Rita Moreno is an EGOT winner, meaning she has won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony. The Chronicle describes her as a longtime Berkeley resident.

Larry June is a San Francisco rapper.

Alanis Morissette has lived in the Bay Area for several years, according to the Chronicle. Her 1995 album "Jagged Little Pill" made her a star.

Too $hort is the Oakland rap pioneer. He has done this gig on the other side: the Las Vegas Aces booked him for halftime of Game 2 of the 2023 Finals in Las Vegas. E! News reported that he drummed before Game 2 for the team that had swept the Aces in the semifinals.

LaRussell is a rapper from Vallejo.

Why the drum matters at Chase Center

The pregame drum is the Valkyries' signature home-game ritual. A guest swings a mallet at a bass drum, and the crowd answers each hit with a letter: "G! S! V!" The New York Times described Angela Davis doing it in 2025. Megan Rapinoe took a turn in the team's first season, and Olympic skier Eileen Gu banged it at the 2026 home opener, according to the team's own announcement. Giving the first two Finals drum slots to Moreno and Too $hort keeps the ritual in local hands.

The crowd they'll play to

NBC Bay Area reported, before the Finals, that the Valkyries had sold out every home game they had played. The series is over. Full Court Buckets' Finals attendance tracker, using the WNBA.com game pages, lists 18,064 at each Chase Center Finals game (Games 1, 2, 5 and 7) and 17,099 at each State Farm Arena game (Games 3, 4 and 6). The seven-game total is 123,553, which passes the prior record of 92,599 from the five-game 2024 Finals.

Tickets have not been cheap. Bay City News reported Friday that the lowest Game 1 price on Ticketmaster's resale market was over $250, and KQED listed Game 1 seats from $223 to more than $1,300. All fans at Game 1 get a violet "This is Ballhalla" T-shirt, the team says.

The series

This is the Valkyries' first Finals, in their second season, and the team says no other franchise has reached the Finals that fast. Golden State went 32-12, beat Dallas 2-1 in the first round and swept the defending champion Aces.

Atlanta comes in on a franchise-best 10-game winning streak. The Dream swept Washington and New York, and they went 30-14 in the regular season. Atlanta was also the league's previous expansion team before Golden State, and it went 4-30 in its 2008 debut, according to the Valkyries' preview. The Dream have reached the Finals three times before (2010, 2011 and 2013) and were swept each time, per WNBA.com.

Golden State won all three regular-season meetings, but the last one was July 4, before Atlanta added DeWanna Bonner. Dream guard Allisha Gray missed the last two semifinal games with a left-hand injury and was listed day-to-day this week.

Those dates have passed. The Valkyries won the series 4-3, with Game 7 on Oct. 31 at Chase Center, 68-63 (team results page). The pre-series picture above, including Atlanta's winning streak and Allisha Gray's day-to-day listing, is what was known when this lineup story was filed.

The lineup also circulated on TikTok Friday, including in a video from NBC Bay Area reporter Alyssa Goard (@alyssamgoard).

Attendance figures come from Full Court Buckets' own compiled data.

item.title: Gabby Williams scores 8 of the last 9 as Valkyries beat Dream 68-64 in Finals Game 1
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals on Saturday at Chase Center, and they did it by holding Atlanta scoreless for the final 3:12.
item.content:encoded:
newsFull Court Buckets

Gabby Williams scores 8 of the last 9 as Valkyries beat Dream 68-64 in Finals Game 1

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 17, 2026

The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals on Saturday at Chase Center, and they did it by holding Atlanta scoreless for the final 3:12. Gabby Williams scored 8 of Golden State's last 9 points, including the free throws at 1:18 that gave the Valkyries their first lead since the third quarter.

Every play from this game is on the Game 1 play-by-play page, searchable by player, quarter and play type. Game 2 plays will post on the Game 2 play-by-play page.

Atlanta led for most of the afternoon in front of a sellout crowd of 18,064. The Dream were up 64-61 with 3:12 left and never scored again. Golden State now leads the best-of-seven series 1-0, and it has beaten Atlanta in all four meetings this season, counting three regular-season wins.

The last 3:12

Rhyne Howard hit two free throws at 3:12 to make it 64-61 Dream. That was Atlanta's last point.

Williams answered right away. She had already scored on a running layup at 3:22, and at 2:15 she made two free throws to cut it to 64-63. At 1:21 Allisha Gray missed a driving layup, Williams grabbed the rebound and drew a foul on Angel Reese. Two more free throws, 65-64 Valkyries.

Atlanta still had chances. Howard missed a 25-foot three at 1:09. Reese then stole the ball from Williams with 46.1 seconds left, but Naz Hillmon missed a 26-foot three at 25.9. Kiah Stokes rebounded, got fouled and made 1 of 2 at 23.8 for a 66-64 lead.

Gray missed a 25-footer at 7.9 that would have won it. Howard fouled on purpose at 4.1, Williams made both, and Gray's step-back three at 2.1 missed. Atlanta missed all seven of its field-goal attempts after the 3:12 mark.

How it got there

This was a game of runs. Golden State went on a 9-0 burst in the first quarter to lead 14-11, then Atlanta closed the quarter on an 11-0 run to go up 22-14.

The Valkyries flipped it in the second. They won that quarter 28-17, with a 10-0 run from 3:43 to 1:29 that turned a 37-32 deficit into a 42-37 lead. It was 42-39 Golden State at the half.

Then the Valkyries went cold. They scored 9 points in the third quarter. Atlanta scored the first 5 points of the second half, Howard hit a 27-foot running jumper, and Isobel Borlase's jumper at 4:27 made it 50-44. Golden State answered with a 7-0 run, capped by a Laeticia Amihere layup for a 51-50 lead at 2:58. Atlanta closed on an 8-0 run that carried into the fourth, and Howard's free throws at 9:07 made it 58-51.

From there, Atlanta made two field goals the rest of the way: a Hillmon layup at 7:16 and a Jordin Canada jumper at 4:23. Golden State won the fourth quarter 17-8.

The numbers that decided it

Neither team could shoot. Golden State made 25 of 78 shots (32%) and 7 of 33 threes. Atlanta made 21 of 64 (33%) and 4 of 25 threes (16%). The 132 combined points came in well under the 154.5 DraftKings total listed in our preview.

21+. Gamble responsibly. 1-800-GAMBLER.

Three numbers explain why the worse-shooting team on the scoreboard still won:

  • Turnovers. Atlanta turned it over 12 times, and Golden State scored 17 points off them. The Dream scored 8 off Golden State's mistakes.
  • Second chances. The Valkyries grabbed 12 offensive rebounds to Atlanta's 7. Kaila Charles had 10 rebounds, and three of them came on the defensive glass in the final 67 seconds.
  • Rim protection. Golden State blocked 10 shots. Stokes had 4.

Williams finished with 26 points on 8-of-22 shooting, made 7 of 8 free throws and was +16 in 33 minutes. Gray led Atlanta with 19 points and went 8-for-8 at the line, but shot 5 of 19 from the field. Reese had 14 points and 12 rebounds, 5 of them offensive. Howard scored 12 on 3-of-14 shooting.

Atlanta's three starting guards, Gray, Howard and Canada, went 11 of 42 combined. One game is a small sample, but that is the clearest gap Golden State created.

What's next

My preview picked Atlanta to win Game 1 and Dream +2.5 as a betting lean. Both missed, since Atlanta lost by four.

Game 2 is Monday, Oct. 19, at 5 p.m. PT at Chase Center, on USA Network, CNBC and Peacock.

My pick is Golden State in Game 2. The Valkyries won Game 1 while making just 21% of their threes, because their offensive rebounding and shot blocking didn't depend on shots falling.

TV: NBC · Stream: Peacock

item.content:encoded:
WNBA PlayoffsFull Court Buckets

2026 WNBA Finals schedule: Dream vs. Valkyries results, TV and tip times

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 16, 2026

WNBA Finals schedule and results

The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.

GameDateMatchupResult or tip timeLinks
Game 1Oct. 17Dream at ValkyriesFinal: Valkyries 68, Dream 64Recap · Play-by-play
Game 2Oct. 19Dream at ValkyriesFinal: Dream 79, Valkyries 65Recap · Play-by-play
Game 3Oct. 21Valkyries at DreamFinal: Dream 97, Valkyries 71Recap · Play-by-play
Game 4Oct. 24Valkyries at DreamFinal: Valkyries 67, Dream 62Recap · Play-by-play
Game 5Oct. 26Dream at ValkyriesFinal: Valkyries 64, Dream 55Recap · Play-by-play
Game 6Oct. 29Valkyries at DreamFinal: Dream 80, Valkyries 69Recap · Play-by-play
Game 7Oct. 31Dream at ValkyriesFinal: Valkyries 68, Dream 63Recap · Play-by-play

The best-of-seven series uses a 2-2-1-1-1 format, with Golden State holding home court. On Oct. 13 the league moved Games 3 and 4 to State Farm Arena, moved Game 3 up from Thursday, Oct. 22, to Wednesday, Oct. 21, and moved Game 4’s tip from 12:30 PM PT to 10:00 AM PT (WNBA release). The league said the change “dramatically expands the seating capacity.”

Written before the series, October 16, 2026

The WNBA Finals start Saturday, Oct. 17, at 12:30 PM PT, when the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries host the No. 4 Atlanta Dream at Chase Center in San Francisco (NBC and Peacock). Both teams swept their semifinals on Oct. 9, so the league will crown a first-time champion.

The number that stands out in FCB’s Finals database: Atlanta is 0-9 in Finals games. Its last Finals home game, in 2013, drew 5,040 at the Gwinnett Center. This time Games 3 and 4 are at State Farm Arena, and Gray’s status for Saturday is still open.

How both teams got here

Dream 85, Liberty 83 (Brooklyn). Atlanta finished a 3-0 sweep and reached its first Finals since 2013. Jordin Canada had 19 points and 11 assists with no turnovers, Angel Reese had 22 points and 9 rebounds, and Rhyne Howard scored 21. Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones scored 26 each for New York. Read the full recap.

Valkyries 87, Aces 77, OT (Las Vegas). Golden State won overtime 16-6 to sweep the defending champions. Kayla Thornton scored 18, Gabby Williams had 16 with 3 steals, and Kiah Stokes went 5 for 5 for 11 points and 10 rebounds. Tiffany Hayes added 11. A’ja Wilson scored 21 on 6-of-19 shooting. Read the full recap.

The Valkyries got here in their second season, the fastest an expansion team has reached the Finals. Final seeds are on our standings page.

Allisha Gray is day-to-day

Allisha Gray, Atlanta’s leading scorer at 19.0 points a game, is day-to-day after a minor procedure on her left hand. She hurt it in Game 1 of the semifinals and played 11 minutes in that series. She was a full participant in practice on Friday, Oct. 16, after a limited session Thursday, and said she felt good, but the Dream want to see how her hand handles game pace before deciding on Saturday (USA TODAY’s Meghan L. Hall, via RotoWire, Oct. 16). Earlier reporting: USA TODAY, Oct. 15.

Five things FCB’s box-score data shows

FCB compiles its data from official box scores. These come from three regular-season games and five or six playoff games per team, so treat them as context, not predictions.

1. Golden State won the season series with threes. The Valkyries made 33 threes to Atlanta’s 18 across the three meetings, a 45-point edge from beyond the arc in a series they won by a combined 19. Atlanta had more offensive rebounds in all three games (31 to 20 overall).

2. The season series is old. The last meeting was July 4, when Atlanta was 12-9 and on a five-game losing streak. The Dream finished 30-14, have lost once since Aug. 18 and arrive on a franchise-best 10-game winning streak.

3. Atlanta has the bigger playoff margin. The Dream are 5-0, scoring 92.6 points a game and allowing 83.0 (+9.6). The Valkyries are 5-1, scoring 87.0 and allowing 79.8 (+7.2), so the Valkyries allow fewer points and the Dream score more.

4. Atlanta has owned the finishes. Across their five playoff games, the Dream outscored opponents by 16 in fourth quarters and overtime. Golden State is minus-3 in the same stretch over six games, though it’s 1-1 in overtime, losing at Dallas and winning at Las Vegas. Both teams are unbeaten in playoff games decided by three points or fewer (Atlanta 2-0, Golden State 1-0).

5. The crowd gap is about 2 to 1. Chase Center drew 18,064 for both regular-season meetings and all four Golden State home playoff games. The July 4 game in College Park, at Gateway Center, drew 3,596. Atlanta’s three home playoff games at State Farm Arena averaged 9,695.

The awards on the floor

Reese is the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year, the first Dream player to win it (WNBA release). Williams finished second in that vote. Reese, Howard and Williams all made the All-Defensive First Team. Wilson, whose Aces Golden State just eliminated, won a record fifth MVP and became the first player to win three in a row.

What FCB’s Finals data says about the crowds

FCB compiles its data from official box scores. Three numbers frame this series:

  • Chase Center has drawn 18,064 for all four of Golden State’s 2026 home playoff games.
  • Atlanta’s three Finals home games before this year drew 10,522 (2010), 11,543 (2011) and 5,040 (2013).
  • The prior record for a single Finals is 92,599 total, set in 2024 (18,520 a game).

Two sold-out Chase Center games would put the series at 36,128 before it reaches Atlanta. Whether the Finals pass the prior record of 92,599 depends on how many games are played and what State Farm Arena draws for Games 3 and 4. We’ll log every game in the Finals attendance database, which is free to cite.

The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3. Game 7 (Oct. 31): Valkyries 68, Dream 63. Game 7 drew 18,064 at Chase Center. Through 7 games with reported attendance the Finals have drawn 123,553 combined. That passes the prior record of 92,599, set in 2024 over 5 games.

  • Game 4 source: official WNBA.com box score for Game 4 (attendance 17,099, sellout), matching the official scorer’s report (final box), checked Oct. 25, 2026, 8:00 a.m. PT. Combined reported attendance through four games: 70,326 (18,064 + 18,064 + 17,099 + 17,099). The prior record to tie was 92,599 across five games in 2024 (FCB Finals attendance CSV, each row linked to its official game record); 92,599 (the prior record) − 70,326 = 22,273.
  • Game 3 source: official WNBA.com game record for Game 3; the 17,099 attendance (sellout) is from the official scorer’s report (final box), checked Oct. 22, 2026, 8:30 a.m. PT. Game 1 (Valkyries 68, Dream 64, Oct. 17) and Game 2 (Dream 79, Valkyries 65, Oct. 19) each drew 18,064 at Chase Center (Game 1 box score, Game 2 box score). Combined reported attendance through three games: 53,227.
  • Atlanta record: the earlier Finals games hosted by the Dream drew 10,522 (2010 Game 3, game record), 11,543 (2011 Game 3, game record) and 5,040 (2013 Game 3 at Gwinnett Center, game record).
  • Audience: Game 1 averaged 2.1 million viewers on NBC and Peacock, peaking at 3.0 million (NBC Sports release); Game 2 averaged 1.33 million on USA Network, CNBC, E! and Peacock (USA Sports release); Game 3 averaged 1.71 million on USA Network, CNBC and Peacock (USA Sports release); Game 4 averaged 1.9 million on NBC and Peacock, peaking at 2.5 million (NBC Sports release); Game 5 averaged 1.43 million on USA Network, CNBC and Peacock (WNBA.com, Nov. 4, 2026); Game 6's final average is 1.49 million viewers across USA Network, E!, and SYFY, plus streaming led by Peacock (Sports Media Watch, Nov. 3, 2026). USA Sports on Oct. 31, 2026 reported 1.5 million for that live window (USA Sports release), up 4% vs. last year's series-clinching game (LV-PHX Game 4), based on Nielsen panel-only data and digital data from Adobe Analytics. No peak was released. The same release calls the Game 6 coverage the fifth most-watched WNBA Finals game on cable on record, and 1.7 million viewers once the 8 p.m. ET encore on USA Network and CNBC is included. Myles Ehrlich quoted the USA Sports note on X the same day. Game 7 drew 3.3 million viewers on USA Network and CNBC, plus streaming led by Peacock (USA Sports release, Nov. 3, 2026), based on Nielsen Panel + Big Data and digital data from Adobe Analytics. No peak was released. USA Sports called it the most-watched WNBA playoff game ever. WNBA.com on Nov. 4, 2026 reports the seven-game series averaged 1.88 million viewers, the most since 1999 and up 30 percent from 2025, and the postseason at 1.49 million viewers, up 27 percent from 2025, the most-watched postseason since the inaugural 1997 season. Sports Media Watch reports the Game 7 audience at 3.28 million, the most-watched WNBA playoff game on record and a cable record. USA Network's hour-long postgame show averaged 1.0 million viewers, kept separate from the game average.
  • the 2026 Finals averaged 1.88M viewers, the most since 1999 (WNBA.com, Nov. 4, 2026).
  • The Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA championship, 4-3.
  • The prior record, the highest Finals series attendance in FCB's 2002–2025 database, is 92,599, across five games in 2024. The single-game high is 22,076, reached in 2003 Game 3 and 2007 Game 5 (FCB Finals attendance CSV, each row linked to its official game record).

How this is calculated

R = prior record (92,599). C = combined reported attendance of completed 2026 Finals games (pending reports count as unknown, not zero). g = remaining future games in the selected series length. To tie: R − C. To exceed: R − C + 1, the exact required total. Approximate average across g games: (R − C + 1) ÷ g, shown to two decimals. A uniform whole-number target rounds that up, which is sufficient but not the minimum possible average. With no remaining games the result is final; no per-game target is shown.

What the numbers say

  • The prior record, the highest WNBA Finals series total in this 2002–2025 database, is 92,599 combined reported attendance, over five games in 2024 (18,520 average). It is also the highest average per game in the database, and 10,581 above No. 2 by total (2009).Scope: Finals archive: through 2025🔗 Copy link
  • Scenario, not a forecast: under the default assumptions, a seven-game 2026 Finals would total 123,553, 33.4% more than the prior record, 2024’s 92,599, while averaging 17,650 per game, 4.7% below 2024’s 18,520. A longer series can pass the total without a bigger average crowd.Scope: Finals archive: through 2025; 2026 Finals: through Game 7; scenario uses default assumptions🔗 Copy link
  • The largest single-game Finals attendance since 2002 is 22,076, reported twice, both in Detroit (2003 G3, 2007 G5).Scope: Finals archive: through 2025🔗 Copy link
  • Five WNBA Finals games since 2002 have gone to overtime in this database (2005 G2, 2009 G1, 2021 G2, 2024 G1, 2024 G5).Scope: Finals archive: through 2025🔗 Copy link
  • The 2026 WNBA playoffs had three overtime games before the Finals (First Round DAL–GSV G2, Semis GSV–LVA G3, Semis ATL–NYL G2).Scope: 2026 playoffs: through semifinals🔗 Copy link
  • Finals games from 2002 to 2025 have a combined reported attendance of 1,191,363 across the 90 games with published attendance. This sums game figures; it is not a count of unique people.Scope: Finals archive: through 2025🔗 Copy link

item.title: How the Valkyries’ league-best defense takes away the next option, not just the first
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Golden State led the WNBA with a 99.1 defensive rating. Film of Caitlin Clark and Breanna Stewart possessions shows the help, recovery and box-outs behind it.
item.content:encoded:
WNBAFull Court Buckets

How the Valkyries’ league-best defense takes away the next option, not just the first

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 14, 2026

Golden State finished the 2026 regular season 32-12 with the WNBA’s best defensive rating, 99.1 points allowed per 100 possessions, then held A’ja Wilson to 41.1% shooting in a semifinal sweep of Las Vegas (she shot 52.7% in the regular season). Two possessions, one against Caitlin Clark’s Fever and one against Breanna Stewart’s Liberty, show how: the first rotation takes away the easy play, and the next defender is already moving before the offense finds the second one. That habit is what Atlanta has to beat starting with Game 1 of the Finals on Saturday, Oct. 17.

  • 99.1 regular-season defensive rating, 1st in the WNBA (team release)
  • 104.1 playoff defensive rating, 2nd behind Atlanta’s 102.0 (same release)
  • 79.8 points allowed per playoff game, fewest (same release)
  • 41.1% Wilson’s field-goal percentage against Golden State in the semis, down from 52.7% in the regular season (same release)

Jump to: Early offense · Middle offense · Finishing the stop · How offenses can attack it · What it means for the Finals

Small-sample note: the film covers two possessions. They show habits, not how often each coverage works. The season numbers above are the evidence for the overall result.

Film credit: breakdown by Jeremy Lin (@jlin7 on TikTok, posted Sept. 16, 2026; also on Instagram). The clips are described here. This page does not embed the video or republish stills.

Three phases of the same habit.
PhaseWhat Golden State doesWhat the offense loses
Early offenseGets bodies between the ball and the rimThe clean transition drive
Middle offenseHelps on the first action, then resets as the ball movesThe easy roll pass and the next driving lane
Finishing the stopFinds the rebound threat before chasing the ballA simple second chance

1. Early offense: take away the first clean drive

In Golden State’s 79-60 win at New York on Aug. 27 (Valkyries up 46-34, 7:20 left in the third quarter), Stewart catches in transition with room to attack. By the time she squares up, Golden State’s retreating defenders are between her and the rim, so driving means driving into traffic. She passes, New York swings it, and the possession ends in a corner three.

That’s a win for the defense in one specific way: it removed the first clean option and made the Liberty use more passes. Whether a corner three is a good trade depends on the shooter and the contest, and the clip alone can’t settle that.

What to watch: where the defenders land as the ball is caught. If those first steps are late, help never matters.

2. Middle offense: help, recover, help again

In Golden State’s 88-75 win at Indiana on July 15 (Valkyries up 20-18 in the second quarter), Clark runs a pick-and-roll, moves the ball, gets it back and attacks a closeout. Golden State has to defend four actions in one trip.

The weak-side I puts help at two depths

As Clark comes off the screen, one helper sits at the nail (the middle of the free-throw line) and another sits low near the rim. The higher one discourages a middle drive. The lower one protects the rim and the roller. With both jobs covered, the pocket pass to the screener isn’t there, and Clark swings it across the floor. The diagram at the top of this story is that shape. The spots are a schematic, not tracking data.

The skip pass starts the next job

A skip pass is supposed to beat the first layer of help. Here it doesn’t, because Tiffany Hayes gets back toward the nail while Indiana attacks off the catch. The ball goes back to Clark, now attacking a defender closing out on her.

Clark attacks the closeout and finds another crowd

Clark drives the gap and three nearby Valkyries shrink her shot and passing windows. The trip ends in a turnover. The shape looks like a triangle in that moment. One clip isn’t enough to call it a zone or a standard coverage.

3. Finish the stop: find a body before chasing the ball

Back to the Liberty possession. When the corner three goes up, three Golden State defenders turn to find their man first. Two of them put bodies on Stewart, and Kiah Stokes collects the miss.

Stokes gets the rebound in the box score. Her teammates made it available. That matters against Atlanta, which our Game 1 preview shows wins with pressure while Golden State wins on the glass.

The personnel behind it

The team’s September awards case names Gabby Williams and Veronica Burton as its perimeter defensive leaders and Stokes as the backline anchor. That Sept. 23 release listed her second in the league with 73 blocks. She finished the regular season second, with 74 blocks in 43 games. In both clips the decisive defender, Hayes recovering or a teammate pinning Stewart, never touches the ball.

How an offense can attack it

These are my reads from the spacing in the clips, not plays shown in the video.

  • Move it before help resets. Catch-and-shoot or catch-and-drive right away, before the helper reaches the nail.
  • Make the weak-side helper choose. A cut behind her, timed with the drive, makes her guard two things. Cut too early and you just add a body to the lane.
  • Use the screener as a passer. If the roll is covered, the short roll puts the decision in the screener’s hands.
  • Punish help with shooting and a surprise rebounder. It costs transition defense at the other end.

What it means for the Finals

My pick (as of Oct. 14): Atlanta’s best path is the first counter, quick decisions before Golden State’s second rotation arrives. The Dream had the playoffs’ best defensive rating (102.0), so this series is likely to be decided by which offense creates a clean second option. Follow the numbers game by game in our 2026 WNBA Finals ratings tracker and the Valkyries team page.

Season and playoff figures: Golden State Valkyries team releases (Sept. 23 and Oct. 13, 2026), checked Oct. 14, 2026 PT. Film concept credit: Jeremy Lin (@jlin7), Sept. 16, 2026. Game results gathered and verified by Full Court Buckets. Clip scores and records were read from the broadcast scorebugs in the video. Diagrams are original Full Court Buckets illustrations.

item.title: Liberty lost the turnover battle by 18 in the sweep. Here are 5 moves I'd make as GM
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Atlanta swept the Liberty while shooting 42.0% to New York's 47.1%. The gap was 18 turnovers. Five offseason moves I would make.
item.content:encoded:
Opinion and roster analysis

Liberty lost the turnover battle by 18 in the sweep. Here are 5 moves I'd make as GM

By Ryan MoalemiUpdated November 4, 2026

Fast Facts for Media & Citations

  • Team field-goal percentage: New York Liberty 47.1%, Atlanta Dream 42.0%.
  • Series turnover margin: New York -18 (45 turnovers to 27).
  • Series result: Atlanta sweeps 3-0. Game 3: Dream 85, Liberty 83.

Updated October 13, 2026: The Stewart contract report now cites Newsweek, because the Sports Condensed page did not return the article.

Updated November 4, 2026: The head-coaching seat is open. The note is under the series table. Contract and draft figures below are still the Oct. 12 set.

Atlanta swept the New York Liberty in the semifinals, 92-82, 101-98 in overtime, and 85-83, while shooting worse, 42.0% to 47.1%. The Dream attempted 33 more shots. New York committed 18 more turnovers and collected nine fewer offensive rebounds. Three games are a small sample. The five moves are: keep the five, trade for Elizabeth Williams, give Pauline Astier and Marine Fauthoux a real share of the offense, draft Oluchi Okananwa, and set spending limits before the last spots are filled.

I would keep Sabrina Ionescu, Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones, Satou Sabally, and Leonie Fiebich, offer a second-round pick for Williams, play Astier and Fauthoux beside Ionescu, use the No. 8 pick on Okananwa if she is available, and set the budget before filling the rest of the roster.

Totals across three games, the same counts as the semifinal table lower on this page. Effective field-goal percentage, turnover percentage, offensive-rebound percentage, and free-throw rate are not in this story, so they are not shown.
MeasureNew York LibertyAtlanta Dream
Field-goal percentage47.1%42.0%
Turnovers4527
Turnover margin-18+18
Series resultSwept, 0-3Sweep, 3-0
Game 38385
Download CSV

Free to use and republish (CC0).

The head-coaching seat is open

The Associated Press reported that the Liberty announced on Nov. 3, 2026 that they had fired head coach Chris DeMarco after one season. He arrived in December from the Golden State Warriors staff and had no prior WNBA experience, the AP reported, and he was under contract for 2027. Jonathan Kolb did not keep Sandy Brondello after 2025, so this is the franchise's third head coach in three seasons and Kolb's fourth coaching search since 2019, according to that report. Checked Nov. 4, the Liberty staff directory still listed DeMarco as head coach and did not name a replacement. The five moves below were written on Oct. 12. The instruction to the coaching staff in move 3 is for whoever is hired next.

1. Keep the five and address the lost possessions

Sabrina Ionescu, Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones, Satou Sabally, and Leonie Fiebich would all return. The case for keeping them starts with what happened against the Atlanta Dream.

Totals across three games; Game 2 includes overtime; turnovers are team totals.
2026 semifinal totalsLibertyDream
Field goals90 of 19194 of 224
Field-goal percentage47.1%42.0%
Turnovers4527
Offensive rebounds2029
Download CSV

Free to use and republish (CC0).

Jonquel Jones had 26 points and 14 rebounds in the elimination game. I would look for someone who can cover her rest minutes before shopping her. Sabally's return would also change the available lineups. The Liberty ruled her out for the rest of the season after a concussion (AP), so this plan depends on her being medically cleared.

2. Offer a second-round pick for Elizabeth Williams

My opening offer to the Chicago Sky would be the 2027 No. 23 pick for Elizabeth Williams. My ceiling would be that pick plus New York's 2028 third-rounder. I would walk away if the Sky required a first-round pick.

Williams is under contract for a listed $600,000 cap hit in 2027, the figure that counts against the salary cap rather than base salary, then an unrestricted free agent, according to the Her Hoop Stats WNBA Salary Cap Database. This would require a trade and sufficient cap room. She is not a free agent New York can simply sign.

I would ask her to screen, protect the rim, and give Jonquel Jones roughly 12 dependable minutes on an ordinary night. She would play mainly beside Breanna Stewart or Satou Sabally, keeping shooting around a center whose job is to work near the basket.

Chicago's reason to consider it would be a younger, cheaper roster spot and more spending flexibility around Kamilla Cardoso and Azura Stevens, who are both on the Sky's 2027 sheet. But Williams is useful depth for Chicago too. I have no reporting that Chicago wants to move her.

If the trade fails, I would keep No. 23, draft frontcourt help, and let Han Xu compete for the backup-center job. Williams is my preferred upgrade, not a move worth forcing.

3. Give Astier and Fauthoux a real share of the offense

I would make Pauline Astier a re-signing priority and start camp with Marine Fauthoux in the regular rotation. Fauthoux's 20 points and four assists in Game 2 were encouraging. She followed that with 9 points on 4-of-8 shooting in Game 3. One excellent game does not establish her as the answer at point guard, but it earns her a longer audition.

My instruction to the coaching staff would be to keep one of those guards on the floor whenever Sabrina Ionescu sits. Let Fauthoux or Astier bring the ball up against pressure, then use Ionescu coming off a screen or taking a handoff. That gives Sabrina more chances to attack a moving defense and gives opponents another ballhandler to account for.

Through the first 15 games, I would compare turnover rate, assist-to-turnover ratio, and offensive efficiency in lineups pairing Ionescu with another point guard. If those groups cannot protect the ball, I would revisit veteran point guards. Until then, I would put the available money toward the frontcourt.

4. Draft Okananwa and keep a rebounding prospect in view

My first-round preference is Oluchi Okananwa, subject to her senior season, draft entry, and availability. Maryland's October 1 update credits her with 17.8 points per game and 74 steals in 33 games last season (2.2 steals per game) (Maryland athletics). Her school biography also lists All-Big Ten Defensive Team honors.

I would develop her as the guard who picks up a quick opposing ballhandler early and fights through screens. Against Atlanta, that could mean an assignment on Jordin Canada, freeing Leonie Fiebich to spend more time on Rhyne Howard. College steals do not guarantee that she can handle that job in the WNBA. How well she gets around screens and makes open shots would decide her minutes.

The Oct. 1 salary sheet lists New York's 2027 picks by round and does not lock the numbers. The current board has the Liberty at 8, 23, and 38, and New York still holds each of those picks (Tankathon; WNBAGM, data as of Oct. 12). Picks 1 through 7 are a lottery, so No. 8 is the first selection after it.

At No. 38, I would have NC State forward Khamil Pierre on the board if she remains available. Her 2025-26 line shows 11.9 rebounds per game, including 108 offensive rebounds in 32 games, and 1 of 6 from three (Sports-Reference). That three-point volume raises a spacing question, so I would treat her as a development candidate. A full college season remains before either selection becomes a serious draft-night decision.

2027 contract status on this page

Reported status only. The planning amounts later in this story ($950,000, $400,000, $300,000, and the $7,474,516 total) are the author's budgets, not reported contracts, and they stay in that table.
ItemStatusFigure on this pageWhere this page credits it
2027 salary capNot a published dollar figure on this pageUnavailableHer Hoop Stats WNBA Salary Cap Database, updated Oct. 1, 2026; USA Today
Six listed 2027 cap hitsListed on the Oct. 1 sheet$5,224,516Her Hoop Stats, Oct. 1, 2026
Breanna Stewart, 2026 cap hitDescribed as a three-year standard max that rises if the cap rises$1,190,000 (17% of that page's $7 million cap)Newsweek, April 17, 2026
Elizabeth Williams, 2027 cap hitUnder contract with Chicago, then an unrestricted free agent. A trade in this piece, not a signed Liberty deal.$600,000Her Hoop Stats
Pauline Astier and Han XuReserved. They can only re-sign with New York.No dollar figure listedOct. 1 sheet
Marine JohannesRestricted free agentNo dollar figure listedOct. 1 sheet
Manuela PuochUnsigned 2026 third-rounder$288,600 scale figure for 2027Oct. 1 sheet
Download CSV

Free to use and republish (CC0).

5. Set spending limits before filling the last six spots

After six listed 2027 cap hits totaling $5,224,516, the money left for the other spots is still unknown, because the 2027 cap is not a published dollar figure yet (Her Hoop Stats WNBA Salary Cap Database, updated October 1, 2026, 12:35 p.m. Eastern; USA Today).

My working budget for the proposed roster would be:

The first two lines are listed cap hits. The last three are my budgets, not reported offers or agreed salaries.
Roster allocationPlanning amount
Six returning cap hits as currently listed$5,224,516
Elizabeth Williams via proposed trade$600,000
Astier, Marine Johannes, and Han Xu combined$950,000
No. 8 pick allowance$400,000
Madison Scott, standard contract (a full roster deal)$300,000
Preliminary total for 12 players$7,474,516

The rookie contract must follow the applicable scale. The same sheet still shows the 2027 first-round figure as unset, so $400,000 is only my allowance. I would also seek at least $100,000 of cap room after the full roster is signed.

The Liberty sheet lists Stewart's 2026 cap hit at $1,190,000, 17% of that page's $7 million cap, and she described the deal as a three-year standard max that rises if the cap rises (Newsweek, April 17, 2026).

If the updated numbers cannot accommodate Williams and a complete roster, I would keep the draft pick and use a cheaper center. Astier and Han Xu need new contracts. The Oct. 1 sheet lists both as reserved players, meaning they can only re-sign with New York. Marine Johannes is a restricted free agent, so she can sign another team's offer sheet, but New York can match it. I would bring Johannes back within this budget for her shooting, but I would not match an offer that prevents the other pieces from fitting. The sheet also lists 2026 third-rounder Manuela Puoch as unsigned, with a 2027 scale figure of $288,600. This 12 does not include her.

The 12 players I would take into 2027

Assuming the trade, draft, and contract targets work, this is my preferred opening roster. Madison Scott is my provisional choice for the last standard spot. She would need to earn it in camp.

RolePlayers
Starting fiveSabrina Ionescu, Leonie Fiebich, Satou Sabally, Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones
First reservesPauline Astier, Marine Fauthoux, Elizabeth Williams, Oluchi Okananwa
Situational depthMarine Johannes, Han Xu, Madison Scott

Scott is currently listed as a developmental player (a developmental contract, not a standard contract), signed Sept. 2 and available Sept. 16 on that sheet, so this projects a new standard contract. Elizabeth Balogun, signed Aug. 18, is in the same developmental group. Khamil Pierre and Balogun would be developmental-contract targets if eligible and available after roster cuts. I would leave Rebekah Gardner, a restricted free agent on the sheet, and Anneli Maley, who has no 2027 figure there, out of my preferred 12. Raquel Carrera is listed as reserved, and I would give her a chance to compete for a frontcourt place in camp.

The closing five would depend on the opponent. Against heavy ball pressure, I would use Fauthoux or Astier alongside Ionescu and choose the other three by matchup. Protecting a lead against a fast guard, I would consider Okananwa if she has earned the assignment. The five highest-profile players would not automatically finish every game.

The risk: this plan asks young guards to improve while an expensive veteran group remains intact. I would accept that risk for one more run. By midseason, I would want evidence that New York can reach its offense against pressure and survive Jones sitting down. If those problems persist, the next trade discussion would have to be bigger.

These are my proposed moves, not reported negotiations. Contracts, draft positions, and availability reflect information available on October 12. The Nov. 4 coaching note is the exception.

My take: keep the five one more year, but only if the guards fix the giveaways. 45 turnovers in three games is the clearest gap I can fix without breaking up the stars.

Full Court Buckets gathers and verifies its own game data. Audience, contract, and college figures above are credited to the dated sources linked in the story.

item.title: WNBA Finals arrive after 51 games topped 1 million viewers
item.dc:creator: Ryan Moalemi
item.description: Atlanta faces Golden State in the 2026 WNBA Finals after 51 regular-season games topped 1 million viewers. See the numbers, our audience estimate and the TV schedule.
item.content:encoded:
WNBA PlayoffsFull Court Buckets

WNBA Finals arrive after 51 games topped 1 million viewers

By Ryan MoalemiOctober 11, 2026

Fast Facts for Media & Citations

  • 51 regular-season telecasts averaged at least 1 million viewers in 2026, up from 19 in 2025 (WNBA, Oct. 14).
  • ESPN/ABC regular season: 1.37 million over 29 games, up 17%, separate from ESPN's 1.4 million for eight postseason games through the semifinals (ESPN, Oct. 15). The first round averaged 1.3 million (WNBA), up 37% from 944,000 across ESPN/ABC, Prime Video and USA Sports, per Sports Media Watch.
  • October 2026 US search estimates: Atlanta Dream 1.22 million, Angel Reese 1.0 million, Golden State Valkyries 550,000.

The WNBA reported 51 regular-season telecasts averaging at least 1 million viewers in 2026, compared with 19 in 2025.

  • Source: WNBA release, Oct. 14, 2026. This is a count of qualifying telecasts, not total audience growth.
  • The Valkyries lead the series 3-2 after beating the Dream 64-55 in Game 5 on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, at Chase Center (Game 5 recap).
  • Game 6 is Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. PT (12:30 p.m. ET) at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on USA Network, E!, Syfy and Peacock (Game 6 preview). 2026 Finals audience: Game 2 averaged 1.33 million viewers across USA Network, CNBC, E! and streaming on Peacock, which USA Sports calls the most-watched WNBA Finals Game 2 ever on cable. USA Sports says that was up 9% vs. the 2025 WNBA Finals Game 2 on broadcast television, so the comparison is cable plus streaming against a broadcast game (USA Sports release, Oct. 21, 2026). Game 1 averaged 2.1 million on NBC and Peacock (NBC Sports release). Game 4 averaged 1.9 million on NBC and Peacock and peaked at 2.5 million, the most-watched WNBA Finals Game 4 ever, according to NBC Sports (NBC Sports release, Oct. 27, 2026). See all games on the WNBA viewership page.

The WNBA Finals arrive after a regular season with 51 telecasts averaging at least 1 million viewers, up from 19 in 2025 (WNBA release, Oct. 14). That is 32 more qualifying telecasts, and it measures how often the league cleared that threshold, not 51 million different people.

Angel Reese and her Atlanta Dream teammates spent Sunday night in a suite at the Falcons–Ravens Sunday Night Football matchup. A Sports on Prime TikTok post, crediting the Atlanta Falcons, showed the WNBA finalists together. Reese already attracts attention beyond basketball, and appearing with teammates gives people who recognize her another reason to notice the team around her. That appearance cannot tell us how many football fans will watch Game 1, so Saturday, six days later, is the measurable test.

The Dream visit the Golden State Valkyries for Game 1 on Saturday, Oct. 17, at 12:30 p.m. PT on NBC and Peacock. Both teams swept their semifinals. Atlanta is back for the first time since 2013; Golden State has reached the Finals in its second season. One franchise will leave with its first championship.

There is plenty for new viewers to watch on the court. Reese brings her Defensive Player of the Year credentials. Golden State counters with Gabby Williams, who is averaging 22.7 points in the playoffs after helping eliminate the defending champion Aces.

Williams vs. Reese in the 2026 playoffs

Per game, except games played and shooting percentages.

Angel Reese518.08.42.21.643.338.587.1

Reese has played five playoff games and Williams six. That is a small sample. Full Court Buckets gathers and verifies its own data.

The audience is growing beyond Indiana

The most useful numbers come with a clear label. ESPN's regular-season average, a playoff-round average and an individual game's peak audience measure different things. Here is what the reported averages show:

Download CSV

Free to use and republish (CC0).

Sources: ESPN release, Sept. 25, 2026 (rows 1–2); Just Women's Sports, Oct. 8, 2026 (row 3); Front Office Sports, Oct. 7, 2026 (row 4).

Caitlin Clark's drawing power remains substantial. Indiana appeared in all five ESPN-network games that averaged more than 2 million viewers this season. But the 24% increase for games without the Fever is especially relevant to this Finals: those audiences were growing, too. ESPN also reported growth of 27% among viewers ages 18–24 and 29% among those ages 2–17.

The semifinal openers provide a more immediate test. Atlanta–New York averaged 1.17 million viewers on ABC, while Golden State–Las Vegas drew 1.12 million across NBC and Peacock. That NBC figure combines a Nielsen TV audience of 1.01 million with 111,000 streaming viewers measured by Adobe Analytics (Sports Media Watch, Oct. 2026), so the two games were not measured the same way. Both played against the NFL's Sunday schedule. Those results give the finalists a recent audience baseline without borrowing the ratings of a Fever elimination game.

These are the sources' reported comparisons, and broadcasters, distribution and Nielsen's methods all changed this year, so they show growth in measured audiences without isolating where it came from.

Search interest is a different count

Television averages count viewers. Search volume counts queries. Full Court Buckets keyword research estimates US monthly Google searches for October 2026 at 1.22 million for the Atlanta Dream, 1.0 million for Angel Reese, 550,000 for the Golden State Valkyries, and 60,500 each for Gabby Williams and WNBA Finals.

Download CSV

Free to use and republish (CC0).

What audience should the Finals draw

Full Court Buckets' working estimate is a series average of roughly 1.2 million to 1.6 million viewers per game. This is an editorial forecast, not a league or network projection, and it is not a statistical confidence interval.

The range starts near the 1.15 million average for this year's semifinal openers and brackets the 1.5 million four-game 2025 Finals average on ABC and ESPN ESPN reported; that release lists 2025 Game 1 separately at 1.9 million. A 2026 Game 1 figure should be compared with that Game 1, not the series average. Two semifinal games are a thin baseline, so treat the low end as a rough anchor, not a floor. The range allows for a championship bump while accounting for a different matchup and a move away from an all-ABC/ESPN series.

Distribution could matter as much as the names on the jerseys. Games 1 and 4 air on NBC and Peacock. Games 2 and 3 air on USA, CNBC and Peacock. Games 5, 6 and 7 are not listed in the Oct. 13, 2026 WNBA release, so this page does not assign them a network. A long, close series gives casual viewers time to get invested. A sweep removes those later opportunities.

A decisive game approaching or exceeding 2 million viewers would be a strong upside result, rather than the expectation for every night. For context, the deciding game of the 2024 Finals drew 2.15 million. College football, NFL games and baseball's postseason will compete for attention during this series.

Series length also changes the business result. Seven games provide 75% more telecasts than a four-game sweep. That means more opportunities for viewing and advertising even if the average audience stays flat. It does not mean 75% more unique fans.

The finalists are turning attention into repeat customers

Golden State's ticket numbers are unusually strong for a team this new. The Valkyries sold out all 22 regular-season home games, averaging 18,064 fans at Chase Center. They also reported more than 12,000 season-ticket holders and a renewal rate above 90% for 2027 (Valkyries release).

That renewal figure matters. A full arena can reflect opening-year curiosity; customers committing to another season are evidence of a habit taking hold. Golden State has now sold out every regular-season home game in each of its first two years.

Sportico reported on Oct. 7 that the Valkyries brought in $100 million in revenue before the playoffs, making them the first women's sports team to reach that mark, and that a Finals run could push gross revenue past $130 million. That is reported revenue, not profit, but it gives the league a concrete example of what a successful expansion market can support.

Atlanta has its own evidence. In its Oct. 6 arena announcement, the Dream reported more than 400% growth in season-ticket membership over five years and three consecutive seasons of sellouts at Gateway Center Arena. All 25 regular-season home games will move to State Farm Arena in 2027 as the WNBA expands to 50 games per team.

On Oct. 11, USA Today reported that State Farm Arena was booked, with a concert on Oct. 22 and Hawks games on Oct. 24 and Oct. 29, and that Games 3, 4 and 6 would stay at Gateway Center Arena unless that changed. Gateway seats 3,500 for basketball. The Chase Center average of 18,064 minus 3,500 is 14,564 fewer seats per Atlanta game. That is seats, not revenue. The WNBA release of Oct. 13, 2026 moved Game 3 (Wednesday, Oct. 21, 8:00 p.m. ET) and Game 4 (Saturday, Oct. 24, 1:00 p.m. ET) to State Farm Arena. Games 5, 6 and 7 are not in that release. Game 6 is also at State Farm Arena, on Thursday, Oct. 29, at 12:30 p.m. ET.

Game-by-game Finals ratings

This page is the season-long audience story. The game-by-game sheet, using the WNBA release of Oct. 13, 2026, is the 2026 WNBA Finals ratings tracker. Multi-year attendance and viewership stay on the viewership and attendance page.

2026 WNBA Finals schedule

Games 1 through 4 are the games in the WNBA release of Oct. 13, 2026. Golden State has home court in the best-of-seven, 2-2-1-1-1 series. Peacock streams the games that release lists. Games 5, 6 and 7 are if necessary, and that release does not list a date, a tip time, or a network for them.
